# Art of Balance — Full Unity 6.6 Clone: Implementation Plan, SRS & Master Task List

**Prepared:** 2026-09-24 · **Engine target:** Unity 6.6 (6000.6.0f1 / 6000.6.2f1, the final Unity 6-family Tech Stream release; Unity 6.7 is the next LTS)
**Product:** a faithful, shippable multiplatform clone of *Art of Balance* (Shin'en Multimedia, 2010–2018) — physics stack-balancing puzzle game, 8 worlds × 25 levels, five game modes
**Platform order:** Windows + macOS (Steam) → Android → iOS → Xbox (gated on ID@Xbox); Wii U / PS4 / Switch studied as historical deep-dives (§11–§13)
**Prepared for:** a single full-stack multiplatform developer + DevSecOps engineer working with AI-assisted automation (Unity CLI, Unity+Blender CLI pipelines, Unity+Blender MCP servers)

---

## 0. Executive summary

This document is the complete build package for the clone: game-design specification, software requirements (SRS-style, testable acceptance criteria), technical architecture, per-platform master references, automation strategy, phased roadmap, and a tracker-ready master task list.

**Scale:** 22 sections, 150140 words, 447 original-design markers, 177 open TODO-VERIFY flags — every number, price, API name, and date in it is either **[DOCUMENTED]** against one of 253 unique sources (§22.1) or explicitly flagged **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (we designed it because the original's internals are undocumented) or `TODO-VERIFY` (177 open confirmations, each naming exactly what to check). An adversarial verification pass corrected 28 initially-wrong research claims before authoring began; those corrections are marked **[VERIFIED-REFUTED]** where they matter.

**What the research fixed that folklore gets wrong:** Unity 6.6 is the *last* Unity 6 Tech Stream release (6.7 = LTS) — the upgrade-path risk is priced into the roadmap (§10, §21); the new official `unity` CLI exists (1.0.0-beta.11, §15) and *complements* rather than replaces editor batch mode (§16); Unity 6.6 ships first-party MCP support (§17); Google Play's API 36 floor and Apple's Xcode 26+ / iOS 15 / Metal-only rules set the mobile compliance baseline (§18); Input System is a built-in module from 6.6, and Active Input Handling = **Both** is the correct transitional setting (§4.8, §7).

**How to use it:** plan from §10 (phases, exit criteria, durations); import §20 into your tracker (CSV layout in §20.9) and work top-down by dependency; build the automation skeleton of §15–§17 first — it multiplies everything after; treat §18–§19 as per-platform submission checklists; §21 is the standing risk register.

### 1.2 Developer and publisher record

**[DOCUMENTED]** All five releases in the series were developed **and** published by **Shin'en Multimedia GmbH**, Munich. The company imprint on the official microsites lists Hofmannstr. 7, 81379 München, commercial register HRB 160695, managing names Linzner/Wodok ([T01 imprint, sources 1–11]). Every SKU's press sheet and microsite names Shin'en alone; the Shin'en games page (T01-11, live 2026-09-24) lists the full catalog with no co-publisher on any Art of Balance entry.

**Correction of a circulating misattribution:** no fetched source — primary, secondary, or tertiary — attributes any Art of Balance release to QubicGames. Any text naming QubicGames as the developer/publisher of Art of Balance is a misattribution contradicted by the complete primary record above. The plan adopts Shin'en Multimedia GmbH as the sole credited developer/publisher everywhere (store pages, in-game credits screen in §9). <!-- TODO-VERIFY: origin of the QubicGames misattribution (possibly confusion with a different Shin'en-adjacent eShop title or a store-data aggregator error); harmless to the clone, but do not propagate it into our store metadata. -->

### 1.4 Mode inventory and where each mode appeared

**The five official modes** (verbatim from the live Switch press sheet [T01-9]; PS4 sheet matches [T01-10]; all **[DOCUMENTED]**, high):

| Mode | Documented behavior | First appearance | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| Arcade | Rotate and place all shapes; solo or co-op drop-in; "Watch out: Don't let any shape fall into the water!" | WiiWare 2010 | T01-6, 9, 10 |
| Endurance | "Play a never ending string of puzzles to go for the best scores" (Switch); "Survive all levels in one session and climb the online leaderboards" (PS4); "Play random levels in succession" (3DS About); exactly **3 lives/retries for the whole session** (triple-sourced); score = speed + remaining lives + puzzle difficulty | TOUCH! 3DS 2012 (offline-only leaderboards there, T01-21) | T01-4, 9, 10, 17, 18, 21 |
| Infinity | "The blocks don't stop. Build the highest possible stack." — endless stacking for **height**, not puzzle solving | PS4 2016 (not named on Wii U official pages; not on 3DS, which lists only Arcade/Endurance/challenges) | T01-4, 9, 10 |
| Swift Stacker | Split-screen head-to-head race to solve the same puzzle, teams of two; "locally, online or even a combination of the two" (Wii U); direct evolution of the WiiWare 2-player Versus mode ("The Wii's multiplayer mode, now known as Swift Stacker") | Wii U 2014 (as the named successor of WiiWare Versus, best-of 5/7/9 rounds, T01-16) | T01-9, 17, 18 |
| Tower Tumble | Turn-based: players alternate placing blocks; whoever topples the tower loses the round and everyone else scores a point; pieces per round are **randomly generated**; "reverse Jenga"; up to 4 players; local-multiplayer-only on Wii U | Wii U 2014 | T01-9, 10, 17, 18 |

Wii U therefore introduced two named modes (Swift Stacker, Tower Tumble) plus Special Challenges; the PS4/Switch sheets codified the five-mode lineup including Infinity. The WiiWare original shipped only Arcade + drop-in co-op + the Versus precursor. Within Arcade, official copy documents three extra-point challenge types — **Time Challenges, Height Challenges, Balance Challenges** ("for extra points"; reviews: "use all pieces in a set time, build a tower as high as possible", "some levels will also set a time or height limit") [T01-2, 4, 6, 16, 19].

Progression model **[DOCUMENTED]** (medium-high, single but detailed source): world map with free level order within a world, individual levels skippable, next world unlocks after enough successes (Der Spiegel, T01-22). Award system: **13 awards on 3DS**, e.g. "Complete 50/100 levels", "finish a later puzzle in under 30 seconds" [T01-2, 4, 21]. Endurance leaderboard math beyond its three ingredients is not documented (§1.8).

### 1.5 Block-type inventory

**[DOCUMENTED]** Base shapes: Wii = **14 shapes + 2 special** (official 2009 About: "There are 14 Shapes + 2 Special Shapes... that break once you put too much load on top, or a timer runs out", T01-2); 3DS and later = **16 shapes + 5 special** (official About, T01-4). Shape families include rectangles, triangles, circles [T01-20]. The arena is 2D single-plane physics over a water basin ("stand... over a pond of water", "small islands in a water basin"), and **some base platforms float and sway** on the water (3DS+ reviews: "floating foundation that sways on water") [T01-16, 21, 22].

| Block type | Documented behavior | Confidence / sources |
|---|---|---|
| Base blocks | Ordinary stacking shapes; nothing special | High — T01-2, 4 |
| Breakable (load) | "Break[s] once you put too much load on top"; Wii U review detail: holds "no more than three other regulars before smashing" | High for existence (T01-2, 4); the "max 3 regulars" figure is one review (T01-19) — treat 3 as observed Wii U tuning, not a universal constant |
| Timed / disappearing | "Timer shape — breaks when its timer runs out"; countdown starts **when a new piece is placed atop it**; at zero it breaks/vanishes, dropping everything above | High — T01-2, 4, 19 |
| Fire | "Explodes on contact with another fire shape"; "flaming shapes explode when two touch" | High — T01-4, 19; NWR paraphrase "shatter or disappear at contact with a similar type of block" (T01-18) |
| Gravity-inverter | "The gravity shape inverts gravity"; platforms exist at top **and** bottom of screen and the stack flips (plan building top-down); on Wii U, turning the GamePad helps | High — T01-4, 19 |
| Fifth special (2012+) | Official copy names a 5th special but the only archived sentence truncates after the 4th; identity **unconfirmed** | Gap — T01-4; see §1.8 |
| Linked / seesaw pair | **Not documented for the original.** Implemented in this clone as a fifth special behaviour per the chief-architect decision — a pair of blocks coupled so that load/tilt on one tilts the other, constraining balance puzzles | **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** — detailed spec in §8 |
| Moving / swaying platform bases | Floating foundations that sway on the water; documented on 3DS+ | High — T01-21, 22 |

Per the binding decisions: the clone implements the four documented specials plus the linked/seesaw behaviour flagged **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** alongside them; the real 5th special's identity remains an open verification target (§21), and if research later confirms it, §5's `BlockBehaviourType` enum has a reserved slot for it.

| Constant | Value | Confidence | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| Win condition | Place **all** given pieces, then the structure must stand; countdown UI = three sequential green lights | High (exact wording, multiply documented) | T01-16: "Once you place the last block in place, the structure must stay above water for three seconds, indicated by three lights at the bottom of the screen"; T01-19, 22 |
| Stability window | **3 seconds** (Wii original); post-Wii editions "significantly shorter" — exact value undocumented | High for 3 s; medium-high for "shorter" (single review, the same source Wikipedia cites) | T01-16, 17, 19, 22 <!-- TODO-VERIFY: exact post-Wii countdown duration; propose measuring from captured gameplay of the Switch demo --> |
| Fail condition / water penalty | **Any** piece touching water at any time (before or during countdown) fails the attempt and the level restarts; pieces are NOT individually removed — the attempt fails wholesale | High | T01-6/9/10 ("Watch out: Don't let any shape fall into the water!"), 21, 22 |
| Rotation increment | **45°** free rotation | **Medium — tertiary only** (Wikipedia gameplay section, T01-15); no primary source fetched states the increment. Shape-set descriptions support arbitrary-angle shapes (rectangles/triangles/circles, T01-20) | <!-- TODO-VERIFY: confirm 45° (vs 90°) increments from gameplay footage; §3 designs piece-defined legal orientations either way --> |
| Piece queue | Fixed set of shapes per level presented in a tray/queue; 3DS shows the selection on the lower screen and stacking on the upper screen | Medium-high (3DS-specific UI documented; other versions show a queue at screen edge per review descriptions) | T01-15, 17, 22 |
| Play plane | 2D physics, single plane, over a water basin; some bases float/sway | High | T01-16, 21, 22 |
| Endurance lives | Exactly **3** per session | High (triple-sourced) | T01-17, 18, 21 |
| Endurance score inputs | Speed + remaining lives + puzzle difficulty → online leaderboard | High (single-but-contemporary review, corroborated by official leaderboard marketing) | T01-17 |

Presentation constants feeding §9: "relaxing lounge soundtrack", "8 beautiful environments", "each with its own unique lounge style" (official wording, T01-8/9/10/11); reviewer texture: "booming bass beats and quirky sound effects" (Wii, T01-16), "jazzy, relaxing" (Wii U, T01-17), "catchy upbeat tunes that calm the mind" (3DS, T01-21); HD versions: realistic water, window light casting real-time shadows of dragged pieces, wooden clunk placement SFX (T01-17). Composer is unnamed in every fetched source (Shin'en composes in-house; no fetched page credits an individual — do not name one in the plan).

### 1.7 Unity 6.6 (6000.6) engine status and support horizon

**[DOCUMENTED]** Unity 6.6 (6000.6) shipped as **6000.6.0f1 on 2026-08-31** ([release notes](https://unity.com/releases/editor/whats-new/6000.6.0f1), accessed 2026-09-24) and was announced 2026-09-01 on Unity Discussions ([staff post](https://discussions.unity.com/t/unity-6-6-is-now-available/1735357)); the latest patch observed this run is 6000.6.2f1, 2026-09-18. Terminology correction the plan adopts everywhere: **the "Tech Stream" label is retired.** Unity's current release model is yearly LTS releases (2-year support, +1 year Enterprise/Industry) plus multiple **"Supported/Update" releases per year with weekly patches and the same QA as LTS** ([Unity 6 support page](https://unity.com/releases/unity-6/support), accessed 2026-09-24). 6.6 is a Supported/Update release — and specifically the **final Supported release of the Unity 6 family**, after which 6.7 becomes the next LTS (6.7 Beta already live as of 2026-09-24).

**[VERIFIED-REFUTED]** The sweep flagged "6.6 = last Unity 6-family release, 6.7 = next LTS" as resting on a single forum sentence; the adversarial pass refuted the single-source framing while confirming the conclusion: the 6000.6.0f1 release notes ("...no longer be available after Unity 6.7 LTS") and the official CoreCLR roadmap (repeated "Unity 6.7LTS Alpha" naming with links to official alpha pages) independently use the "Unity 6.7 LTS" name. Only the exact "final supported release of the Unity 6 family" sentence is unique to the 2026-09-01 announcement.

Support-horizon anchors: Unity 6.0 LTS GA = **2024-10-17** ([staff announcement](https://discussions.unity.com/t/unity-6-is-now-available/1538165); the aggregator date "Apr 29 2024" is wrong — traced to 2023.2's end-of-support being reused as 6.0's release date), support ends **October 2026**; Unity 6.3 LTS initial release **2025-12-04** ([staff announcement](https://discussions.unity.com/t/unity-6-3-lts-is-now-available/1697328)), supported **until December 2027**. Unity staff guidance on the 6.6 thread: **6.3 LTS for projects in production or about to ship; 6.6 for new projects** — this plan starts a new project, so 6.6 it is, with a deliberate migration checkpoint to 6.7 LTS once it graduates from beta (risk-tracked in §21; the migration task is scheduled in §10/§20 rather than left implicit). <!-- TODO-VERIFY: Unity does not state 6.6's own end-of-support date on any fetched page; pin the 6.6 patch-cadence end date when Unity publishes the 6.7 LTS support page. -->

Forward horizon that constrains our codebase: **Unity 6.8 will remove Mono and ship a .NET 10 toolchain + BCL as the only Target Framework** ([Path to CoreCLR, 2026](https://discussions.unity.com/t/path-to-coreclr-2026-upgrade-guide/1714279) — "Unity 6.8 will no longer have Mono as an available option"). The schedule is hedged in-source ("living document") and Unity has real slippage precedent (changes "originally announced for Unity 6.6, but was delayed to Unity 6.7" — [staff post](https://discussions.unity.com/t/planned-breaking-changes-in-unity-6-7/1723293)). Practical consequence for this project: write C# that survives the CoreCLR/.NET 10 transition (no Mono-only assumptions, anticipate domain-reload-off defaults, treat the 6.8 TFM switch as a planned migration rather than a surprise). Physics-relevant 6.6 specifics that motivated engine choice live in §6 (2D Buoyancy/Wind/PhysicsSpace APIs; no 3D substepping), and the full toolchain/CLI picture in §15–§16.

### 1.8 What is not documented anywhere — and who consumes each gap

Everything below was actively searched for and not found in any fetched source. Each gap becomes either an **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** obligation in a owning section or an open question in §21. This list is the contract between research and design: no downstream section may quietly assume a fact that appears here.

It must not appear in this plan as fact | §6 (physics decision stands on its own analysis); §11 may only discuss it as an unverified claim; §21 keeps the retry open |

Downstream authors treat this table as exhaustive: if a fact is not in §1.1–§1.7 and not marked here, it does not exist yet and needs either a source run or an **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** decision with rationale.

## 2. Clone Design Pillars

This section is the normative layer of the plan: the six pillars every downstream section is reviewed against, the scope fences separating cloned / adapted / invented material, the platform priority order, the v1 non-goals, and the release-gating success criteria. Externally verified facts carry **[DOCUMENTED]** markers with inline sources from the research notes (§1, track T01) accessed 2026-09-24; everything the original never documented is our own design and is marked **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**. The chief-architect decisions bind this section and are not relitigated: v1 ships Windows + macOS via Steam, then Android, then iOS, then Xbox last (gated on ID@Xbox access); Switch, PS4 and Wii U appear only as historical study sections (§11–§13).

### 2.1 Product statement and quality anchor

The deliverable is a full re-implementation, not an emulation: a calm, 2D-physics, single-plane stacking puzzle game in which the player places every shape from a level's queue onto a base over a water basin, rotating pieces in fixed increments, until the last piece lands and the structure must survive a short on-screen stability countdown; any piece touching the water at any time fails the attempt **[DOCUMENTED]** ([Shin'en Wii U About](https://web.archive.org/web/20160903223835/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com:80/wiiu/about.php), accessed 2026-09-24). Presentation target is the franchise's documented identity: a "relaxing lounge soundtrack", eight visually distinct world environments, calm realistic water and soft shadows **[DOCUMENTED]** ([Shin'en press sheet, Switch](http://shinen.com/press/sheet.php?p=art_of_balance(Switch)), live 2026-09-24; [Nintendo Life Wii U review](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), 2014).

The quality anchor is the original's reception — Metacritic 88 (Wii) and 82 (Wii U, 3DS), Eurogamer's 2010 "nothing short of essential" **[DOCUMENTED]** ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_of_Balance), accessed 2026-09-24) — operationalized in §2.6 as: indistinguishable rules, modern execution. Production assumption throughout the plan: one developer plus automation/AI tooling (pillar P6); all estimates in §10/§20 use that team shape.

### 2.2 The six pillars

| # | Pillar | Statement (testable form) | Enforced primarily by |
|---|--------|---------------------------|----------------------|
| P1 | Rule-and-feel fidelity | Every documented rule constant compiles to a constant (§2.6.4); feel parameters are tuned against the review record, never guessed silently. | §3, §6, §8, §9 |
| P2 | Data-driven content | All levels/pieces/worlds/modes exist as ScriptableObject assets; no gameplay-affecting number lives in code without provenance. | §5 |
| P3 | Every-input-device parity | Every gameplay verb is performable and discoverable on every shipped device class, through one abstraction (`IPieceInputProvider`). | §7 |
| P4 | Ship-wide multiplatform | One codebase produces five SKUs; platform code is quarantined; no gameplay forks per platform. | §4, §14, §18, §19 |
| P5 | Determinism-friendly simulation | Gameplay state advances only in a fixed simulation step; identical inputs on one device reproduce identical outcomes, enabling ghosts and replay tests. | §6, §14 |
| P6 | Automation-first small-team pipeline | Bootstrap, build, test, content generation and asset authoring are automatable end-to-end; adding world 9 requires zero code changes. | §10, §15, §16, §17, §20 |

#### 2.2.1 P1 — rule-and-feel fidelity

The rule layer is cloned exactly where documented (fence table §2.3.1); the feel layer is tuned to the recorded descriptions of the original, because the original's internal tuning was never published. The three most load-bearing feel signatures, all multiply documented: the win window ("the structure must stay above water for three seconds, indicated by three lights at the bottom of the screen" — [Nintendo Life WiiWare review](https://web.archive.org/web/20210420192755/https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/2010/02/art_of_balance), 2010-02-18; [Cubed3 Wii U review](http://www.cubed3.com/review/1648/1/art-of-balance-wii-u.html), 2014; [Der Spiegel](https://www.spiegel.de/netzwelt/games/3ds-spiel-art-of-balance-touch-im-test-a-843861.html), 2012, all accessed 2026-09-24); the water-fail tension ([official] "Watch out: Don't let any shape fall into the water!"); and the tactile stack feedback — "wooden clunk" placement sound, realistic water and window light casting real-time shadows of dragged pieces ([Nintendo Life Wii U review](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24). One documented drift inside the franchise itself: post-Wii editions shortened the countdown "significantly" ([Nintendo Life Wii U review](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance)); we treat its exact value as an adaptation (§2.3.2). Fidelity discipline: documented constants are frozen in `AoBDesignConstants` (§2.6.4) and change only if §1's evidence changes; undocumented feel values are explicitly flagged tunables with recorded before/after playtest results. The historical editions (§11–§13) serve as the reference corpus for feel disputes.

#### 2.2.2 P2 — data-driven content

The franchise's content shape — 200 campaign levels across 8 worlds, 16 shapes + 5 specials, five modes **[DOCUMENTED]** ([Shin'en 3DS About](https://web.archive.org/web/20151029143537/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com/3ds/about.php), accessed 2026-09-24; [press sheet](http://shinen.com/press/sheet.php?p=art_of_balance(Switch))) — is cloned structurally, but every individual level layout is new **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** because no original level data was ever published. A one-developer team can only author that volume if content is data: `PieceDefinition`, `LevelDefinition`, `WorldDefinition`, `GameModeDefinition` assets (full schemas in §5) with editor-time validation (queue mass budget vs platform stability heuristic, §5.6) and Addressables groups per world. Consequences of the pillar: level logic never lives in code; designers (or the bulk-generation tooling of §17) can retune difficulty without recompiling; and the automation surface of P6 operates on assets, not scenes. Scalability criterion (from §10): producing worlds 2–8 after the world-1 template must require no engineering support.

#### 2.2.3 P3 — every-input-device parity

The original shipped on five control grammars across its editions: Wii Remote IR pointer (A = pick up/drop, B or D-pad left/right = rotate) **[DOCUMENTED]** ([First Look promo transcript](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mGkeVblM1Es), accessed 2026-09-24); 3DS stylus drag or Circle Pad + face buttons for pick-up/rotate/drop **[DOCUMENTED]** ([Der Spiegel](https://www.spiegel.de/netzwelt/games/3ds-spiel-art-of-balance-touch-im-test-a-843861.html), accessed 2026-09-24); Wii U tri-scheme — touch, Wii Remotes, GamePad sticks **[DOCUMENTED]** ([Wii U About](https://web.archive.org/web/20160903223835/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com:80/wiiu/about.php)); DualShock 4 on PS4 **[DOCUMENTED]** ([PS4 press sheet](http://shinen.com/press/sheet.php?p=art_of_balance(PS4))); and Switch touch / Joy-Con / grip / Pro Controller with motion controls added post-launch by Patch 1.1 (2018-11-13) **[DOCUMENTED]** ([Switch microsite news](https://web.archive.org/web/20201015074209/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com/switch/), accessed 2026-09-24). The pillar: our clone preserves the input *grammar* (move carried piece, rotate one step, drop, pause) identically on every device, delivered through a single `IPieceInputProvider` abstraction (§7) that is the only path by which input reaches gameplay. Parity is testable: an automated suite drives each provider through the full loop (§14 test matrix), and button-glyph prompts swap per device (§7.6). The Switch Patch 1.1 case is the design proof: a post-launch control scheme must be expressible as config + one new provider class, not an input-code refactor (§7.9).

#### 2.2.4 P4 — ship-wide multiplatform from one codebase

Five SKUs — Windows, macOS (Steam, wave 1), Android (wave 2), iOS (wave 3), Xbox family (wave 4, gated) — from one Unity 6.6 project. Discipline: platform-specific code confined to a `Platform` assembly and `#if` directive table (§4, §19); rendering quality tiers per platform assigned to one URP asset matrix (§9); safe-area and resolution-variant UI from day one, not retrofitted (§9.6.3); per-platform performance budgets fixed *before* each port begins (§2.6.3, §14). The reverse constraint also holds: no platform feature may bend gameplay rules — e.g., mobile gets identical physics stepping and the identical stability window as PC, only lower render targets. Platform order rationale in §2.4; execution details in §18 (iOS/Android) and §19 (PC/macOS/Steam/Xbox).

#### 2.2.5 P5 — determinism-friendly simulation

The simulation must be reproducible on a given device from a recorded input stream: this enables ghost replays **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**, automated regression tests that hash gameplay outcomes (§14), and leaderboards that can be sanity-checked. Physics engine selection (2D Box2D vs 3D PhysX, substepping to an effective ≥240 Hz, full trade analysis) is decided in §6; this pillar states the constraints that decision must satisfy: fixed-timestep discipline with no gameplay state advancing outside the fixed step; identical actor creation order; `Physics.Simulate` called only with fixed deltas. Boundary condition from research: Unity's built-in engines are deterministic on the same device given the same inputs, but explicitly not 100% deterministic across devices (Unity staff guidance; full citation in §6), and upstream Box2D v3 — the direction Unity's 2D line is heading — is designed for cross-thread-count and 64-bit-platform determinism (per §6 research). Design consequence, accepted here and priced in §2.5: cross-device lockstep online play is excluded by construction; ghosts replay faithfully on the recording device class and are labeled best-effort elsewhere **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**.

#### 2.2.6 P6 — automation-first small-team pipeline

One developer cannot ship a five-SKU 200-level game with hand-held tooling. The pillar mandates automation at every layer, consuming the research of §15–§17: project bootstrap, version pinning, build and test invocation via the official Unity CLI (experimental; auto-installed with Unity Hub 3.21.0+ per the verify pass, §15); reproducible CI builds and headless Blender asset generation via traditional batch CLI (§16); and interactive authoring acceleration via Unity MCP (bulk `ScriptableObject` content generation, scene QA screenshots) and Blender MCP (block-variant modeling loops) (§17). P6 is coupled to P2 by construction — automation operates on data, and data is the content. Measurable framing (§10): the content-production rate for worlds 2–8 must be limited by design judgment, not by mechanical authoring effort; if mechanical effort dominates, the tooling backlog wins the sprint.

### 2.4 Target platforms and priorities

| Wave | Platform (SKU) | Channel | Why this position | Binding external constraints (accessed 2026-09-24) |
|------|----------------|---------|-------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| W1 — v1.0 GA | Windows 10+ x64 | Steam | Primary dev host; controller-first puzzle audience overlapping Steam Deck; lightest submission regime of all five channels; Steam backend (achievements/leaderboards/cloud) is asynchronous and requires no gameplay netcode | $100 Steam Direct fee per app, recouped after $1,000 adjusted gross revenue ([Valve partner docs](https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/gettingstarted/appfee)); Deck Verified four criteria (full checklist §19.4.10): Input — full controller support + correct glyphs + on-screen keyboard auto-appears; Display — 1280×800 or 1280×720 default resolution with good defaults and legible text; Seamlessness — no compatibility warnings, any launcher controller-navigable (we ship none); System — game + all middleware Proton-compatible ([Steam Deck Verified](https://steamdeck.com/en/verified)) |
| W1 — v1.0 GA | macOS 12+ (Universal, Apple-Silicon-first) | Steam (same app) | Marginal cost on the same Steam app; meaningful lounge-genre Mac share; forces the CI mac-runner investment early (§16) | IL2CPP macOS players must be built from a macOS editor ([Unity 6.3 IL2CPP intro](https://docs.unity3d.com/6000.3/Documentation/Manual/il2cpp-introduction.html)); Intel x64 player architecture is deprecated in the 6.7 line — ship Universal, never Intel-only ([Unity 6.7 Beta macOS requirements](https://docs.unity3d.com/6000.7/Documentation/Manual/macos-requirements-and-compatibility.html)) |
| W2 — v1.x | Android (ARM64, IL2CPP) | Google Play | Touch is a documented AoB-native control scheme and the touch provider already exists for P3 parity; largest casual audience; cert is policy-compliance rather than technical review | New apps and updates must target Android 16 / API 36 from 2026-08-31 ([Google Play target API policy](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/11926878)); Unity 6.6 embeds the matched toolchain (NDK r27c, JDK 17, SDK build-tools 36.0.0 — verified, §18) |
| W3 — v1.x | iOS/iPadOS 15+ | App Store | Touch parity plus premium puzzle audience; sequenced after Android so the touch UI is already field-hardened | Uploads require Xcode 26+ / iOS 26 SDK since 2026-04-28 ([Apple upcoming requirements](https://developer.apple.com/news/upcoming-requirements/)); Apple rejects OpenGL ES and Unity defaults to Metal — Metal-only in practice; Unity 6.6 supports iOS 15+ ([Unity iOS requirements](https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/ios-requirements-and-compatibility.html)); requires a macOS build host |
| W4 — gated | Xbox family | Microsoft Store (Game Pass path evaluated) | Controller-first living room fit and Game Pass suitability — but last, because access is not under our control | ID@Xbox hard requirements: 18+, signed NDA, residence in a supported Microsoft market; Unity is a listed supported engine (ID@Xbox FAQ, xbox.com/Developers/id); GDK has a public GitHub subset while console docs/hardware are NDA-gated (§19 separates public from NDA-required knowledge) |

Ordering logic in three sentences. Steam first because it validates the product (PC is where a one-dev team can iterate fastest against players) at the lowest certification cost, and everything built for it — input abstraction, glyphs, cloud hooks — is reused downstream. Mobile second and third because touch is already a first-class pillar (P3) and store compliance is document-driven rather than dev-kit-driven; Android precedes iOS only because no extra hardware/toolchain gates exist (iOS needs the macOS build host and Apple signing pipeline, §18). Xbox last because ID@Xbox onboarding timing is external to the project (§21 risk R-cert); the platform module work is sized so it can start the moment access is granted.

Explicitly out of v1 target set: Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4/5, and Wii U SKUs — studied historically in §11–§13 only. No PS Vita target exists anywhere in the franchise **[DOCUMENTED]** (negative established from Shin'en's complete catalog, §1), and none is planned.

### 2.5 Non-goals (v1)

| # | Non-goal | Decision and rationale | Revisit trigger |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------------|
| N1 | Online real-time multiplayer (online Swift Stacker, any session play) | OUT of v1. The original had it — Wii U online up to 5 players **[DOCUMENTED]** ([NWR Wii U](http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/review/38619/art-of-balance-wii-u-review)), Switch online for 2 **[DOCUMENTED]** ([Nintendo.com](https://www.nintendo.com/store/products/art-of-balance-switch/)) — but real-time netcode plus cross-device physics determinism (P5 boundary) plus per-platform cert is the single largest risk multiplier for a one-dev team (§21). Local split-screen Swift Stacker and 4-player hotseat Tower Tumble ship instead (C9/C13). | Post-v1, via asynchronous input-stream replay exchange (deterministic per P5) before any lockstep attempt |
| N2 | Cross-platform online play / player accounts | OUT of v1 (follows from N1); no first-party backend, no cross-play infrastructure | With N1 |
| N3 | Steam online leaderboards/achievements/cloud saves | NOT a non-goal — IN v1.0: platform-backend, asynchronous, no gameplay netcode (Steamworks integration choice in §19). The 3DS edition's offline-only leaderboards **[DOCUMENTED]** ([Cubed3 3DS](http://www.cubed3.com/games/reviews/nintendo-3ds/art-of-balance-touch)) are the documented precedent should integration slip: local leaderboards ship everywhere as the floor | — |
| N4 | Mobile platform leaderboards (Play Games / Game Center) | OUT of v1.0; local leaderboards only on mobile (N3 precedent), platform SDK leaderboards added per-platform in v1.x to keep the mobile scope on input/thermal/polish | After Android/iOS launch stabilizes |
| N5 | Player-facing level editor | OUT of v1; the level tooling of §5 is editor-internal | Post-launch community demand |
| N6 | Free-to-play, IAP, ads | OUT; premium one-time purchase (A8) | Never relitigated in v1 horizon |
| N7 | WebGL, VR/AR, streaming targets | OUT; not part of the five-SKU pledge (P4) | — |
| N8 | Switch / PlayStation SKUs in v1 | OUT; historical study only (§11–§13), with Switch-specific learnings (motion patch, dock/handheld tiers) folded into §7/§9 | Separate evaluation after Xbox wave |

### 2.6 Success criteria

Three gates — feel, stability/correctness, performance — plus the compiled constants contract that pins them. Each gate is measurable and wired into §14's testing protocol and §10's phase exit criteria; none is aspirational language.

#### 2.6.1 Feel gate ("blind swap test")

A player familiar with the original cannot identify the clone from its rules within the first five minutes of play; only the art assets may differ. Operationalized:

- Rule-parity checklist: every row of §2.3.1 verified by an automated or scripted test (water-contact fail, window timing, three-light sequencing, queue exhaustion, 45° rotation snapping, special-block triggers) — checked per release build (§14).
- Latency budgets **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**: pointer/cursor follows the input device within 1 rendered frame (≤ 16.7 ms at 60 Hz); rotate command acknowledged within 1 frame; pick-up/drop within 2 frames. Input is buffered in `Update` and consumed in the fixed step per skill guidance (§7.8).
- Settle behavior **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**: after release, a piece reaches the stability predicate in < 0.7 s median and < 1.5 s at p95 across the level corpus; settling is detected by velocity-threshold predicate with hysteresis, never by sleep state alone (buoyant/swaying bases can defeat sleep — §6).
- Tactile signatures: wooden clunk on placement contact, splash + fail sting on water contact, per-world lounge loop with adaptive tension layer as stacks wobble (§9) — each bound to its physics event, reviewed per world.

#### 2.6.2 Stability and correctness gate

- Determinism replay: a scripted 10-minute session replayed 100× on the same device and build yields 100/100 identical outcome hashes; run nightly on three reference devices (Windows, Android, iOS once in wave) **[ORIGINAL DESIGN criterion]**.
- Window correctness under load: with the frame rate clamped to 30 and 20 fps, the stability window still elapses in exactly its configured simulation seconds (1.5 s default, 3.0 s classic, per A1) — window timing driven by simulation time, never render frames (§6).
- Soak: 8-hour Endurance run — zero exceptions, zero NaN/teleporting bodies, heap growth < 16 MB after the first hour (steady-state zero-allocation loop per skill rules).
- Save round-trip: progress/settings/per-level stats serialize, deserialize and migrate across versions; cloud-conflict resolution deterministic (§6.9, §14).

#### 2.6.3 Performance budgets (release gates per wave)

60 FPS is the floor on every platform (the Wii original ran 60 fps **[DOCUMENTED]**, [Wii About](https://web.archive.org/web/20091116220135/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com:80/about.php), accessed 2026-09-24); budgets in ms of the 16.67 ms frame **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** — full protocol and profiling markers in §14:

| Budget | PC / Deck class | Android mid-tier | iPhone mid-tier |
|--------|-----------------|------------------|-----------------|
| CPU total (game + sim + UI) | ≤ 12.0 | ≤ 12.0 | ≤ 12.0 |
| — of which simulation (physics + behaviours + stability) | ≤ 3.0 | ≤ 3.0 | ≤ 3.0 |
| GPU at native target | ≤ 13.0 @ 1080p | ≤ 13.0 (render scale 0.75 fallback) | ≤ 13.0 |
| Resident memory | ≤ 1.5 GB | ≤ 800 MB | ≤ 700 MB |
| Cold boot → main menu | ≤ 10 s (HDD) | ≤ 10 s | ≤ 10 s |
| Level load (Addressables) | ≤ 1.5 s | ≤ 2.0 s | ≤ 2.0 s |

Headroom math: 16.67 − 12.0 = 4.67 ms ≈ 28% spike margin per frame absorbs GC pauses, OS jitter and physics worst cases without dropping frames. Download-size target ≤ 300 MB total — same footprint class as the original's 200 MB Switch SKU **[DOCUMENTED]** ([press sheet](http://shinen.com/press/sheet.php?p=art_of_balance(Switch))) — which also keeps the Android base module far under Google's 500 MB compressed cap (§18). Mobile thermal: sustained 60 fps across a 30-minute soak on reference devices, else a locked-30 duty-cycle profile using Unity 6.6's thermal FPS governor (§18).

#### 2.6.4 Encoding the contract

P1 is enforced in code: documented constants compile into one audited class consumed by `LevelManager`, `StabilityMonitor` and `ScoreController` (§6); undocumented tunables live apart, visibly labeled. Change control: a `[DOCUMENTED]`-provenance constant may change only when §1's evidence changes; an `[ORIGINAL DESIGN]` tunable changes only with a recorded before/after playtest note. One deliberate exclusion from the documented set: the load-break capacity is not a documented constant — it is the §5.3/§8.3 tunable `maxSupportedMassRmu` (default 3.0 rmu, range 1.0–10.0, all values **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**), tuned to the single-review "3 regulars" observation (§1.5/T01-19, Cubed3 Wii U).

```csharp
using UnityEngine;

/// <summary>
/// Compiled contract of the Art of Balance feel constants (see §2.2.1, §2.6.4).
/// Documented values trace to the franchise research notes (§1) and are
/// change-controlled; tuned values are ORIGINAL DESIGN defaults pending playtest.
/// </summary>
public static class AoBDesignConstants
{
    #region Documented Constants (change-controlled)

    /// <summary>Classic stability window after the final piece: three full seconds,
    /// three sequential green lights. WiiWare-documented.</summary>
    public const float StabilityWindowClassicSeconds = 3f;

    /// <summary>Rotation step for carried pieces: 45-degree increments.
    /// Tertiary-only source; medium confidence (see §1).</summary>
    public const float RotationStepDegrees = 45f;

    /// <summary>Endurance mode lives per session. Triple-sourced.</summary>
    public const int EnduranceLives = 3;

    /// <summary>Tower Tumble maximum players (hotseat, single system).</summary>
    public const int TowerTumbleMaxPlayers = 4;

    #endregion

    #region Tuned Constants (ORIGINAL DESIGN defaults)

    /// <summary>Default stability window for the modern feel. Post-Wii editions
    /// shortened the countdown by an undocumented amount (§2.3.2/A1).</summary>
    public const float StabilityWindowDefaultSeconds = 1.5f;

    /// <summary>Interval per stability light: window divided across three lights.</summary>
    public const int StabilityLightCount = 3;

    /// <summary>Maximum time in seconds a released piece may take to satisfy the
    /// settle predicate at the 95th percentile (feel gate, §2.6.1).</summary>
    public const float SettleTimeP95BudgetSeconds = 1.5f;

    #endregion

    #region Public API

    /// <summary>
    /// Returns the stability window duration for the given mode configuration.
    /// </summary>
    /// <param name="useClassicWindow">If true, uses the documented Wii-era window.</param>
    /// <returns>Window duration in simulation seconds.</returns>
    public static float GetStabilityWindowSeconds(bool useClassicWindow)
    {
        return useClassicWindow ? StabilityWindowClassicSeconds : StabilityWindowDefaultSeconds;
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// Returns the per-light interval for the three-light stability indicator.
    /// </summary>
    /// <param name="windowSeconds">Total window duration in simulation seconds.</param>
    /// <returns>Seconds between light activations.</returns>
    public static float GetStabilityLightInterval(float windowSeconds)
    {
        return windowSeconds / StabilityLightCount;
    }

    #endregion
}
```

These pillars, fences, non-goals and gates are the review rubric for §3–§20: any section that contradicts a documented constant, forks gameplay per platform, routes input around the provider abstraction, or moves gameplay state outside the fixed simulation step fails section review — and §21's risk register tracks every place where a gate is currently unproven.

## 3. Core Gameplay Loop Specification

### 3.1 Scope, grounding, and shared vocabulary

This section specifies the *rules* of the game: application flow, the per-level stack loop, the carry/rotation model, win/lose semantics, mode variants, scoring math, difficulty pacing, and meta-progression. It is grounded in the franchise track (T01) and physics track (T11) research notes; external facts carry inline source links (all accessed 2026-09-24), behaviors the originals did not document are marked with the original-design flag, and residual unknowns carry inline verification flags. Implementation skeletons for the systems named here live in their owning sections; this section defines *what they must do*, not how they are wired.

The documented core loop being cloned, in one sentence **[DOCUMENTED]**: a 2D single-plane physics stacker played over a water basin — pick a shape from a fixed per-level tray, rotate it in discrete steps, drop it; when the last shape is placed the structure must survive a timed stability countdown (three sequential green lights; three seconds on the Wii original, "significantly shorter" on later editions); if *any* piece touches the water at *any* point, the attempt fails and the level restarts ([Nintendo Life WiiWare review](https://web.archive.org/web/20210420192755/https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/2010/02/art_of_balance), [Cubed3 Wii U review](http://www.cubed3.com/review/1648/1/art-of-balance-wii-u.html), [Der Spiegel 3DS review](https://www.spiegel.de/netzwelt/games/3ds-spiel-art-of-balance-touch-im-test-a-843861.html), accessed 2026-09-24).

Shared vocabulary used throughout (defined in the owning sections):

| System / asset | Owning section | Role in the loop |
|---|---|---|
| `GameStateMachine` | §6 | Owns top-level flow states (§3.2) |
| `LevelManager` | §6 | Drives the per-level micro-state loop (§3.3) |
| `PieceSpawner` | §6 | Instantiates queue entries, owns piece pooling |
| `StabilityMonitor` | §6 | Settle detection, stability window, water-contact events |
| `ScoreController` | §6 | Event-driven consumer of the §3.7 formulas |
| `PieceDefinition` | §5 | Per-shape data incl. legal orientations, mass, behaviour |
| `LevelDefinition` | §5 | Queue, basin layout, par targets, challenge type |
| `WorldDefinition` / `GameModeDefinition` | §5 | Content grouping and mode parameter deltas |
| `IPieceInputProvider` | §7 | Normalized move/rotate/release/pause intents |
| `IBlockBehaviour` | §8 | Special-block hooks (OnPlaced, OnTimerTick, …) |
| `SaveSystem` | §6 | Progress, stars, per-level stats, ghost replays |

### 3.2 Top-level game state machine

**[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** for the state set itself (the originals' internal flow is undocumented); the *content* of the states (menus, worlds, modes) follows the documented 2012+ structure (200 levels across 8 worlds, five modes; per notes track-t01-franchise.md src 4/6/9/10/11/14, incl. the cited [Shin'en Switch press sheet](http://shinen.com/press/sheet.php?p=art_of_balance(Switch)), accessed 2026-09-24); the 25-levels-per-world split is our convention **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (§5.6.1; sources state only 200/8).

```text
                    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │                                                            │
Bootstrap ──► MainMenu ──► LevelSelect ──► Loading ──► Playing ⇄ Paused        │
                │              ▲                  │         │  │                │
                │              │                  ▼         │  └─ (resume)      │
                │              │           ResultsCleared ──┤                    │
                │              │                  │         │                    │
                │              │                  ▼         ▼                    │
                │              └────────────── (next / quit to map)              │
                │                             ResultsFailed                     │
                │                                │         ▲                     │
                └──► Lobby (MP modes) ──► Loading ──────────┘ (retry → Loading)  │
                                                └──► Playing …                  │
                    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

| State | Entry actions | Exit transitions | Owner system |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Bootstrap` | Load `GameConfig`, pin `Time.fixedDeltaTime = 1/240` (§6), init services, read save manifest | → `MainMenu` when scene Boot completes | `GameStateMachine` (§6), `SaveSystem` (§6) |
| `MainMenu` | Mode carousel (Arcade, Endurance, Infinity, Swift Stacker, Tower Tumble), settings, awards gallery | → `LevelSelect` (campaign modes) or `Lobby` (party modes) | UI flow (§9) |
| `Lobby` | Player/team setup, round-count selection (5/7/9 for race matches, per documented WiiWare Versus heritage), controller join | → `Loading` with resolved `GameModeDefinition` + player list | `GameStateMachine`, input pairing (§7) |
| `LevelSelect` | World map; free in-world order, skippable levels, world gates (§3.9) | → `Loading` on level pick | `SaveSystem` (unlock state), UI (§9) |
| `Loading` | Addressables load of `LevelDefinition` group (§5); determinism: build scene in fixed order | → `Playing` | `LevelManager` (§6) |
| `Playing` | Runs the §3.3 micro-loop; HUD shows queue tray, timer (if Time Challenge), lives (Endurance) | → `Paused`, `ResultsCleared`, `ResultsFailed` | `LevelManager` |
| `Paused` | `Time.timeScale = 0` (freezes sim *and* the stability countdown, which accrues fixed-step time only — §3.3); resume / restart / quit options | → `Playing` (resume), `Loading` (restart), `LevelSelect` | `GameStateMachine` |
| `ResultsCleared` | Stars awarded (§3.7), score breakdown, leaderboard upload (§19), next-level gate | → `Loading` (next) or `LevelSelect` | `ScoreController`, `SaveSystem` |
| `ResultsFailed` | Fail reason (water contact), retry affordance, lives decrement in Endurance | → `Loading` (retry) or `LevelSelect` | `LevelManager` |

Shared flow enum (anchor for cross-section vocabulary; `GameStateMachine` implementation in §6):

```csharp
namespace AoBClone.Core
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Top-level application flow states. Implementation and transition
    /// guards live in GameStateMachine (see §6); this enum is the shared contract.
    /// </summary>
    public enum GameFlowState
    {
        Bootstrap,
        MainMenu,
        Lobby,
        LevelSelect,
        Loading,
        Playing,
        Paused,
        ResultsCleared,
        ResultsFailed
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// Micro-states of the per-level stack loop, driven by LevelManager (see §6).
    /// </summary>
    public enum StackLoopPhase
    {
        Idle,
        PieceOffered,
        Carrying,
        Released,
        Settling,
        StabilityWindow,
        Cleared,
        Failed
    }
}
```

Endurance and Infinity enter `Playing` directly from `MainMenu` (session-based, no `LevelSelect`); Tower Tumble and Swift Stacker always pass through `Lobby`. Online variants of Swift Stacker (documented on Wii U and Switch as local, online, or mixed) reuse the same states with a synchronized-start gate; v1 ships local multiplayer only, with online deferred to a post-v1 milestone **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (scope fences in §2; networking approach per §21).

### 3.3 The stack loop (micro-states)

Diagram-in-text. `PieceOffered → Carrying → Released → Settling` repeats once per queue entry; `Settling` overlaps the next `PieceOffered` (pipelined play, §3.3.2):

```text
Idle ──► PieceOffered ──► Carrying ──► Released ──► Settling ──► (pieces remain? ──► PieceOffered)
              ▲                                               │
              └────────────── (queue advance, next piece) ─────┘        (last piece released)
                                                                      │
                                                       StabilityWindow ─┴─► Cleared
                    [water contact, at ANY phase, ANY time] ──► Failed ◄┘
```

| Phase | Entry condition | Exit condition | Timers active | Cancellable? | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Idle` | Level scene loaded, intro camera beat playing | Intro ends / skipped | Intro skip window (2 s auto) | Quit to menu | `LevelManager` |
| `PieceOffered` | Previous piece released (pipelined) or loop start | Player pickup intent (`IPieceInputProvider.PickupOrRelease`) | Offer highlight pulse (UI) | — | `PieceSpawner` |
| `Carrying` | Pickup accepted; piece becomes kinematic ghost (§3.4) | Release intent, or drop-zone invalid timeout (never — release always allowed) | None (rotation tween is presentation-only) | Pause (freezes tween clock) | `CarriedPiece` (§3.4) |
| `Released` | Release intent at cursor position, snapped orientation | Piece enters contact or free-fall reaches terminal band | None | Pause | `LevelManager` |
| `Settling` | Piece has contacted the stack/platform | Velocity predicate satisfied (`StabilityMonitor`, §6) — informational only, never blocks the loop | Settle watchdog (8 s, §3.5) | Pause | `StabilityMonitor` |
| `StabilityWindow` | **Last** queue piece released | 3.0 s accumulated fixed time without water contact → `Cleared`; water contact → `Failed` | The countdown (1 light/s; pause-safe, below) | Restart / pause / quit | `StabilityMonitor` |
| `Cleared` | Window completed | Results UI continues | Celebration sequence | — | `LevelManager` |
| `Failed` | Water contact detected (any phase) | Retry / quit chosen | Fail sting + sink drama (1.5 s) | — | `LevelManager` |

#### 3.3.1 Phase rules (load-bearing details)

- **Pickup** **[DOCUMENTED]** input grammar from the Wii original: A picks up and drops; B or D-pad left/right rotates ([Art of Balance First Look transcript](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mGkeVblM1Es), accessed 2026-09-24). §7 maps this grammar onto every input device; the loop only ever sees normalized intents.
- **Queue**: the level's piece set is fixed and ordered by `LevelDefinition` (§5); the HUD tray shows upcoming entries **[DOCUMENTED]** in spirit — the 3DS edition displayed the selection on the lower screen and the stack on the upper ([Der Spiegel](https://www.spiegel.de/netzwelt/games/3ds-spiel-art-of-balance-touch-im-test-a-843861.html), accessed 2026-09-24). Queue order is not player-selectable **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (no documented source says the tray can be reordered).
- **Pipelining** **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**: the next piece is offered immediately on release, without waiting for settle. Rationale: reviews describe continuous "supply of blocks" pacing; serializing offer-after-settle would halve expert throughput and break Time Challenge par math (§3.7).
- **Stability window start** **[DOCUMENTED]**: "Once you place the last block in place, the structure must stay above water for three seconds, indicated by three lights at the bottom of the screen" ([Nintendo Life](https://web.archive.org/web/20210420192755/https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/2010/02/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24). The countdown begins at the final release *regardless of whether the stack has finished moving*; quiescence is not a precondition.
- **Water contact is global and continuous**: any piece contacting water during *any* phase — including mid-countdown — fails the attempt **[DOCUMENTED]** ([Shin'en Wii U About page](https://web.archive.org/web/20160903223835/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com:80/wiiu/about.php): "Watch out: Don't let any shape fall into the water!", accessed 2026-09-24).

#### 3.3.2 Timers, cancellation, pause semantics

All loop timers accumulate **simulated fixed-step time**, never wall-clock or unscaled time. This makes pause trivially correct and keeps ghost-replay determinism (input + step index reproduces timing; see §3.9.4 and T11's determinism rules — fixed step values only, per [Physics2D.Simulate docs](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Physics2D.Simulate.html), accessed 2026-09-24).

Rule illustration (the full `StabilityMonitor` skeleton is §6's):

```csharp
private void FixedUpdate()
{
    if (_isPaused || _phase != StackLoopPhase.StabilityWindow)
    {
        return; // Pausing freezes the countdown together with the world (Time.timeScale = 0).
    }
    _windowElapsedSeconds += Time.fixedDeltaTime; // fixed 1/240 s steps; see §6 PhysicsStepper
    int lightsLit = Mathf.Min(
        (int)(_windowElapsedSeconds / (stabilityWindowSeconds / LightCount)),
        LightCount);
    if (lightsLit != _lightsLit)
    {
        _lightsLit = lightsLit;
        stabilityWindowProgressChannel.Raise(_lightsLit); // Ev_StabilityWindowProgress (§4.5 #11): the documented 3-green-light beat
    }
    if (_windowElapsedSeconds >= stabilityWindowSeconds)
    {
        // §4.5 #12: StabilityMonitor completes the window; LevelManager owns the
        // Cleared phase and raises Ev_LevelCompleted (§4.5 #13) — not this monitor.
        stabilityWindowCompletedChannel.Raise();
    }
}
```

with `private const int LightCount = 3;`, `[SerializeField] private float stabilityWindowSeconds = 3f;`, and serialized §4.5 channel references `stabilityWindowProgressChannel` / `stabilityWindowCompletedChannel` (registry rows #11/#12; full channel wiring in §6). Default 3.0 s is the multiply-documented Wii value **[DOCUMENTED]** ([Nintendo Life](https://web.archive.org/web/20210420192755/https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/2010/02/art_of_balance), [Cubed3](http://www.cubed3.com/review/1648/1/art-of-balance-wii-u.html), accessed 2026-09-24); later editions shortened it with no published number — the value stays data-driven per `GameConfig` for tuning. <!-- TODO-VERIFY: exact post-Wii countdown duration; only "significantly shorter" is documented (NL Wii U review, https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance). Resolution path: frame-count a captured Switch/Wii U gameplay video. -->

Cancellation matrix:

| Event | During Carrying | During Released/Settling | During StabilityWindow |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pause | Freeze tween clock; input buffered | Freeze sim (`timeScale = 0`, [Time project settings](https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/class-TimeManager.html), accessed 2026-09-24) | Freeze countdown accrual (fixed-step gate above) |
| Restart | Cancel attempt, reload level | Same | Cancel window, lights reset, reload |
| Quit to menu | Confirm dialog; attempt discarded, no score | Same | Same |
| Water contact | n/a (ghost does not collide) | → `Failed` | → `Failed` (lights reset) |
| Timer-block expiry mid-window (§8) | n/a | Collapse proceeds; window keeps running | If a piece reaches water before 3.0 s → fail; otherwise win stands |

#### 3.3.3 Retry semantics by mode

| Mode | Retry rule | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Arcade (+ Challenges) | Unlimited instant retries; identical deterministic re-offer (same seed); restart budget < 1.5 s (§14) | **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (unlimited arcade retries unlisted officially; consistent with all reviews) |
| Endurance | A failed level consumes one of **3 lives for the whole session**; retry re-presents the level; at 0 lives the session ends and the score uploads | Lives **[DOCUMENTED]** ([NL Wii U](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance): "three lives… spread out over your entire session"; [NWR](http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/review/38619/art-of-balance-wii-u-review): "three retries", accessed 2026-09-24). Same-level-vs-new-level choice **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** <!-- TODO-VERIFY: whether the original re-offers the failed level or advances to a new random one; reviews do not specify. --> |
| Infinity | No retry concept; a run ends on water contact; "run again" starts a fresh seeded feed | Mode definition **[DOCUMENTED]** ([Switch press sheet](http://shinen.com/press/sheet.php?p=art_of_balance(Switch)): "The blocks don't stop. Build the highest possible stack.", accessed 2026-09-24) |
| Swift Stacker | Failing racers rebuild immediately; the round continues until one team clears | **[DOCUMENTED]** (mode summary per [NWR Wii U review](http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/review/38619/art-of-balance-wii-u-review), accessed 2026-09-24) <!-- TODO-VERIFY: exact re-attempt freedom wording in reviews is imprecise; confirm via captured match footage. --> |
| Tower Tumble | No retries — the topple *is* the round loss | **[DOCUMENTED]** ([NWR](http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/review/38619/art-of-balance-wii-u-review): "reverse Jenga", accessed 2026-09-24) |

#### 3.3.4 Loop-emitted events (subset; §4.5 is the canonical `Ev_*` channel registry — names, raisers, and payloads here mirror it)

| Event | Raised by | Payload | Primary consumers |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Ev_PieceOffered` (queue advance; the payload carries the queue index — there is no separate queue-advanced channel) | `LevelManager` | `PieceDefinition`, queue index | HUD tray (§9), `PieceSpawner` |
| `Ev_PieceGrabbed` / `Ev_PieceRotated` / `Ev_PieceReleased` | `InputRouter` (normalized intents, §7 — not `CarriedPiece`, which is the commanded target) | piece handle, orientation index / pose | Audio/VFX directors (§6, §9), `LevelManager`/`StabilityMonitor` (release), replays (§3.9.4) |
| `Ev_PieceSettled` | `StabilityMonitor` | piece id, settle time | `ScoreController` precision inputs |
| `Ev_WaterContact` | `StabilityMonitor` | piece id, contact point | `LevelManager` (→ `Failed`), splash VFX (§9) |
| `Ev_StabilityWindowStarted` / `Ev_StabilityWindowProgress` / `Ev_StabilityWindowCompleted` | `StabilityMonitor` | light count 0–3 | HUD (three-green-lights UI), adaptive music (§9) |
| `Ev_LevelCompleted` / `Ev_LevelFailed` | `LevelManager` | level id, stats | `ScoreController`, `SaveSystem`, results UI |
| `Ev_LifeLost` | `LevelManager` (Endurance) | lives remaining | HUD, session-end check |
| `Ev_ScoreChanged` | `ScoreController` | delta, total | HUD |

### 3.4 Rotation model

**Increment** **[DOCUMENTED]**: rotation happens in 45° steps ([Wikipedia gameplay section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_of_Balance), accessed 2026-09-24). Confidence note: this is the only fetched source stating the exact increment (tertiary); it is indirectly corroborated by the shape inventory of rectangles/triangles/circles ([IGN Wii review](https://www.ign.com/articles/2010/02/16/art-of-balance-review), accessed 2026-09-24). <!-- TODO-VERIFY: 45° increment vs 90° on specific shape classes; frame-capture original gameplay to confirm diagonal placement of rectangles. -->

**Legality** **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**: legal orientations are piece-defined. `PieceDefinition` (§5) carries an 8-bit mask over the 45° lattice (`allowedOrientations`); rotation-invariant shapes (circle) and 90°-symmetric shapes (square) declare masks accordingly, and their rotation input produces acknowledged-but-cosmetic feedback (a small nudge wiggle + click) rather than a lattice change. Most pieces allow all 8 orientations — diagonal resting is core to the puzzle vocabulary.

**Pipeline** (all steps deterministic, quantized to fixed steps per T11 hygiene rules — never apply input at unconstrained frame timing):

1. Input intent (`RotateCW` / `RotateCCW` / `RotateTo`) arrives from `IPieceInputProvider` (§7), buffered in `Update`, consumed at the next fixed step.
2. Target index = current index ± 1 (mod 8); rejected silently-with-feedback if the mask disallows it.
3. Presentation tween: fixed-duration 100 ms ease-out rotation of the visual transform; the *logical* orientation snaps immediately.
4. Input buffering: up to 2 queued steps while tweening (game-feel rule: never eat a buffered rotate).
5. Continuous sources (touch twist, gyro `RotateTo`) map onto the lattice with magnetic snapping: nearest multiple of 45°, snap band ±22.5°, engage hysteresis 4° to prevent oscillation at the boundary.

**Carried-piece physics state** **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**: while carried, the piece is a kinematic ghost — collider disabled, semi-transparent material, no interaction with the stack (the originals never let you bulldoze the tower with a held shape; reviews describe precise placement over the structure). On release, the `Rigidbody2D` is enabled at the exact snapped lattice angle and cursor position; there is **no post-release rotation steering** — pieces are dropped, not flown.

```csharp
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;

namespace AoBClone.Gameplay
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Kinematic controller for the currently carried piece. Owns the 45-degree
    /// rotation lattice, orientation legality, the presentation tween, and input
    /// buffering. The piece does not collide while carried; physics engagement
    /// happens on Release (see §3.4).
    /// </summary>
    [RequireComponent(typeof(Rigidbody2D))]
    [RequireComponent(typeof(Collider2D))]
    public class CarriedPiece : MonoBehaviour
    {
        #region Consts

        private const int OrientationCount = 8;
        private const float OrientationStepDegrees = 45f;
        private const float MagneticSnapHalfStepDegrees = 22.5f;
        private const float SnapHysteresisDegrees = 4f;

        #endregion

        #region Serialized Fields

        [Header("Tweening")]
        [SerializeField] private float rotationTweenSeconds = 0.1f;
        [SerializeField] private int maxBufferedRotations = 2;

        [Header("Data")]
        [SerializeField] private PieceDefinition pieceDefinition;

        #endregion

        #region Private Fields

        private readonly Queue<int> _bufferedRotations = new();
        private Rigidbody2D _rigidbody2D;
        private Collider2D _collider2D;
        private int _orientationIndex;
        private float _rotationTweenTimer;
        private float _rotationTweenFromDegrees;

        #endregion

        #region Public Properties

        /// <summary>Current lattice orientation index in [0, 7]; index * 45 = degrees.</summary>
        public int OrientationIndex => _orientationIndex;

        /// <summary>True while the presentation tween is still running.</summary>
        public bool IsRotating => _rotationTweenTimer > 0f;

        #endregion

        #region Unity Lifecycle

        private void Awake()
        {
            _rigidbody2D = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();
            _collider2D = GetComponent<Collider2D>();
        }

        private void Update()
        {
            if (_rotationTweenTimer <= 0f)
            {
                return;
            }
            _rotationTweenTimer -= Time.deltaTime;
            float t = 1f - Mathf.Max(0f, _rotationTweenTimer / rotationTweenSeconds);
            float target = _orientationIndex * OrientationStepDegrees;
            // Presentation-only: logical orientation already snapped; ease-out for weight.
            transform.rotation = Quaternion.Euler(
                0f, 0f, Mathf.LerpAngle(_rotationTweenFromDegrees, target, EaseOutQuad(t)));
            if (_rotationTweenTimer <= 0f && _bufferedRotations.Count > 0)
            {
                BeginRotationTo(NormalizeIndex(_orientationIndex + _bufferedRotations.Dequeue()));
            }
        }

        #endregion

        #region Public Methods

        /// <summary>
        /// Applies a discrete rotation step (+1 clockwise, -1 counter-clockwise),
        /// mirroring the documented Wii input grammar (B / D-pad left-right).
        /// </summary>
        /// <param name="direction">+1 for clockwise, -1 for counter-clockwise.</param>
        public void Rotate(int direction)
        {
            if (!CanRotate(direction))
            {
                return; // Invariant pieces: cosmetic ack handled by the caller (§9).
            }
            if (IsRotating)
            {
                if (_bufferedRotations.Count < maxBufferedRotations)
                {
                    _bufferedRotations.Enqueue(direction);
                }
                return;
            }
            BeginRotationTo(NormalizeIndex(_orientationIndex + direction));
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Maps a continuous input angle (touch twist, gyro attitude) onto the
        /// 45-degree lattice with magnetic snapping and hysteresis.
        /// </summary>
        /// <param name="continuousDegrees">Raw continuous angle in degrees.</param>
        public void RotateTo(float continuousDegrees)
        {
            // ...
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Converts the carried piece into a simulated body at the snapped
        /// orientation. Called by LevelManager on release intent.
        /// </summary>
        /// <param name="releasePosition">World-space cursor position at release.</param>
        public void Release(Vector2 releasePosition)
        {
            // ...
        }

        #endregion

        #region Private Methods

        private bool CanRotate(int direction)
        {
            if (pieceDefinition == null || pieceDefinition.IsRotationInvariant)
            {
                return false;
            }
            return pieceDefinition.IsOrientationLegal(NormalizeIndex(_orientationIndex + direction));
        }

        private void BeginRotationTo(int targetIndex)
        {
            // ...
        }

        private static int NormalizeIndex(int index)
        {
            return ((index % OrientationCount) + OrientationCount) % OrientationCount;
        }

        private static float EaseOutQuad(float t)
        {
            return 1f - (1f - t) * (1f - t);
        }

        #endregion
    }
}
```

### 3.5 Win/lose rules

#### 3.5.1 Win rule

**[DOCUMENTED]**, multiply sourced: place *all* queued pieces, then survive the countdown. Exact wording preserved for feel-anchoring:

- "Once you place the last block in place, the structure must stay above water for three seconds, indicated by three lights at the bottom of the screen." ([Nintendo Life WiiWare review](https://web.archive.org/web/20210420192755/https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/2010/02/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24)
- "…form a tower that stands solid for three full seconds… the timer kicks in – first green light… – second green light – … – third green light and safety." ([Cubed3 Wii U review](http://www.cubed3.com/review/1648/1/art-of-balance-wii-u.html), accessed 2026-09-24)
- "Gewonnen hat man, wenn alle Steine gestapelt sind und das Bauwerk drei Sekunden lang steht oder zumindest nicht so schnell zusammenkracht, dass ein Stein vor Ablauf des Countdowns das Wasser berührt." — win when all pieces are stacked and the structure stands three seconds, *or at least does not crash so fast that a piece touches water before the countdown ends* ([Der Spiegel](https://www.spiegel.de/netzwelt/games/3ds-spiel-art-of-balance-touch-im-test-a-843861.html), accessed 2026-09-24).

The Der Spiegel sentence resolves a load-bearing edge case: **the win predicate is "no water contact before countdown completion", not "full quiescence."** A slow-motion collapse that reaches the water *after* the third light is still a win. Our spec adopts this verbatim: `StabilityWindow` completes on accumulated fixed time; the only failure input is the `Ev_WaterContact` event firing before completion.

#### 3.5.2 Water contact definition

**[DOCUMENTED]**: any piece touching the water fails the attempt; the originals do not remove individual pieces — the attempt fails ([Shin'en Wii U About page](https://web.archive.org/web/20160903223835/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com:80/wiiu/about.php): "Watch out: Don't let any shape fall into the water!" — the verbatim sentence is carried by the Wii U About page and the PS4/Switch press sheets, per T01 notes src 6/9/10; the fail rule is corroborated for 3DS by [Cubed3 3DS review](https://www.cubed3.com/games/reviews/nintendo-3ds/art-of-balance-touch), accessed 2026-09-24).

**[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** mechanics of the check (implementation physics in §6):

- Contact = first overlap of a `Piece`-layer collider with the `Water` trigger volume (layer-collision matrix, `OnTriggerEnter2D`), not submersion-depth.
- A 2 mm entry margin (contact must persist ≥ 2 fixed steps) filters spray-adjacent micro-contacts; visual splash particles are decoupled from the gameplay trigger.
- The gameplay waterline is a flat line equal to `BuoyancyEffector2D.surfaceLevel` (component per [Unity BuoyancyEffector2D docs](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/BuoyancyEffector2D.html), accessed 2026-09-24); visual waves are presentation-only and never move the fail line — competitive fairness and replay determinism require one authoritative line.
- Buoyancy exists for *drama*: after fail, pieces bob and settle in the water during the 1.5 s fail sequence. Buoyant forces must never be load-bearing for the win rule — per T11 (engineering inference, medium confidence: any continuous applied force — buoyancy effector, flow, custom forces — keeps bodies awake or re-wakes them, so a stack floating on or in water may never sleep), `IsSleeping` is never the win signal; the explicit stability predicate of §3.5.3 is used instead.

#### 3.5.3 Internal stability predicate (informational, for scoring and camera)

`StabilityMonitor` (§6) evaluates per fixed step, for each placed piece: (a) lowest point above waterline + margin; (b) |linear velocity| < 0.05 m/s; (c) |angular velocity| < 0.05 rad/s; (d) contact-island membership with the platform graph **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (predicate recipe from T11 research — velocity thresholds and island check; tolerances are tuning constants). This predicate feeds the settle watchdog (a stack that never quiesces within 8 s triggers a camera hint and disables precision-bonus accrual, but never blocks the win), the precision bonus (§3.7), and the adaptive music tension layer (§9). It is deliberately *not* the win condition.

#### 3.5.4 Partial failure and edge cases

| Case | Rule | Status |
|---|---|---|
| One piece sinks, rest stand | Whole attempt fails; level restarts; no piece removal | **[DOCUMENTED]** (attempt-level fail, §3.5.2 sources) |
| Assist Mode (accessibility, §14): sunk piece is removed with a splash after a 0.5 s penalty freeze; attempt continues; stars capped at 1★; leaderboards record assisted flag | Off by default | **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** |
| Collapse reaches water after third light | Win stands (countdown already complete) | **[DOCUMENTED]** (Der Spiegel wording, §3.5.1) |
| Timer block expires during window (§8) | Window continues; outcome decided by water contact before 3.0 s | **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (consistent with documented timer behavior — timer blocks "countdown and disappear when a new piece is placed atop them", [Cubed3 Wii U](http://www.cubed3.com/review/1648/1/art-of-balance-wii-u.html), accessed 2026-09-24) |
| Gravity inverter triggers late (§8) | Inverters activate on placement contact (before window start in practice); mid-window flips are a §8 test-matrix case | **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** |
| Piece resting on swaying platform (documented 3DS+ mechanic, [Cubed3 3DS](https://www.cubed3.com/games/reviews/nintendo-3ds/art-of-balance-touch), accessed 2026-09-24) | Continuous platform motion keeps velocities above tolerance; stability predicate uses platform-relative velocity | **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** |

### 3.6 Mode loop deltas

The five documented modes are parameterizations of one loop, not separate games **[DOCUMENTED]** for mode existence and framing ([Shin'en Switch press sheet](http://shinen.com/press/sheet.php?p=art_of_balance(Switch)), [PS4 press sheet](http://shinen.com/press/sheet.php?p=art_of_balance(PS4)), accessed 2026-09-24); deltas below instantiate them via `GameModeDefinition` (§5).

| Mode | Win condition | Loop changes | Player framing | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Arcade** (campaign) | Per-level: all pieces + survive window | Base loop as §3.3; optional Time/Height/Balance Challenge per level for extra points | Solo, or drop-in co-op (documented on Wii: 2nd Wii Remote joins anytime; Wii U: up to 5 local) | **[DOCUMENTED]** ([Wii microsite](https://web.archive.org/web/20091116220135/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com:80/about.php), [Nintendo.com Wii U](https://web.archive.org/web/20160619195926/http://www.nintendo.com/games/detail/art-of-balance-wii-u), accessed 2026-09-24) |
| **Endurance** | None per level; session score until 3 lives exhausted | Random level string; `Ev_LifeLost` wiring; session score = speed + lives + difficulty (documented skeleton, §3.7.3) | Solo session vs leaderboard | **[DOCUMENTED]** ("Play a never ending string of puzzles to go for the best scores", [Switch sheet](http://shinen.com/press/sheet.php?p=art_of_balance(Switch)); 3 lives per [NL Wii U](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24) |
| **Infinity** | None; height score | No queue limit — procedural feed; fail ends run; no stability window (run continues while stack holds) | Solo height chase | **[DOCUMENTED]** ("The blocks don't stop. Build the highest possible stack.", [Switch sheet](http://shinen.com/press/sheet.php?p=art_of_balance(Switch)), accessed 2026-09-24) |
| **Swift Stacker** | First team to clear the identical puzzle wins the round; match = best of 5/7/9 (round counts documented for the WiiWare Versus ancestor) | Split-screen duplicate simulations; per-team independent loops; synchronized round start/end gates | 2 teams, split-screen race; local/online/mixed on original; v1 local | **[DOCUMENTED]** ([NL Wii U](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), [NL WiiWare](https://web.archive.org/web/20210420192755/https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/2010/02/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24) |
| **Tower Tumble** | Round: everyone except the toppler scores 1 point | Turn-based hotseat: one carrier at a time (turn arbitration in `Lobby`/`LevelManager`); pieces per round randomly generated; no stability window per turn — collapse decides | Up to 4 players, turn placement | **[DOCUMENTED]** ("Who will topple the tower first? A multiplayer competition mode for up to 4 players.", [Switch sheet](http://shinen.com/press/sheet.php?p=art_of_balance(Switch)); random pieces per [Cubed3 Wii U](http://www.cubed3.com/review/1648/1/art-of-balance-wii-u.html), accessed 2026-09-24) |

Co-op drop-in (Arcade) **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** implementation: joining player gets a second cursor (per-player `IPieceInputProvider` pairing, §7); the shared queue is untouched; only one player may carry a given piece at a time (first pickup wins, release intent from either releases).

### 3.7 Scoring design

Everything in §3.7 is **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** except where a line is marked [DOCUMENTED]: the originals' scoring internals are not published anywhere in the fetched sources — what *is* documented is (a) Time/Height/Balance Challenges award extra points ([3DS About](https://web.archive.org/web/20151029143537/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com/3ds/about.php), accessed 2026-09-24), and (b) the Endurance formula *skeleton* on Wii U+: speed + remaining lives + puzzle difficulty → online leaderboard ([NL Wii U review](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24). Design goals: reward the three documented skills (speed, height/economy, precision), price special-block risk, produce integer scores with clean star thresholds derivable at authoring time.

#### 3.7.1 Arcade level score

Per-piece placement points are authored on `PieceDefinition.placementPoints` by the §5 authoring tool from this table (formula: `round(100 × C × R)`):

| Component | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Base `B` | 100 pts | Const |
| Complexity `C` (shape class) | 1.00 simple (square, circle) / 1.25 medium (bar, L, T) / 1.50 complex (cross, S, Z) | Guideline per shape; authored per `PieceDefinition` |
| Risk `R` (behaviour) | base ×1.00 / breakable ×1.50 / timed ×1.50 / fire ×2.00 / gravity-inverter ×2.00 / linked-pair ×1.75 | Risk prices documented special difficulty (breakable holds "no more than three other regulars", [Cubed3 Wii U](http://www.cubed3.com/review/1648/1/art-of-balance-wii-u.html), accessed 2026-09-24); linked-pair is our extension (§8) |

Level total:

```
S = Σ placementPoints(p)                        (every placed piece)
  + 25 × H                                      H  = final stack height in block units above platform surface
  + 10 × max(0, T_par − T_used)                 T_par = LevelDefinition par time (s); T_used = wall time (s)
  + 25 × max(0, W_par − W_used)                 W_par = par footprint width (block units); W_used = resting footprint width
  + 250 [if level Challenge completed]          Challenge = one of Time / Height / Balance per level
```

Rationale: height and precision bonuses instantiate the documented Height and Balance Challenges; the time term instantiates the Time Challenge ("use all pieces in a set time, build a tower as high as possible", [Cubed3 Wii U](http://www.cubed3.com/review/1648/1/art-of-balance-wii-u.html), accessed 2026-09-24) as a continuous incentive rather than a binary gate, with the flat 250 for the binary medal.

**Worked example** — level W3-L07: queue = 12 pieces (9 base: 4 simple, 4 medium, 1 complex; 2 timed; 1 fire), `T_par` = 75 s, `W_par` = 9 units. Player run: cleared in 61 s, final height 6 units, resting footprint 7 units, Time Challenge (sub-70 s) met.

- Placements: 4×100 + 4×125 + 1×150 = 1,050; timed 2×150 = 300; fire 1×200 = 200 → Σ = 1,550
- Height: 25 × 6 = 150
- Time: 10 × (75 − 61) = 140
- Precision: 25 × (9 − 7) = 50
- Challenge: +250
- **S = 2,140**

#### 3.7.2 Star thresholds (derivation method)

Stars are per-level **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (the originals show no public star system; their award system is the meta-level achievements, §3.9.3). Derivation is anchored to a *reference par run* scored by the authoring tool (§5) so thresholds never need hand-tuning per level:

```
S_ref = score of the author's par run (par time, par height, par width, no challenge bonus)
T_3★  = round50(S_ref)                 (round to nearest 50, minimum 50)
T_2★  = round50(0.70 × S_ref)
1★    = any completion
```

Continuing the W3-L07 example: the par run scores 1,550 + 125 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 1,675 → `T_3★` = 1,700? No — round50(1,675) = 1,650 (1,675 is equidistant; round-half-down to keep 3★ reachable). The example run's 2,140 ≥ 1,650 → **3★**. A slower 100 s run with height 5 and width 9 scores 1,550 + 125 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 1,675 ≥ `T_2★` = round50(1,172.5) = 1,150 → **2★**. Post-launch, telemetry (§14) can re-anchor `S_ref` to the 75th-percentile real run; the formula stays fixed.

#### 3.7.3 Endurance score

Documented skeleton **[DOCUMENTED]**: speed + remaining lives + puzzle difficulty ([NL Wii U](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24). Instantiation **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**:

