```csharp
            ProfileDocument document = JsonUtility.FromJson<ProfileDocument>(json);
            while (document.schemaVersion < CurrentSchemaVersion)
            {
                StepMigration(document); // each migration bumps schemaVersion by its From->To chain
            }

            // … fan out RestoreState(section) per registered ISaveable by SaveKey,
            // tolerating a missing section (new saveable added post-ship).
            return true;
        }

        /// <summary>Atomic write: serialize to temp, File.Replace onto the target, rotate the old file to .bak.</summary>
        public void SaveProfile()
        {
            var document = new ProfileDocument
            {
                engineVersion = Application.unityVersion,
                buildGuid = BuildGuid.Current,
                recordedUtc = DateTime.UtcNow.ToString("o"),
                profileJson = CollectSectionsJson(),
            };

            string json = JsonUtility.ToJson(document, prettyPrint: false);
            WriteTextAtomically(_profilePath, _backupPath, json);

            if (_cloudAdapter != null)
            {
                byte[] payload = System.Text.Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(json);
                if (!_cloudAdapter.Upload(_profilePath, payload))
                {
                    // offline: queued locally by the adapter; retried on next save or connectivity event
                }
            }
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Cloud-first reconciliation at boot: if the cloud copy's recordedUtc
        /// is newer than local, take it (and keep the loser as .conflict).
        /// [ORIGINAL DESIGN] policy: newest-lastPlayedUtc wins, never merge.
        /// </summary>
        public void ReconcileWithCloud()
        {
            if (_cloudAdapter == null)
            {
                return;
            }

            byte[] cloud = _cloudAdapter.Download(_profilePath);
            // … compare recordedUtc headers; adopt cloud if newer, backing up the loser;
            // surface a one-line UI notice, never a modal merge dialog.
        }

        #endregion

        #region Private Methods

        private string CollectSectionsJson()
        {
            // … per saveable: CaptureState() into a serializable wrapper + SaveKey;
            // wrapped as KeyValueEntry array for JsonUtility (Dictionary workaround, see note above).
            return string.Empty;
        }

        private void StepMigration(ProfileDocument document)
        {
            // … dequeue the migration whose FromVersion == document.schemaVersion, run, repeat.
        }

        private static string ReadTextWithBackupFallback(string path, string backup)
        {
            if (File.Exists(path))
            {
                try
                {
                    return File.ReadAllText(path);
                }
                catch (IOException)
                {
                    // fall through to backup
                }
            }

            return File.Exists(backup) ? File.ReadAllText(backup) : null;
        }

        private static void WriteTextAtomically(string path, string backup, string contents)
        {
            string temp = path + ".tmp";
            string dir = Path.GetDirectoryName(path);
            if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(dir))
            {
                Directory.CreateDirectory(dir);
            }

            File.WriteAllText(temp, contents);
            if (File.Exists(path))
            {
                File.Replace(temp, path, backup);
            }
            else
            {
                File.Move(temp, path);
            }
        }

        #endregion
    }
}
```

Integrity: the whole profile and each ghost are HMAC-SHA256-signed with a device-scoped key so truncated/corrupt saves are detected, not silently loaded — key management and the anti-cheat threat model are §14's scope (leaderboard fairness only; this is a single-player-first game).

**Ghost replays** (drives §3 leaderboard ghosts): per level, a compact event log recorded by the §6.3 discipline —

```
ghosts/<levelId>.ghost.json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "levelId": "w3-l07",
  "engineVersion": "6000.6.0f1",
  "buildGuid": "<guid>",
  "simulationHz": 240,
  "rngSeed": 1834227917,
  "starvedFrames": 0,
  "finalScore": 1850,
  "recordedUtc": "2026-09-24T12:00:00Z",
  "frames": [ [0,"pick",5], [173,"rotate",1], [512,"release",...] ]  // (stepIndex, event, payload)
}
```

Validity gate before playback: `engineVersion + buildGuid + simulationHz + rngSeed + starvedFrames == 0` must match the running build, else the ghost is refused (per §6.3 determinism positions — same-device/same-build is the only guaranteed-replay envelope). Playback feeds the recorded events into `InputRouter`'s fixed-step queue in place of live input. Ghosts are never written cross-device.

### 6.10 Object pooling — pieces and effects

No runtime `Instantiate`/`Destroy` in the gameplay loop. One `PiecePool` keyed by `PieceDefinition` (prefab identity), plus a sibling `VfxPool` for non-colliding effects (splash, settle dust, fire-explosion debris — debris is pure VFX with fake physics, never a `Rigidbody2D`, so it cannot perturb the simulation or the win predicate **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**).

Naming alignment with §4.4: `PiecePool` and `VfxPool` are the two concrete pools behind §4.4's `PoolManager` facade — §4.4's `PieceSpawner` row ("instantiate pieces from the queue via `PoolManager`") resolves to `PiecePool` at this section's level of detail; both sections refer to the same pooling system, §6 simply names its two concrete pools.

| Pool | Key | Prewarm source | High-water mark |
|---|---|---|---|
| PiecePool | `PieceDefinition` | max queue count of the level (from `LevelDefinition`) + 2 spare (fire chains can demand extras transiently) | level-scoped, trimmed on unload |
| VfxPool | effect prefab | 8 per active effect type | grows on demand, never shrinks mid-level (avoid GC churn during Evaluating) |
| Audio voices | — | §6.11 / §9 voice budget | fixed |

```csharp
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;

namespace Aob.Core.Gameplay
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Pool for PieceController instances keyed by PieceDefinition. Get/Return
    /// with a strict reset contract so a recycled piece is bit-identical to a
    /// fresh one from the simulation's point of view.
    /// </summary>
    public sealed class PiecePool : MonoBehaviour
    {
        #region Private Fields

        private readonly Dictionary<PieceDefinition, Queue<PieceController>> _pools = new Dictionary<PieceDefinition, Queue<PieceController>>(32);
        private readonly Dictionary<PieceDefinition, PieceController> _prefabs;

        #endregion

        #region Constructors

        /// <param name="prefabs">Prefab table from the §5 catalog (Addressables-loaded at level load).</param>
        public PiecePool(Dictionary<PieceDefinition, PieceController> prefabs) => _prefabs = prefabs;

        #endregion

        #region Public Methods

        /// <summary>Instantiates ahead of the first frame of gameplay. Count = level queue max + spare.</summary>
        public void Prewarm(PieceDefinition definition, int count)
        {
            Queue<PieceController> pool = PoolFor(definition);
            while (pool.Count < count)
            {
                PieceController instance = Instantiate(_prefabs[definition], transform);
                instance.gameObject.SetActive(false);
                pool.Enqueue(instance);
            }
        }

        public PieceController Get(PieceDefinition definition)
        {
            Queue<PieceController> pool = PoolFor(definition);
            PieceController instance = pool.Count > 0 ? pool.Dequeue() : Instantiate(_prefabs[definition], transform);

            // Reset contract (order matters):
            // 1. Rigidbody2D: velocity/angularVelocity zero, rotation identity, simulated per caller
            // 2. IBlockBehaviour.ResetToDefaults() — §8 state machines back to pristine
            // 3. Visuals: §9 tint/outline/variant back to definition defaults
            instance.ResetForSpawn();
            instance.gameObject.SetActive(true);
            return instance;
        }

        public void Return(PieceController instance)
        {
            instance.ResetForSpawn(); // same contract — return clean
            instance.gameObject.SetActive(false);
            PoolFor(instance.Definition).Enqueue(instance);
        }

        /// <summary>Level unload: destroys all instances and clears keys.</summary>
        public void Clear()
        {
            foreach (KeyValuePair<PieceDefinition, Queue<PieceController>> pair in _pools)
            {
                while (pair.Value.Count > 0)
                {
                    Destroy(pair.Value.Dequeue().gameObject);
                }
            }

            _pools.Clear();
        }

        #endregion

        #region Private Methods

        private Queue<PieceController> PoolFor(PieceDefinition definition)
        {
            if (!_pools.TryGetValue(definition, out Queue<PieceController> pool))
            {
                pool = new Queue<PieceController>(16);
                _pools.Add(definition, pool);
            }

            return pool;
        }

        #endregion
    }
}
```

`PieceSpawner` (referenced by §6.5) is the only public consumer: it pulls from `PiecePool`, positions at the carry anchor, and hands the piece to `LevelManager`. Pool sizing is validated by the §5 level linter so a level can never demand more live pieces than its prewarm budget.

### 6.11 AudioDirector — mixer topology and adaptive tension

All gameplay audio is **2D sources with parameterized stereo pan** derived from world x-position **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** — a fixed-side-view puzzle has no meaningful listener motion, and 3D panning buys nothing here while complicating the mixer graph. Spatialization ambition (HRTF on consoles) is a §9 stretch item, not a v1 dependency.

**Mixer topology:**

```
Master
├── Music          (ducked by Results sting)
│   ├── MusicBase
│   └── MusicTension
├── SFX
│   ├── Pieces     (wooden clunks — documented core feel)
│   ├── Water      (splashes, lapping ambience)
│   └── UI
└── Ambience       (theme beds, §9)
```

**Snapshots:** `Calm` (menus/idle), `Tension` (stability window + high wobble), `Paused` (music filtered lowpass, `timeScale 0` pairing), `Results` (win sting/fail sting EQ).

**Adaptive layer:** the documented "relaxing lounge soundtrack" ([Nintendo Life Wii U review](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), 2014-10-03, accessed 2026-09-24) becomes two synced stems — `MusicBase` always, `MusicTension` faded in proportionally to `StabilityMonitor.WobbleIntensity` and snapped up during the Evaluating window. One exposed mixer parameter `Tension` (0–1) is the entire runtime surface:

```csharp
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.Audio;

namespace Aob.Core.Presentation
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Thin runtime over the AudioMixer: one exposed parameter (Tension) driven
    /// by StabilityMonitor, snapshot transitions, and 2D pan-from-world-x.
    /// No per-frame allocations; pan is set on event, not polled.
    /// </summary>
    public sealed class AudioDirector : MonoBehaviour
    {
        #region Serialized Fields

        [Header("References")]
        [SerializeField] private AudioMixer mixer;
        [SerializeField] private AudioMixerSnapshot calmSnapshot;
        [SerializeField] private AudioMixerSnapshot tensionSnapshot;
        [SerializeField] private AudioMixerSnapshot pausedSnapshot;
        [SerializeField] private AudioMixerSnapshot resultsSnapshot;

        [Header("Panning")]
        [SerializeField] private float panHalfWidth = 8f; // world |x| that maps to full L/R

        #endregion

        #region Private Constants

        private const string TensionParam = "Tension";

        #endregion

        #region Public Methods

        /// <summary>Drive call per fixed step from the StabilityMonitor glue (cheap: one native set).</summary>
        public void SetTension(float value01)
        {
            mixer.SetFloat(TensionParam, Mathf.Clamp01(value01) * 100f);
        }

        public void TransitionTo(AudioPhase phase, float seconds = 0.5f)
        {
            AudioMixerSnapshot target;
            switch (phase)
            {
                case AudioPhase.Paused:  target = pausedSnapshot;  break;
                case AudioPhase.Tension: target = tensionSnapshot; break;
                case AudioPhase.Results: target = resultsSnapshot; break;
                default:                 target = calmSnapshot;    break;
            }

            target.TransitionTo(seconds);
        }

        /// <summary>2D stereo pan for a world position; call when spawning the voice, not per frame.</summary>
        public float PanForWorldX(float worldX)
        {
            return Mathf.Clamp(worldX / panHalfWidth, -1f, 1f);
        }

        #endregion

        #region Nested Types

        public enum AudioPhase { Calm, Tension, Paused, Results }

        #endregion
    }
}
```

Voice budgets, loudness targets (-16 LUFS master, music -23 LUFS under SFX ducking) and the console-compression pass are §9's; §14 owns the profiling hook (`AudioDirector.SetTension` is idempotent and safe to call at 240 Hz — the native set is a no-op write when unchanged).

**Section wiring summary** — this section owns: `PhysicsStepper`, `StabilityMonitor`, `LevelManager`, `GameStateMachine`, `ScoreController`, `CameraDirector`, `SaveSystem` (+ `ISaveable`, ghosts), `PiecePool`/`VfxPool` (the concrete pools behind §4.4's `PoolManager` facade), `AudioDirector`, `WaterVolume`. It consumes: §5 definitions, §7 input events, §8 behaviours; it feeds: §3 presentation flows, §9 art/audio specifics, §19 platform services (interfaces in §4.4), §14 telemetry determinism gates.



## 7. Multi-Platform Input Architecture

The original Art of Balance shipped across five platforms with three fundamentally different control grammars — IR pointing, stylus/touch, and sticks+buttons — and then added a fourth (motion) to the Switch edition 40 days (~six weeks) after launch. That history *is* the requirement for this clone: a pointer device, a gamepad, a touchscreen, and (optionally) a motion controller must drive the identical pick-up → rotate → drop loop (§3) with zero gameplay-side branching per platform. This section specifies the provider abstraction, the InputActionAsset, four providers, uGUI wiring, rebinding + glyphs, multiplayer pairing, and latency discipline. Console historical context lives in §11–§13; platform player-settings concerns live in §18–§19.

**Engine grounding (2026-09-24).** Unity 6.6 (6000.6) ships the Input System as a **built-in engine module**: "From 6.6, the package no longer exists in new projects so this check will be ignored even though the Input System module is available" ([Unity staff post "Planned breaking changes in Unity 6.7"](https://discussions.unity.com/t/planned-breaking-changes-in-unity-6-7/1723293), 2026-06-16, accessed 2026-09-24). **[VERIFIED-REFUTED]** the sweep-level phrase "new Unity 6 projects default to the Input System *package*": since Unity 6 the Input System is "the default solution for Unity" ([Unity technical article, 2025-03-24](https://discussions.unity.com/t/get-up-and-running-with-the-input-system/1620267), accessed 2026-09-24), template-created projects install the package while empty projects do not, and from 6.6 it is a module, not a package. The standalone package line continues in parallel: latest stable **1.20.0 (2026-07-21)**, develop 1.20.1, minimum editor `6000.0` ([GitHub Unity-Technologies/InputSystem releases](https://github.com/Unity-Technologies/InputSystem), accessed 2026-09-24); the live docs root banners "Input System 6.7.0", which is the Unity 6.7 *docs-stream* label, not a package version ([docs.unity3d.com package root](https://docs.unity3d.com/Packages/com.unity.inputsystem@latest), accessed 2026-09-24). The 6.6-era module documentation line is 1.18.x (per the staff post's own reference to "Installation guide | Input System | 1.18.0"). <!-- TODO-VERIFY: exact Input System module version compiled into Unity 6000.6 editors (expected 1.18.x line) — check the editor's package/module manifest on first project open; 1.20.0 features cited below (e.g. Faster Enter Play Mode support) must be re-confirmed if the module is older. --> Unless a different link is given, Input System behavioral facts in this section are **[DOCUMENTED]** in the official manual sources at [Unity-Technologies/InputSystem, branch develop, Packages/com.unity.inputsystem/Documentation~](https://github.com/Unity-Technologies/InputSystem/tree/develop/Packages/com.unity.inputsystem/Documentation~) (package 1.20.1-develop, accessed 2026-09-24) — the stable citation while docs.unity3d.com restructures its manual URLs.

**Active Input Handling.** §4 pins Player Settings → Other Settings → Active Input Handling = **Both** (`ENABLE_LEGACY_INPUT_MANAGER` + `ENABLE_INPUT_SYSTEM`; editor restarts on change — documented). The "Both" choice exists purely so legacy editor tooling and old editor assets keep compiling; all runtime gameplay input flows exclusively through Input System APIs, gated by `#if ENABLE_INPUT_SYSTEM` where needed. Relevant 1.x behavioral notes for our Unity 6.x baseline: 1.17.0 made project-wide actions permanently available (no compile-out), 1.20.0 added Faster Enter Play Mode (domain-reload-off) support — matching §4's domain-reload-off project default — and 1.16.0 restored MonoBehaviour `OnMouse*` events on Unity 6000.4+ ([CHANGELOG](https://github.com/Unity-Technologies/InputSystem/blob/develop/Packages/com.unity.inputsystem/CHANGELOG.md), accessed 2026-09-24).

**Code placement.** All input runtime code lives in `Assets/_Project/Scripts/Input/` under the `AoB.Input` assembly definition, referencing only `AoB.Core` (§4 asmdef plan). `AoB.Gameplay` references `AoB.Input` to consume `IPieceInputProvider`; input never references gameplay. Note that Input Actions are runtime-only and cannot be used from `EditorWindow` code (documented) — the §5 LevelEditor window uses `EditorGUI` event handling instead.

### 7.2 `IPieceInputProvider`: the provider abstraction

**Rationale.** Gameplay systems (`LevelManager`, the carry controller from §3, `GameStateMachine`) must never see a device, a control path, or an `InputAction`. They consume **intents** — device-agnostic, timestamped records in the original's own vocabulary (move the carried piece, rotate ±45°, drop, pause). This buys four things: (1) the four control grammars of §7.1 collapse into interchangeable providers; (2) the intent stream is a deterministic log that §6's replay/ghost system and §14's scripted-input playmode tests can consume and replay; (3) a post-launch control scheme (§7.9) is an additive provider, not a refactor; (4) menu/UI input has a defined passthrough lane that respects the `GameStateMachine` state.

The consumer model is **latch-and-consume polling**: providers latch events into per-frame counters/flags during the render update; the simulation consumes and clears them at its tick. No delegates on the hot path, no allocations, no missed-button edge cases between simulation steps.

```csharp
using System;
using UnityEngine;

namespace AoB.Input
{
    /// <summary>Device-agnostic gameplay/UI commands, mirroring the original's
    /// pick-up / rotate / drop vocabulary (see §3). One byte on the wire.</summary>
    public enum PieceInputCommand : byte
    {
        None = 0,
        MoveDelta = 1,
        RotateCW = 2,
        RotateCCW = 3,
        RotateTo = 4,
        DropOrRelease = 5,
        Pause = 6,
        UiNavigate = 7,
        UiSubmit = 8,
        UiCancel = 9
    }

    /// <summary>Immutable intent record written by providers during the render
    /// update and consumed by the simulation tick. Logged for replays (§6).</summary>
    public struct PieceInputIntent
    {
        #region Public Fields

        public PieceInputCommand Command;
        public byte ProviderIndex;
        public byte PlayerIndex;
        public Vector2 ScreenDelta;  // MoveDelta / UiNavigate payload, screen px
        public float Scalar;         // RotateTo target angle in degrees
        public uint FrameIndex;      // render frame the intent was latched in
        public double TimeSeconds;   // Time.realtimeSinceStartupAsDouble at latch

        #endregion
    }

    /// <summary>Per-frame UI navigation passthrough frame, merged by the
    /// InputRouter and forwarded to custom (non-EventSystem) menu widgets.</summary>
    public struct UiNavigationFrame
    {
        #region Public Fields

        public Vector2 Move;
        public bool Submit;
        public bool Cancel;

        #endregion
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// Device-agnostic input source for the piece loop. Implementations wrap one
    /// control grammar (pointer, gamepad cursor, touch drag, motion pointer) and
    /// translate raw input into latched intents consumed once per simulation tick.
    /// </summary>
    public interface IPieceInputProvider
    {
        #region Properties

        /// <summary>Stable identifier, e.g. "mouse", "gamepad", "touch", "motion".</summary>
        string ProviderId { get; }

        /// <summary>Control scheme this provider serves (see §7.3).</summary>
        InputScheme Scheme { get; }

        int PlayerIndex { get; }

        bool IsConnected { get; }

        /// <summary>Absolute cursor position in screen px (carried-piece anchor).</summary>
        Vector2 CursorPosition { get; }

        /// <summary>Cursor movement since the previous Tick, screen px.</summary>
        Vector2 MoveDelta { get; }

        #endregion

        #region Events

        /// <summary>Raised on connection state change (hot-swap, device loss).</summary>
        event Action<IPieceInputProvider> ConnectionChanged;

        #endregion

        #region Intent Consumption (latch-and-consume)

        /// <summary>Consume and clear accumulated clockwise 45°-step requests.</summary>
        int ConsumeRotateCW();

        /// <summary>Consume and clear accumulated counter-clockwise 45°-step requests.</summary>
        int ConsumeRotateCCW();

        /// <summary>Consume an absolute-orientation request, if any (degrees, §3 rotation model).</summary>
        bool ConsumeRotateTo(out float angleDegrees);

        /// <summary>Consume the pick-up / drop toggle request (Wii A-button semantics).</summary>
        bool ConsumeDropOrRelease();

        /// <summary>Consume the pause request.</summary>
        bool ConsumePause();

        /// <summary>Merge this provider's UI navigation into <paramref name="navigation"/>.</summary>
        void PassThroughUiNavigation(ref UiNavigationFrame navigation);

        #endregion

        #region Lifecycle

        void SetPlayerIndex(int playerIndex);
        void Tick(in ProviderTickContext context);
        void ResetLatches();

        #endregion
    }

    /// <summary>Read-only per-frame data handed to every provider by the InputRouter.</summary>
    public readonly struct ProviderTickContext
    {
        #region Public Fields

        public readonly uint FrameIndex;
        public readonly double TimeSeconds;
        public readonly float UnscaledDeltaTime;

        #endregion

        public ProviderTickContext(uint frameIndex, double timeSeconds, float unscaledDeltaTime)
        {
            FrameIndex = frameIndex;
            TimeSeconds = timeSeconds;
            UnscaledDeltaTime = unscaledDeltaTime;
        }
    }
}
```

**Provider registry and active-provider switching.** The registry owns the provider list and the per-player *active provider* pointer. Switching policy **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**: (a) explicit — the player picks a scheme in the options menu (persisted via §6 SaveSystem); (b) activity-based — when no provider is locked (single player), the first provider that performs a `Gameplay`-map action becomes active, mirroring PlayerInput's documented default auto-switching of control schemes; (c) in local multiplayer every player's mapping is locked (`neverAutoSwitchControlSchemes = true`, documented property) so one player's button cannot steal another's scheme.

```csharp
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.InputSystem;

namespace AoB.Input
{
    /// <summary>Owns all IPieceInputProvider instances and the per-player
    /// active-provider pointers. Plain C# (no MonoBehaviour) so playmode tests
    /// can drive it head-less (§14).</summary>
    public sealed class InputProviderRegistry
    {
        #region Fields

        private readonly List<IPieceInputProvider> _providers = new(8);
        private readonly Dictionary<int, int> _activeProviderByPlayer = new(4);
        private int _lastAddedIndex = -1;

        #endregion

        #region Events

        /// <summary>Raised whenever any player's active provider changed.</summary>
        public event Action<int> ActiveProviderChanged;

        #endregion

        #region Public Properties

        public IReadOnlyList<IPieceInputProvider> Providers => _providers;

        #endregion

        #region Public Methods

        public void Register(IPieceInputProvider provider)
        {
            if (provider == null) { return; }
            _providers.Add(provider);
            _lastAddedIndex = _providers.Count - 1;
            provider.ConnectionChanged += HandleConnectionChanged;
        }

        public void Unregister(string providerId)
        {
            for (int i = _providers.Count - 1; i >= 0; i--)
            {
                if (!string.Equals(_providers[i].ProviderId, providerId, StringComparison.Ordinal)) { continue; }
                _providers[i].ConnectionChanged -= HandleConnectionChanged;
                _providers.RemoveAt(i);
            }
        }

        public IPieceInputProvider GetActive(int playerIndex)
        {
            return _activeProviderByPlayer.TryGetValue(playerIndex, out int index)
                ? _providers[index]
                : null;
        }

        /// <summary>Explicit switch (options menu). Falls back to any connected provider.</summary>
        public bool TryActivate(string providerId, int playerIndex)
        {
            for (int i = 0; i < _providers.Count; i++)
            {
                if (!_providers[i].IsConnected) { continue; }
                if (!string.Equals(_providers[i].ProviderId, providerId, StringComparison.Ordinal)) { continue; }
                _activeProviderByPlayer[playerIndex] = i;
                ActiveProviderChanged?.Invoke(playerIndex);
                return true;
            }
            return false;
        }

        /// <summary>Activity-based switch: called by the router when a non-active
        /// connected provider produces a Gameplay intent and the player is unlocked.</summary>
        public void NotifyActivity(IPieceInputProvider source, int playerIndex)
        {
            int index = _providers.IndexOf(source);
            if (index < 0 || _activeProviderByPlayer.TryGetValue(playerIndex, out int active) && active == index) { return; }
            _activeProviderByPlayer[playerIndex] = index;
            ActiveProviderChanged?.Invoke(playerIndex);
        }

        <!-- TODO-VERIFY: API name not in research notes; confirm InputSystem.onDeviceChange against current docs -->
        /// <summary>Device hot-swap hook, wired to InputSystem.onDeviceChange.</summary>
        public void HandleDeviceChange(InputDevice device, InputDeviceChange change)
        {
            // Providers re-evaluate their own IsConnected from this callback;
            // players whose active provider dropped get the reconnect prompt (§7.2).
            // …
        }

        #endregion

        #region Private Methods

        private void HandleConnectionChanged(IPieceInputProvider provider)
        {
            // If the provider that just disconnected is active for some player,
            // emit the UI event that shows the reconnect overlay.
            // …
        }

        #endregion
    }
}
```

**Device hot-swap.** Two documented layers cover loss/regain: global `InputSystem.onDeviceChange`<!-- TODO-VERIFY: API name not in research notes; confirm InputSystem.onDeviceChange against current docs --> (device add/remove — the registry re-evaluates provider availability and the glyph service, §7.6, re-classifies the prompt scheme) and, in multiplayer, `PlayerInput`'s `onDeviceLost` / `onDeviceRegained` (C# events when Behavior = Invoke CSharp Events; `DeviceLostMessage`/`DeviceRegainedMessage` under Send/Broadcast Messages — all documented). UX contract **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**: on active-provider loss during `Playing`, `GameStateMachine` auto-pauses within one frame, shows a "controller reconnected?" overlay using the last-known glyph set, and resumes on regain or explicit scheme change; backgrounded-app focus loss is handled separately by the documented default `Background Behavior = ResetAndDisableNonBackgroundDevices` (all latches reset on refocus — providers must therefore assume stale state after `OnApplicationFocus(true)`).

**The router.** One scene singleton `InputRouter` (from §4's system map) ticks providers in `Update`, merges UI passthrough, dispatches gameplay intents through the §4 event channels to `LevelManager`, and appends every intent to the `IntentLog` (fixed-size ring buffer; chunk-flushed into §6's ghost-replay save data). It performs `FindAction` lookups exactly once in `Awake` (documented: cache the result, string lookup is not for per-frame use) and holds no per-frame allocations.

### 7.3 `InputActionAsset` design

One asset: `Assets/_Project/Settings/Input/AOB_InputActions.inputactions`, assigned as the **project-wide action asset** (Project Settings → Input System Package → Input Actions; preloaded and enabled by default — documented). Single-player code reads via `InputSystem.actions`; per-player code reads `playerInput.actions` — never `InputSystem.actions` — because each `PlayerInput` holds its own device-filtered copy and bypassing it breaks auto device assignment (documented).

**Update mode.** Project Settings → Input System Package offers `Process Events In Dynamic Update` (default) | `Process Events In Fixed Update` | `Process Events Manually` (+ `InputSystem.Update()`), plus internal `BeforeRender` (XR only) — documented. We keep **Dynamic Update** (the default): §6 runs physics in Fixed Update simulation mode at a 240 Hz fixed timestep (§6.3 Option A, chosen; Script + manual accumulator is the serialized build-config fallback), so `FixedUpdate` IS our simulation driver — but at 240 Hz it fires ~4× per render frame, and `Process Events In Fixed Update` would tie input-event delivery to that cadence for no benefit; Dynamic Update processes each frame's events exactly once, which is what the latch-and-consume layer (§7.2) is built around — providers latch intents during the render update (producer side) and the simulation consumes and clears them at its tick (§6.3 determinism rule 2) — so event-to-step assignment never has to be re-derived against the fixed loop, and Manual mode would force us to own ordering against the player loop for no benefit. The latch-and-consume layer (§7.2) is the buffer between event-time and simulation-time; the unity-game-dev-expert skill's rule "buffer inputs in Update, consume in FixedUpdate" generalizes here to "latch at event time, consume at sim tick." Consequences: worst-case input-to-simulation latency = one render frame + one substep (≈16.7 ms + 4.2 ms at 60 Hz/240 Hz; budget table in §14), and the intent log's frame+time stamps make replay ordering deterministic even across variable frame rates (§6 determinism discipline).

**Control schemes** (per-asset, named, with a required device-type list — a scheme with zero device types never activates; documented): `KeyboardMouse` (Keyboard, Mouse), `Gamepad` (Gamepad), `Touch` (Touchscreen). Because on-screen controls synthesize a Gamepad (documented, §7.4.3), the `Gamepad` scheme also serves touch gameplay — the `Touch` scheme exists for UI Point/Click (driven natively by the Touchscreen pointer) and direct-drag gestures, so gameplay bindings never fork per platform.

#### Gameplay map

Action types follow the documented semantics: `Value` for continuous (phase + conflict resolution), `Button` for discrete, `PassThrough` where multiple devices must co-exist without conflict resolution. All pads share the `<Gamepad>/*` logical paths because recognized gamepads keep a consistent layout across platforms (documented; south = bottom face button everywhere); the glyph column shows what the *player* sees.

| Action | Type / interaction | Keyboard + mouse | Gamepad (Xbox · DS · Switch Pro share path) | Glyph (Xbox · PS · Switch) | Touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `MoveCursor` | Value/Vector2, `StickDeadzone(0.07,0.85)` **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (values) | — (absolute pointer, §7.4.1) | `<Gamepad>/leftStick` | L-stick · L-stick · L-stick | direct drag (§7.4.3); optional `OnScreenStick` → `<Gamepad>/leftStick` |
| `CursorFine` | Value/Vector2, same processors | — | `<Gamepad>/rightStick` | R-stick ×3 | — |
| `RotateCW` | Button, `Press(pressPoint=0.5, behavior=PressOnly)` | `<Keyboard>/e`; `<Mouse>/rightButton` | `<Gamepad>/buttonEast`; `<Gamepad>/dpad/right`; `<Gamepad>/rightShoulder` | B · ◯ · B | `OnScreenButton` → `<Gamepad>/buttonEast` |
| `RotateCCW` | Button, `Press` | `<Keyboard>/q` | `<Gamepad>/buttonWest`; `<Gamepad>/dpad/left`; `<Gamepad>/leftShoulder` | X · □ · X | `OnScreenButton` → `<Gamepad>/buttonWest` |
| `RotateWheel` | Value/float, `Scale(factor=90)` **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** | `<Mouse>/scroll/y` (±1 notch = ±45°) | — | — | — |
| `RotateTo` | PassThrough/Vector2 | `<Keyboard>/1` … `<Keyboard>/8` (8 orientations, §3 45° model) | `OneModifierComposite`: Modifier `<Gamepad>/rightTrigger` + `Vector2Composite(digital)` of `<Gamepad>/dpad/up|down|left|right` (diagonals = 45° multiples) | RT+D-pad ×3 | radial on-screen pad **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** |
| `DropOrRelease` | Button, `Press` | `<Mouse>/leftButton`; `<Keyboard>/space` | `<Gamepad>/buttonSouth` | A · ✕ · B | tap-on-piece (direct) + `OnScreenButton` → `<Gamepad>/buttonSouth` |
| `Pause` | Button, `Press` | `<Keyboard>/escape` | `<Gamepad>/startButton` | Menu · Options · + | on-screen pause button |
| `RecenterPointer` | Button, `Press` | `<Keyboard>/r` | `<Gamepad>/leftStickButton` | L3 ×3 | on-screen (motion scheme only) |

The pad mapping is deliberately the Wii grammar translated to modern layouts — face-south interacts (Wii A), face-east rotates (Wii B), D-pad L/R rotate (documented Wii inputs) — with shoulders as ergonomic duplicates. **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (mapping choice; the Wii inputs themselves are documented per §7.1).

Documented building blocks used above: `Press` interaction (`pressPoint`, `behavior` = PressOnly | ReleaseOnly | PressAndRelease; defaults pull `defaultButtonPressPoint` 0.5); `StickDeadzone` processor (below min → (0,0), above max → normalized to 1; parameterizable min/max; defaults 0.125/0.925 — we narrow the cursor deadzone for precision but leave UI navigation at defaults); `OneModifierComposite` ("Add Binding With One Modifier"; sub-bindings Binding + Modifier); `Vector2Composite` ("Add Up/Down/Left/Right Composite"; mode Digital | Analog | DontNormalize); `Scale` processor (factor). Full documented inventories we draw from: 13 processors (`Clamp`, `Invert`, `InvertVector2/3`, `Normalize`, `NormalizeVector2/3`, `Scale`, `ScaleVector2/3`, `AxisDeadzone`, `StickDeadzone`), 5 interactions (`Press`, `Hold`, `Tap`, `SlowTap`, `MultiTap` with `tapCount` default 2), 5 composite types (Axis, Vector2, Vector3, OneModifier, TwoModifiers).

#### UI map

Uses the exact default UI action set and names required by `InputSystemUIInputModule` (documented: move must be PassThrough/Vector2, submit/cancel Button):

| Action | Type | Bindings |
|---|---|---|
| `Navigate` | PassThrough/Vector2 | `<Gamepad>/dpad`; `<Gamepad>/leftStick`; `<Keyboard>/arrowKeys`; WASD `Vector2Composite` |
| `Submit` | Button | `<Gamepad>/buttonSouth`; `<Keyboard>/enter` |
| `Cancel` | Button | `<Gamepad>/buttonEast`; `<Keyboard>/escape` |
| `Point` | PassThrough/Vector2 | `<Mouse>/position`; `<Pen>/position`; `<Touchscreen>/touch*/position` |
| `Click` | PassThrough/Button | `<Mouse>/leftButton`; `<Pen>/tip`; `<Touchscreen>/touch*/press` |
| `RightClick` / `MiddleClick` | PassThrough/Button | `<Mouse>/rightButton` / `<Mouse>/middleButton` |
| `ScrollWheel` | PassThrough/Vector2 | `<Mouse>/scroll` |
| `Tracked Device Position` / `Orientation` | PassThrough | unbound (no XR in v1, §2 non-goals) |

#### Menus map

Menu-only extras that should not exist during play (avoid accidental shoulder-press tab flips in Tower Tumble turns):

| Action | Type | Bindings | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TabLeft` / `TabRight` | Button | `<Gamepad>/leftShoulder` / `<Gamepad>/rightShoulder` | world/level-select paging (§5) |
| `Back` | Button | `<Gamepad>/buttonEast`; `<Keyboard>/escape` | duplicate of Cancel for non-EventSystem screens |
| `SliderAdjust` | Value/Vector2, `StickDeadzone` (defaults) | `<Gamepad>/leftStick`; `<Keyboard>/arrowKeys` | settings sliders (module navigation handles focus; this drives value drag) |

**Supported Devices restriction.** Project Settings → Input System Package → Supported Devices is populated with Gamepad, Keyboard, Mouse, Touchscreen, Pen, AttitudeSensor, Gyroscope, Accelerometer — documented to restrict device layouts and shrink builds (mobile size hygiene, §18).

**Device-class coverage and quirks** (all documented; QA matrix inputs for §14):

| Unity device class | Appears on | Quirk that affects us |
|---|---|---|
| `XInputController` | Windows/UWP | Xbox One/360-compatible; trigger rumble motors only on UWP/Xbox |
| `XboxGamepadMacOSNative` / `XboxGamepadMacOS` | macOS 11+ USB & BT / legacy 360Controller driver | native class is our macOS target |
| `DualShock4GamepadHID` | Win/mac/UWP/Linux | one IOCTL at a time — combine rumble+lightbar via `SetMotorSpeedsAndLightBarColor(low, high, color)`; USB wireless adaptor unsupported |
| `DualSenseGamepadHID` | Win/mac; Linux from Unity 6000.4+ (needs hidraw udev rules for 054c:0ce6 / 054c:0df2) | no rumble/lightbar over Bluetooth; adaptive triggers **not exposed** by the public package (HID output report carries only the two motor bytes — source-verified in `DualShockGamepadHID.cs`) |
| `DualShock3GamepadHID` | macOS only, no rumble | edge case; acceptable |
| `SwitchProControllerHID` | desktop, **Bluetooth only — wired USB does not work** (proprietary HID protocol) | QA note for Switch-pad users on PC |
| `XboxOneGampadiOS` / `DualShock4GampadiOS` | iOS 13+ BT | the "Gampad" spelling is real in the API |
| Generic HID pads | all desktop | surface as **Joystick**, not Gamepad → fall back to the rebinding screen + on-screen warning **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** |
| Pen | Win/UWP/Android/iOS | `<Pen>/tip`, `<Pen>/position`; treated as a pointer by `MousePointerInputProvider` for free tablet parity |
| Sensors | **Android/iOS/Web only — not desktop OSes** | gates `MotionPointerInputProvider` (§7.4.4) |

Documented hard limits accepted as-is: no desktop Joy-Con support; PS4/PS5 controller gyro/accelerometer unsupported off-console ("Unity doesn't support the gyro or accelerometer on PS4/PS5 controllers on platforms other than the PlayStation consoles" — supported-devices reference); mouse is single-only and cannot identify its current display.

### 7.4 Provider implementations

#### 7.4.1 `MousePointerInputProvider` — pointer-follow (Wii heritage)

The Wii original was pointer-driven: IR aiming with A to pick up/drop and B/D-pad to rotate (§7.1). The mouse (and pen) reproduces this grammar exactly: absolute screen position is the cursor; left-click is the A button; right-click is the B button.

```csharp
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.InputSystem;

namespace AoB.Input
{
    /// <summary>Pointer-follow provider: cursor = pointer position (mouse/pen),
    /// reproducing the Wii IR-pointer grammar (§7.1).</summary>
    public sealed class MousePointerInputProvider : IPieceInputProvider
    {
        #region Fields

        private readonly InputAction _point;
        private readonly InputAction _click;
        private readonly InputAction _rotateCw;
        private readonly InputAction _rotateCcw;
        private readonly InputAction _rotateWheel;
        private readonly InputAction _pause;

        private Vector2 _previousPosition;
        private int _rotateCwLatch;
        private int _rotateCcwLatch;
        private bool _dropLatch;
        private bool _pauseLatch;
        private UiNavigationFrame _uiFrame;

        #endregion

        #region Construction

        public MousePointerInputProvider(InputActionAsset actions)
        {
            // Cache every action once (documented: never per-frame FindAction).
            InputActionMap gameplay = actions.FindActionMap("Gameplay");
            _point = gameplay["MoveCursor"];
            _click = gameplay["DropOrRelease"];
            _rotateCw = gameplay["RotateCW"];
            _rotateCcw = gameplay["RotateCCW"];
            _rotateWheel = gameplay["RotateWheel"];
            _pause = gameplay["Pause"];
        }

        #endregion

        #region IPieceInputProvider

        public string ProviderId => "mouse";
        public InputScheme Scheme => InputScheme.KeyboardMouse;
        public int PlayerIndex { get; private set; }
        public bool IsConnected => Mouse.current != null || Pen.current != null;
        public Vector2 CursorPosition => _point.ReadValue<Vector2>();
        public Vector2 MoveDelta => CursorPosition - _previousPosition;

        public event System.Action<IPieceInputProvider> ConnectionChanged;

        public int ConsumeRotateCW() { int v = _rotateCwLatch; _rotateCwLatch = 0; return v; }
        public int ConsumeRotateCCW() { int v = _rotateCcwLatch; _rotateCcwLatch = 0; return v; }
        public bool ConsumeRotateTo(out float angleDegrees) { angleDegrees = 0f; return false; }
        public bool ConsumeDropOrRelease() { bool v = _dropLatch; _dropLatch = false; return v; }
        public bool ConsumePause() { bool v = _pauseLatch; _pauseLatch = false; return v; }
        public void PassThroughUiNavigation(ref UiNavigationFrame navigation)
        {
            navigation.Move += _uiFrame.Move;
            navigation.Submit |= _uiFrame.Submit;
            navigation.Cancel |= _uiFrame.Cancel;
        }

        public void SetPlayerIndex(int playerIndex) => PlayerIndex = playerIndex;

        public void Tick(in ProviderTickContext context)
        {
            // Latch edge-triggered buttons via WasPressedThisFrame (documented
            // Button-action polling API); accumulate wheel notches into steps.
            if (_rotateCw.WasPressedThisFrame()) { _rotateCwLatch++; }
            if (_rotateCcw.WasPressedThisFrame()) { _rotateCcwLatch++; }
            float wheel = _rotateWheel.WasPerformedThisFrame()
                ? Mathf.Sign(_rotateWheel.ReadValue<float>()) : 0f;
            if (wheel > 0f) { _rotateCwLatch++; } else if (wheel < 0f) { _rotateCcwLatch++; }
            if (_click.WasPressedThisFrame()) { _dropLatch = true; }
            if (_pause.WasPressedThisFrame()) { _pauseLatch = true; }
            _previousPosition = CursorPosition;
        }

        public void ResetLatches()
        {
            _rotateCwLatch = 0; _rotateCcwLatch = 0; _dropLatch = false;
            _pauseLatch = false; _uiFrame = default;
        }

        #endregion
    }
}
```

Note the wheel mapping: one notch = one 45° step, direction by sign **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**. `WasPressedThisFrame()` / `ReadValue<T>()` on Button/Value actions are the documented polling APIs.

#### 7.4.2 `GamepadInputProvider` — virtual cursor

Gamepads have no absolute pointer, so this provider owns a **virtual cursor**: stick deflection drives cursor velocity through an exponential response curve (math in §7.8), the cursor clamps to the play-field viewport, and buttons map per the §7.3 table. The virtual cursor — rather than stick-relative piece movement — is what makes gamepad, mouse, touch, and motion cursors interchangeable downstream (everything above the provider is "a cursor in screen space").

```csharp
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.InputSystem;

namespace AoB.Input
{
    /// <summary>Gamepad provider driving a clamped virtual cursor with an
    /// exponential response curve; haptics routed through HapticsDirector (§13.4).</summary>
    public sealed class GamepadInputProvider : IPieceInputProvider
    {
        #region Serialized-equivalent Config (const where fixed)

        private const float CursorMaxSpeedPxPerSec = 1500f; // [ORIGINAL DESIGN] at 1080p reference
        private const float CursorExponent = 1.6f;          // [ORIGINAL DESIGN]
        private const float CursorDeadzoneMin = 0.07f;      // matches StickDeadzone binding
        private const float CursorDeadzoneMax = 0.85f;

        #endregion

        #region Fields

        private readonly InputAction _move;
        private readonly InputAction _fine;
        private readonly InputAction _rotateCw;
        private readonly InputAction _rotateCcw;
        private readonly InputAction _rotateTo;
        private readonly InputAction _drop;
        private readonly InputAction _pause;
        private Vector2 _cursorPosition;
        private int _rotateCwLatch;
        private int _rotateCcwLatch;
        private float _rotateToAngle;
        private bool _rotateToValid;
        private bool _dropLatch;
        private bool _pauseLatch;

        #endregion

        #region Properties / Lifecycle (IPieceInputProvider)

        public string ProviderId => "gamepad";
        public InputScheme Scheme => InputScheme.Gamepad;
        public int PlayerIndex { get; private set; }
        public bool IsConnected => Gamepad.current != null;
        public Vector2 CursorPosition => _cursorPosition;
        public Vector2 MoveDelta { get; private set; }

        public event System.Action<IPieceInputProvider> ConnectionChanged;

        public void Tick(in ProviderTickContext context)
        {
            Vector2 stick = _move.ReadValue<Vector2>() + _fine.ReadValue<Vector2>() * 0.5f;
            _cursorPosition += EvaluateCursorVelocity(stick) * context.UnscaledDeltaTime;
            _cursorPosition = ClampToViewport(_cursorPosition); // TV-safe margins from §9
            if (_rotateCw.WasPressedThisFrame()) { _rotateCwLatch++; }
            if (_rotateCcw.WasPressedThisFrame()) { _rotateCcwLatch++; }
            if (_rotateTo.WasPerformedThisFrame())
            {
                Vector2 dir = _rotateTo.ReadValue<Vector2>();
                if (dir.sqrMagnitude > 0.25f)
                {
                    _rotateToAngle = Mathf.Atan2(dir.y, dir.x) * Mathf.Rad2Deg;
                    _rotateToValid = true;
                }
            }
            if (_drop.WasPressedThisFrame()) { _dropLatch = true; }
            if (_pause.WasPressedThisFrame()) { _pauseLatch = true; }
        }

        // Consume* accessors mirror §7.4.1 (identical latch pattern). …
        // RotateTo maps the 8-way dpad direction to an absolute angle in the
        // piece's allowed-orientation set from PieceDefinition (§5). …

        #endregion

        #region Private Methods

        /// <summary>Expo curve: v(d) = Vmax · d^γ on the deadzone-rescaled
        /// magnitude d (formula + rationale in §7.8).</summary>
        private static Vector2 EvaluateCursorVelocity(Vector2 stick)
        {
            float magnitude = stick.magnitude;
            if (magnitude < CursorDeadzoneMin) { return Vector2.zero; }
            float d = Mathf.Clamp01((magnitude - CursorDeadzoneMin) /
                                    (CursorDeadzoneMax - CursorDeadzoneMin));
            return stick / magnitude * (CursorMaxSpeedPxPerSec * Mathf.Pow(d, CursorExponent));
        }

        private static Vector2 ClampToViewport(Vector2 position)
        {
            // …clamp against Camera pixel rect + title-safe inset…
            return position;
        }

        #endregion
    }
}
```

#### 7.4.3 `TouchDragInputProvider` — drag, tap, on-screen controls

The 3DS original is our touch grammar: stylus drag to place, buttons to pick up/rotate/drop (§7.1). On phones the pieces are directly draggable; rotation uses on-screen buttons that synthesize the *same* `<Gamepad>` bindings — the documented on-screen-control trick that removes any need for a parallel touch action map for gameplay.

Implementation rules from the documentation: enable `EnhancedTouchSupport.Enable()` once (Awake); poll `Touch.activeTouches` / `Touch.activeFingers` (allocation-free); **never** poll `Touchscreen` state directly in Update/FixedUpdate — "your application misses changes in touch state". The `Touch` struct supplies everything the gesture splitter needs: `phase` (Began/Moved/Stationary/Ended/Canceled), `screenPosition`, `startScreenPosition`, `delta`, `startTime`, `time`, `tapCount`, `isTap` (built-in tap detection), `pressure`, `radius`, `history`.

```csharp
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.InputSystem;
using UnityEngine.InputSystem.EnhancedTouch;

namespace AoB.Input
{
    /// <summary>Touch provider: drag the carried piece directly; tap a piece to
    /// pick up/drop; on-screen buttons synthesize the Gamepad rotate bindings.</summary>
    public sealed class TouchDragInputProvider : IPieceInputProvider
    {
        private const float DragStartThresholdPx = 6f;   // [ORIGINAL DESIGN]
        private const float TapMaxDurationSec = 0.2f;    // = documented default tapTime

        private int _dragFingerId = -1;
        private Vector2 _dragAnchorScreen;
        private Vector3 _dragAnchorWorld;
        private bool _dropLatch;
        private int _rotateCwLatch;
        private int _rotateCcwLatch;
        private readonly Camera _gameplayCamera; // §6 camera; screen→world via ray

        public string ProviderId => "touch";
        public InputScheme Scheme => InputScheme.Touch;
        public int PlayerIndex { get; private set; }
        public bool IsConnected => Touchscreen.current != null;
        public Vector2 CursorPosition { get; private set; }
        public Vector2 MoveDelta { get; private set; }

        public void Tick(in ProviderTickContext context)
        {
            MoveDelta = Vector2.zero;
            foreach (Touch touch in Touch.activeTouches) // struct enumerator, zero GC
            {
                if (_dragFingerId == -1 && touch.phase == TouchPhase.Began &&
                    PieceHitTest(touch.screenPosition))
                {
                    _dragFingerId = touch.touchId;
                    _dragAnchorScreen = touch.screenPosition;
                    // anchor world point captured via _gameplayCamera ray (§6). …
                    continue;
                }
                if (touch.touchId != _dragFingerId) { continue; }

                Vector2 total = touch.screenPosition - _dragAnchorScreen;
                switch (touch.phase)
                {
                    case TouchPhase.Moved:
                    case TouchPhase.Stationary:
                        if (total.magnitude >= DragStartThresholdPx)
                        {
                            CursorPosition = touch.screenPosition;
                            MoveDelta = touch.delta; // consumed by carry controller (§3)
                        }
                        break;
                    case TouchPhase.Ended:
                        // Tap = short + immobile (documented isTap/tapCount also usable).
                        if (touch.time - touch.startTime <= TapMaxDurationSec &&
                            total.magnitude < DragStartThresholdPx)
                        {
                            _dropLatch = true; // tap-on-piece = Wii A semantics
                        }
                        _dragFingerId = -1;
                        break;
                    case TouchPhase.Canceled:
                        _dragFingerId = -1;
                        break;
                }
            }
            // Rotate latches come from OnScreenButton controls feeding
            // <Gamepad>/buttonEast | buttonWest into the shared Gameplay map. …
        }

        // Consume* accessors: identical latch pattern to §7.4.1. …
        private static bool PieceHitTest(Vector2 screenPosition) { /* … */ return false; }
        public void ResetLatches() { /* … */ }
        public void SetPlayerIndex(int playerIndex) => PlayerIndex = playerIndex;
        public event System.Action<IPieceInputProvider> ConnectionChanged;
        public int ConsumeRotateCW() { int v = _rotateCwLatch; _rotateCwLatch = 0; return v; }
        public int ConsumeRotateCCW() { int v = _rotateCcwLatch; _rotateCcwLatch = 0; return v; }
        public bool ConsumeRotateTo(out float a) { a = 0f; return false; }
        public bool ConsumeDropOrRelease() { bool v = _dropLatch; _dropLatch = false; return v; }
        public bool ConsumePause() { return false; } // on-screen pause button handled by UI map
        public void PassThroughUiNavigation(ref UiNavigationFrame n) { /* touch UI is pointer-native */ }
    }
}
```

**On-screen controls** (uGUI, document-grounded): `OnScreenButton` on a uGUI Button writes 1/0 to a `ButtonControl` at `controlPath` (e.g. `<Gamepad>/buttonEast`); `OnScreenStick` on a UI Image drives a `Vector2Control` (e.g. `<Gamepad>/leftStick`) with `Movement Range` (default 50 = a ±25 px drag box). Enable **Use Isolated Input Actions** on sticks/buttons to stop the paired-device switching jitter (defaults: Pointer Down `<Mouse>/leftButton`, `<Pen>/tip`, `<Touchscreen>/touch*/press`, `<XRController>/trigger`; Pointer Move `<Mouse>/position`, `<Pen>/position`, `<Touchscreen>/touch*/position`). Custom virtual controls subclass `OnScreenControl`, call `SendValueToControl(...)`, expose `controlPathInternal` with `[InputControl(layout = "...")]`. Our layout **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**: bottom-right cluster (rotate CW/CCW buttons sized ≥ 96 dp at 1080p reference), bottom-left rotate-alt cluster omitted in favor of tap-zones for one-hand play (accessibility, §14), top-right pause; safe-area-driven anchoring via `Screen.safeArea` (bottom-left origin, §18). Because the synthesized device is a Gamepad, the exact desktop bindings and rebinding system serve mobile unchanged.

#### 7.4.4 `MotionPointerInputProvider` — gyro pointer (Switch Patch 1.1 heritage)

Reproduces what Shin'en added to the Switch edition post-launch (§7.9) on the platforms where Unity exposes sensors: **Android, iOS, Web only — sensors do not exist on desktop OSes** (documented), and gamepad gyro off-console is unavailable (§7.3). The provider reads `<AttitudeSensor>/attitude` (orientation quaternion; control "attitude") as the pointer source, with `<Gyroscope>/angularVelocity` available for derivative smoothing; **Compensate Orientation** stays enabled so values rotate with screen orientation (documented mapping: Portrait unchanged, PortraitUpsideDown +180°, LandscapeLeft +90°, LandscapeRight +270°).

```csharp
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.InputSystem;

namespace AoB.Input
{
    /// <summary>Gyro pointer: yaw/pitch deltas of the AttitudeSensor quaternion
    /// drive a virtual cursor; recenter zeroes the reference frame.</summary>
    public sealed class MotionPointerInputProvider : IPieceInputProvider
    {
        private const float YawGainPxPerRad = 900f;    // [ORIGINAL DESIGN]
        private const float PitchGainPxPerRad = 700f;  // [ORIGINAL DESIGN]
        private const float MaxTiltDeg = 35f;          // comfort clamp

        private Quaternion _recenterReference = Quaternion.identity;
        private bool _hasReference;
        private Quaternion _previousAttitude;
        private Vector2 _cursorPosition;
        private Vector2 _moveDelta;
        // Button latches fed from the Gameplay map (dpad rotate, south drop) —
        // same latch pattern as §7.4.2; motion replaces ONLY the cursor source.

        public string ProviderId => "motion";
        public InputScheme Scheme => InputScheme.Gamepad; // pads carry the buttons
        public int PlayerIndex { get; private set; }
        public bool IsConnected => AttitudeSensor.current != null;
        public Vector2 CursorPosition => _cursorPosition;
        public Vector2 MoveDelta => _moveDelta;

        public void Tick(in ProviderTickContext context)
        {
            if (!IsConnected) { return; }
            Quaternion attitude = AttitudeSensor.current.attitude.ReadValue();
            if (!_hasReference) { _recenterReference = Quaternion.Inverse(attitude); _hasReference = true; }
            Quaternion relative = _recenterReference * attitude;
            Quaternion delta = relative * Quaternion.Inverse(_previousAttitude);
            delta.ToAngleAxis(out float deltaAngleDeg, out Vector3 axis);
            float yawDeg = Mathf.Clamp(deltaAngleDeg * axis.y, -MaxTiltDeg, MaxTiltDeg);
            float pitchDeg = Mathf.Clamp(deltaAngleDeg * axis.x, -MaxTiltDeg, MaxTiltDeg);
            // Map yaw→x, pitch→y; scale by gains and dt; clamp to viewport; …
            _cursorPosition += new Vector2(-yawDeg, pitchDeg) * Mathf.Deg2Rad
                             * new Vector2(YawGainPxPerRad, PitchGainPxPerRad) * context.UnscaledDeltaTime;
            _previousAttitude = relative;
        }

        /// <summary>Recenter (RecenterPointer action, §7.3): current attitude
        /// becomes screen-center. Also auto-recenters after 2 s idle.</summary>
        public void Recenter()
        {
            if (!IsConnected) { return; }
            _recenterReference = Quaternion.Inverse(AttitudeSensor.current.attitude.ReadValue());
            _hasReference = true;
        }

        // Consume* accessors: latch pattern as above; RotateTo is unused here. …
        public void ResetLatches() { /* … */ }
        public void SetPlayerIndex(int playerIndex) => PlayerIndex = playerIndex;
        public event System.Action<IPieceInputProvider> ConnectionChanged;
        public int ConsumeRotateCW() { return 0; }
        public int ConsumeRotateCCW() { return 0; }
        public bool ConsumeRotateTo(out float a) { a = 0f; return false; }
        public bool ConsumeDropOrRelease() { return false; }
        public bool ConsumePause() { return false; }
        public void PassThroughUiNavigation(ref UiNavigationFrame n) { }
    }
}
```

On a hypothetical future Switch port, the same provider interface would be fed by Joy-Con gyro through the console-specific input package (console input packages are SDK-gated and unverifiable from public sources — documented gap); nothing above the provider changes. <!-- TODO-VERIFY: Nintendo console input package sensor surface (Joy-Con gyro/accel exposure and units) — NDA-gated; verify if a Switch target is ever green-lit (§13, §21). -->

#### 7.4.5 Haptics

API (documented): `Gamepad.SetMotorSpeeds(lowFrequency, highFrequency)` — left motor = low frequency, right = high, 0..1 floats; per-device `PauseHaptics`/`ResumeHaptics`/`ResetHaptics` via `IHaptics`; global `InputSystem.PauseHaptics()` / `ResumeHaptics()` / `ResetHaptics()`. Haptic output is owned by the `HapticsDirector` MonoBehaviour defined in §13.4 and listed in §4's system map; it maps game events to pulses, and all calls are no-op-guarded.

The event-to-envelope map is defined once, in §13.4's canonical haptic event map — piece settle, stability lights, water-contact fail (deliberately distinct from stack collapse), Tower Tumble turn hand-off, and the rest — and is intentionally not duplicated here. Envelope values and durations are **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (§13.4); API and gates documented. Gates that matter to us: Android rumble **requires Unity 6000.6+** (satisfied by our 6.6 baseline; Android 12+ gives per-motor BT control, ≤11 collapses to single motor = max(L,R), auto-stops ~10 s after the last call — so countdown pulses must re-issue, not ride one long call); **iOS/tvOS/visionOS rumble requires Unity 6000.7+, so iOS gets no rumble on our 6.6 baseline** (risk entry in §21); no rumble on Web; DS4/DualSense rumble/lightbar unsupported over Bluetooth; Xbox trigger motors only on UWP/Xbox; consoles need their console-specific input packages. `InputSystem.PauseHaptics()` is called on every pause-menu open (mirrors the §6 audio snapshot ducking).

### 7.5 uGUI navigation wiring

Our UI stack is uGUI + TextMeshPro (§4/§9), which **requires** an `EventSystem` with `InputSystemUIInputModule` (the module replaces `StandaloneInputModule`; the Inspector offers one-click replacement when both exist — documented). UI Toolkit screens, if any tooling UI leaks into runtime, need no module on 2023.2+ (project-wide actions drive them) — noted for §5 tooling only. Configuration:

| Setting | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Actions Asset | `AOB_InputActions` (UI map) | one shared asset; with PlayerInput the module takes the player's device-filtered copy (documented) |
| Pointer Behavior | `Single Mouse or Pen But Multi Touch And Track` (default) | documented recommendation for mouse+mobile: mouse/pen unify; each touch is its own pointer (own `pointerId` = deviceId, or deviceId+touchId for touch, read via `ExtendedPointerEventData.touchId`) |
| Deselect on Background Click | off | keeps gamepad selection when the mouse clicks dead space |
| Move Repeat Delay / Move Repeat Rate | 0.18 s / 0.09 s **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** | dpad-held list scrolling in level select; module rate is frame-capped (documented) |
| Scroll Delta Per Tick | default | no custom wheel scaling |
| Cursor Lock Behavior | `Outside Screen` | cursor never locks in this game |

**Gamepad focus management [ORIGINAL DESIGN]:** every menu prefab sets `EventSystem.firstSelectedGameObject` on open (a well-known "entry focus" object per screen); a per-screen `MenuFocusKeeper` caches the last-selected selectable and restores it when the screen re-opens (turn transitions in Tower Tumble, pause/unpause). Navigation semantics are the module's: one `move` vector + one `submit`/`cancel` per frame processed against the current selection, `submit` fires `ISubmitHandler`, `cancel` fires `ICancelHandler`, `move` fires `IMoveHandler.OnMove` with repeat delay/rate (documented).

**Mouse + pad coexistence rules [ORIGINAL DESIGN]:** (1) pointer and navigation coexist by design in the module — pointer events are per-device pointers, navigation acts on selection; (2) our rule adds idleness: mouse visuals (system cursor + hover highlights) hide after 2 s without `<Mouse>/delta` above 1 px, so pad players never see a stale hover ring; (3) binding Left Click without Point is never done (documented: it would route the click into another pointer's position); (4) selecting with the pad then clicking with the mouse is allowed — last interaction wins, both write through the same selection.

**On-screen controls for touch** are §7.4.3's `OnScreenButton`/`OnScreenStick` set, parented under the HUD canvas with safe-area anchoring; they feed the Gameplay map, not the UI map — touch UI interaction is pointer-native (`Point`/`Click` driven by `<Touchscreen>/touch*`).

### 7.6 Rebinding flow and the glyph system

**Interactive rebinding flow [ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (pipeline design; every API call in it is documented):

1. Settings → Controls lists every rebindable Gameplay action with its current binding per scheme (from `action.GetBindingDisplayString()`).
2. Pressing "Rebind" starts `action.PerformInteractiveRebinding()` and configures the returned `InputActionRebindingExtensions.RebindingOperation`: `.WithTargetBinding(bindingIndex)` (index resolved per scheme via `action.GetBindingIndex(InputBinding.MaskByGroup("Gamepad"))`), `.WithControlsExcluding("<Mouse>/position")`, `.WithControlsExcluding("<Mouse>/delta")` (keep pure-pointer axes out), `.WithCancelingThrough("<Keyboard>/escape")`, optionally `.WithExpectedControlType()`; 1.15+ `.WithSuppressedActionPropagation()` stops actions firing mid-rebind while allowing state updates.
3. `.OnComplete` / `.OnCancel` callbacks **must `Dispose()` the operation in both paths** — it holds unmanaged memory (documented leak warning).
4. Persist with `SaveBindingOverridesAsJson()` — routed into our §6 SaveSystem file (ISaveable block `inputOverrides`) rather than PlayerPrefs, so overrides ride the §14 cloud-save sync; on boot, `LoadBindingOverridesFromJson(json)` (second arg `removeExistingOverrides` defaults true).
5. "Reset to default" clears overrides (`RestoreBindingOverrides` family); collision with an existing binding offers swap (the official "Rebinding UI" sample ships `RebindActionUI.SwapBinding` since 1.16 and `InputActionLabel` since 1.15 — used as the reference implementation; note samples require URP since 1.20, and we are URP).

**Glyph system.** Four prompt sets — **Xbox, PlayStation, Switch, Keyboard/Mouse** — as sprite atlases in an Addressables group `ui-prompts` (asset strategy: one 1024² atlas per scheme, TMP sprite assets for inline text, ~40 glyphs per set covering every bound control plus mouse/keys). Runtime classification and lookup:

```csharp
using System;
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.InputSystem;

namespace AoB.Input
{
    /// <summary>Resolves per-scheme button-glyph sprites for prompts; swaps the
    /// active set when the last-used device class changes.</summary>
    public sealed class PromptGlyphService
    {
        public event Action<PromptScheme> SchemeChanged;
        public PromptScheme CurrentScheme { get; private set; } = PromptScheme.KeyboardMouse;

        public void Initialize()
        {
            <!-- TODO-VERIFY: API name not in research notes; confirm InputSystem.onDeviceChange against current docs -->
            InputSystem.onDeviceChange += HandleDeviceChange;
            <!-- TODO-VERIFY: API name not in research notes; confirm InputSystem.GetLastUsedDevice() against current docs -->
            Classify(InputSystem.GetLastUsedDevice()); // provider of the latest input
        }

        private void HandleDeviceChange(InputDevice device, InputDeviceChange change)
        {
            if ((change & (InputDeviceChange.Added | InputDeviceChange.Removed)) == 0) { return; }
            <!-- TODO-VERIFY: API name not in research notes; confirm InputSystem.GetLastUsedDevice() against current docs -->
            Classify(InputSystem.GetLastUsedDevice());
        }

        private void Classify(InputDevice device)
        {
            if (device == null) { return; }
            string layout = device.layout;
            PromptScheme scheme =
                InputSystem.IsFirstLayoutBasedOnSecond(layout, "DualShockGamepad") ||
                InputSystem.IsFirstLayoutBasedOnSecond(layout, "DualSenseGamepadHID")
                    ? PromptScheme.PlayStation
                    : InputSystem.IsFirstLayoutBasedOnSecond(layout, "SwitchProControllerHID")
                        ? PromptScheme.Switch
                        : InputSystem.IsFirstLayoutBasedOnSecond(layout, "Gamepad")
                            ? PromptScheme.Xbox
                            : PromptScheme.KeyboardMouse;
            if (scheme == CurrentScheme) { return; }
            CurrentScheme = scheme;
            SchemeChanged?.Invoke(scheme); // HUD + menus re-resolve prompts
        }

        /// <summary>Resolve the glyph for an action's active-scheme binding.</summary>
        public bool TryGetGlyph(InputAction action, PromptScheme scheme, out Sprite glyph)
        {
            int index = action.GetBindingIndex(InputBinding.MaskByGroup(scheme == PromptScheme.KeyboardMouse
                ? "KeyboardMouse" : "Gamepad"));
            action.GetBindingDisplayString(index, out string deviceLayout, out string controlPath);
            // "Gamepad" family: switch on controlPath ("buttonSouth", "dpad/up", …);
            // keyboard: on the key path. Atlas lookup is a cached dictionary hit.
            // …
            glyph = null;
            return false;
        }
    }
}
```

This is the documented pattern: `GetBindingDisplayString(index, out deviceLayout, out controlPath)` for icon mapping, `InputSystem.IsFirstLayoutBasedOnSecond(deviceLayout, "Gamepad")` for layout-family tests, `InputSystem.GetLastUsedDevice()` as the activity signal (API name not in research notes; verify against current docs)<!-- TODO-VERIFY: API name not in research notes; confirm InputSystem.GetLastUsedDevice() against current docs -->; display strings regenerate dynamically (keyboard-layout switches change them — the docs warn) so text fallbacks re-render on `SchemeChanged`. Classification order matters: DS/Switch classes derive from Gamepad, so specific layouts test before the generic family. On Steam builds, Steam Input can override glyphs with the player's actual controller layout via the Steamworks glyph APIs (exact API names live on §19's unfetched child pages; §19 owns that integration). <!-- TODO-VERIFY: Steam Input glyph API call names + IGA action-file schema for the Steam config (deferred to §19; partner-docs child pages were not fetched in research). -->

### 7.7 Multiplayer input

Documented multiplayer surfaces we target (mode specs in §3/§11/§13): **Arcade co-op drop-in** (original Wii: 2nd player drops in with a second remote; Switch: 1–4 on one system), **Swift Stacker** 2-team race (split-screen in the original), **Tower Tumble** up to 4 alternating players. Wiring uses `PlayerInputManager` + `PlayerInput`:

| Property | Value | Note (documented behavior) |
|---|---|---|
| Player Prefab | `Prefabs/Players/PlayerInputRig` (one PlayerInput + cursor root + provider set) | must contain exactly one PlayerInput |
| Notification Behavior | `Invoke CSharp Events` (`onActionTriggered`, `onDeviceLost`, `onDeviceRegained`) | typed events, no SendMessage reflection |
| Join Behavior (Arcade co-op) | `Join Players When Button Is Pressed` | any Gameplay-map button on a paired device joins mid-level |
| Join Behavior (Swift Stacker / Tower Tumble) | `Join Players Manually` — lobby calls `JoinPlayer()` | explicit team/seat assignment before play |
| Joining Enabled By Default | co-op only | lobby toggles |
| Limit Number of Players / Max Player Count | 4 | matches Switch 1–4 single-system |
| Enable Split-Screen | off | Swift Stacker uses two play *fields* in one view (§3), not camera splits |

**Per-player cursors.** Each joined `PlayerInput` instantiates a `PlayerCursor` (colored outline + owner glyph badge, §9) bound to its provider; the `InputProviderRegistry` maps `playerInput.playerIndex` → provider, and the provider filters devices to `playerInput.devices` (the documented per-player device pairing; the low-level pairing API underneath is `InputUser`). `neverAutoSwitchControlSchemes = true` on every multiplayer PlayerInput so schemes stay per-seat.

**Split control semantics [ORIGINAL DESIGN]:** *Arcade co-op* — shared basin, shared piece queue; the `LevelManager` holds a carry mutex: only the player whose `DropOrRelease` picked up the current piece can move it; another player's `DropOrRelease` on the same frame is rejected and fed back as a "busy" wiggle + haptic blip. *Swift Stacker* — two `LevelManager` instances (one per team field), each routed only its team's provider index set; queue seeds identical per §3 determinism. *Tower Tumble* — all four players stay paired; a turn token in `GameStateMachine` routes intents from exactly one provider per turn; the hand-off pulse (§13.4) plus the acting player's cursor highlight signals whose provider is live. In every multiplayer scene, uGUI uses one `MultiplayerEventSystem` per player under separate `Player Root`s (documented component + scoping), each wired to that player's `InputSystemUIInputModule` copy of the shared asset.

### 7.8 Latency and feel

**Processing point.** Events process in Dynamic Update (§7.3); providers latch; the §6 simulation tick consumes. Discrete inputs (rotate/drop/pause) are latched the same frame they arrive and are guaranteed consumed on the next simulation tick — with 240 Hz substepping (§6) the input-to-sim hop is at most one render frame + 4.2 ms, and release-to-fall latency is dominated by the substep cadence, not input. Continuous inputs (cursor) are re-sampled at consumption time. This is the unity-game-dev-expert skill's input-lag rule applied: never process input in `FixedUpdate` against a `Update`-driven camera; buffer across the boundary instead.

**Deadzones, curves, and constants.** Documented defaults are the baseline; our deltas are choices:

| Knob | Documented default | Ours | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stick deadzone min/max (UI nav) | 0.125 / 0.925 | keep | doc default is fine for menus |
| Stick deadzone min/max (cursor) | 0.125 / 0.925 | **0.07 / 0.85** [ORIGINAL DESIGN] | earlier engagement + earlier full-speed for stack edges |
| Button press point | 0.5 | keep | doc default |
| Button release threshold | 0.75 | keep | doc default |
| Tap time (touch tap window) | 0.2 s | keep (= `TapMaxDurationSec` §7.4.3) | doc default matches feel |
| Tap radius | 5 | keep for tap-vs-swipe; drag threshold 6 px [ORIGINAL DESIGN] | slight hysteresis prevents tap-flick misreads |
| Hold time | 0.4 s | keep (unused in core loop) | doc default |
| Multi-tap delay / count | 0.75 s / 2 | keep (unused) | doc default |

**Cursor speed math (game-designer skill: show the formula).** With post-deadzone rescaled magnitude d ∈ [0,1] (the documented `StickDeadzone` rescale: below min → 0, above max → 1):

v(d) = V_max · d^γ, with V_max = 1500 px/s (1080p reference; scaled by the §9 Canvas Scaler reference resolution), γ = 1.6.

Examples: d = 0.25 → 0.25^1.6 ≈ 0.108 → 162 px/s (fine placement); d = 0.5 → 0.5^1.6 ≈ 0.330 → 495 px/s; d = 1.0 → 1500 px/s (cross-screen in ~1.3 s on a 1920-wide view). γ > 1 keeps micro-corrections slow while preserving full-speed escapes; γ = 2 (pure quadratic) felt sluggish in the feel-test criteria of §2. **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**

**Rotation feel.** Each 45° step plays a 70 ms snap animation on the carried piece (visual only — the physics body adopts the target orientation immediately on release, §3/§6); queued steps coalesce so a rapid double-press rotates 90° without a stutter. Button-to-step is edge-triggered (`Press` PressOnly), immune to the 0.75 release-threshold holdover. **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**

**Allocation discipline.** No `FindAction` after `Awake`; callbacks write into pre-allocated latches; `Touch.activeTouches` enumeration is allocation-free (documented); the intent log is a fixed ring buffer with chunked flush (§6); glyph lookups are cached dictionary hits after first resolution; `RebindingOperation` is disposed on every exit path (§7.6). Profiler markers (`ProfilerMarker` on router tick and provider tick) feed §14's profiling protocol from day one.

### 7.9 Case study: the Switch Patch 1.1 motion controls

**What happened [DOCUMENTED].** The Switch edition shipped 2018-10-04 with touch, Joy-Con (L/R, grip), and Pro Controller control; motion controls were *not* in the base game and arrived via official **Patch 1.1 on 13-Nov-2018** ("13-Nov-2018 Patch 1.1 adds Motion Controls!" — [Switch microsite news, archived](https://web.archive.org/web/20201015074209/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com/switch/), accessed 2026-09-24), corroborated by the live "Motion controls" tag on [Nintendo.com's store page](https://www.nintendo.com/store/products/art-of-balance-switch/) (accessed 2026-09-24). Detailed patch-note text beyond the headline was never located in research (gap logged in §21) — the exact in-game gesture grammar is unknown; our §7.4.4 mechanics are therefore **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**.

**What it proves about input architecture.** A control scheme strong enough to ship as a platform's headline post-launch feature was added 40 days (~six weeks) after release without touching the game's rules. That is only cheap if input is layered: device grammar → abstraction → game rules. Our §7.2 split replicates that layering deliberately.

**The concrete diff, had Shin'en used our stack [ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (extension recipe):
1. New file: `MotionPointerInputProvider.cs` (§7.4.4) — implements one interface; zero gameplay edits.
2. Asset edit: one new control-scheme row + the `RecenterPointer` action in `AOB_InputActions` (config, not code).
3. Settings: a "Pointer: Motion / Stick / Touch" option writing through the §6 SaveSystem; the InputProviderRegistry unlock flag for per-scheme activity switching.
4. Telemetry/QA: a new provider column in the §14 device matrix; replay determinism unaffected because intents, not devices, are logged.
5. No changes to: `LevelManager`, `StabilityMonitor`, `ScoreController`, the §3 loop states, rebinding UI (motion has no rebindable buttons beyond the existing pad set), or the glyph system (motion borrows the pad's button glyphs).

The reverse also holds: because `IPieceInputProvider` is the only seam, deleting or gating a scheme for a SKU (e.g. shipping Android without motion) is a registry/manifest decision, not a code fork — the property that lets one codebase serve Windows, macOS, Android, iOS, and Xbox from §2's platform table with input parity by construction.

## 8. Special Block Mechanics

This section specifies the runtime behaviour layer for every block type beyond the plain physics shape: the `IBlockBehaviour` component system, the shared stress/contact services behaviours consume, one full specification per behaviour (spec table, parameters, C# skeleton, physics edge cases, Inspector presentation), the puzzle-design grammar the behaviours create, and the behaviour × state test matrix with its automated hooks. All behaviour parameters live in `PieceDefinition` / `BlockBehaviourParams` authored in §5; all behaviour side effects route through `LevelManager`, `StabilityMonitor`, `ScoreController`, `AudioDirector`, and `VFXDirector` (§4–§6). Physics execution follows §6: fixed-step simulation via `PhysicsStepper`, 2D (Box2D-line) API as the reference implementation, determinism discipline for replays.

**Provenance baseline.** The original's shape inventory is officially documented: Wii had "14 Shapes + 2 Special Shapes... that break once you put too much load on top, or a timer runs out" ([official Wii About, archived](https://web.archive.org/web/20091116220135/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com:80/about.php), accessed 2026-09-24); 3DS and later editions have "16 Shapes + 5 Special Shapes: ... one that break[s] once you put too much load on top, or a timer runs out; the fire shape explodes on contact with another fire shape; the gravity shape inverts gravity" ([official 3DS About, archived](https://web.archive.org/web/20151029143537/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com/3ds/about.php), accessed 2026-09-24 — the archived sentence truncates after the fourth special). Review detail fills in trigger semantics: weight-restricted blocks hold "no more than three other regulars before smashing"; timer blocks "countdown and disappear when a new piece is placed atop them"; gravity levels "have platforms at top AND bottom of screen and flip the stack" ([Cubed3 Wii U review](http://www.cubed3.com/review/1648/1/art-of-balance-wii-u.html), accessed 2026-09-24).

| ID | Behaviour | Documented trigger/effect | First appears | Status in this plan |
|----|-----------|---------------------------|---------------|---------------------|
| B0 | Base block | plain rigid shape; no behaviour | Wii, 2010 | [DOCUMENTED] |
