| Content | 200 levels across 8 worlds — "the 200 arcade levels from the Nintendo 3DS release" | [About page](https://web.archive.org/web/20160903223835/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com:80/wiiu/about.php); [NWR review](http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/review/38619/art-of-balance-wii-u-review), accessed 2026-09-24 |
| Shape set | 16 shapes + 5 specials (documented for the 3DS line; Wii U parity inferred from the shared 200-level content) | [3DS About page, archived](https://web.archive.org/web/20151029143537/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com/3ds/about.php), accessed 2026-09-24 <!-- TODO-VERIFY: Wii U-specific confirmation of the 16+5 shape count (official Wii U copy does not enumerate shapes in fetched captures) --> |
| Modes | Arcade, Endurance, Swift Stacker, Tower Tumble, plus Special Challenges (Time/Height/Balance) | About page + reviews (below) |
| Players | 1–5 local (1 GamePad + 4 Wii Remotes); online 1–5 | [NWR review](http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/review/38619/art-of-balance-wii-u-review), accessed 2026-09-24 |
| Controls | Wii Remote (pointer), GamePad touch, GamePad analog sticks/buttons; play on TV or GamePad | [About page](https://web.archive.org/web/20160903223835/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com:80/wiiu/about.php), accessed 2026-09-24 |
| Reception | Metacritic 82; Nintendo Life 9/10; Cubed3 9/10 | [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_of_Balance), [NL review](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), [Cubed3 review](http://www.cubed3.com/review/1648/1/art-of-balance-wii-u.html), accessed 2026-09-24 |
| Presentation | HD; realistic water; window light casting real-time shadows of the dragged piece; wooden "clunk" placement SFX; "jazzy, relaxing" lounge soundtrack | [NL review](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24 |

Two Wii U-generation deltas over the Wii original matter for our feel target. First, the post-placement stability countdown is **"significantly shorter"** than the WiiWare edition's documented 3 seconds — the exact Wii U value is not published **[DOCUMENTED]** ([NL review](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24) <!-- TODO-VERIFY: exact post-Wii countdown duration; only "significantly shorter" is documented -->. Second, Endurance mode matured here: score = speed + remaining lives + puzzle difficulty, posted to **online** leaderboards (the 3DS edition's Endurance leaderboards were offline-only), with exactly 3 lives per session **[DOCUMENTED]** ([NL review](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24). Our StabilityWindow duration is therefore a per-profile tunable in GameModeDefinition (§5), defaulting to the multiply-documented 3.0 s with the three-green-light UI (§3), not a hard constant.

### 11.2 Control system — the tri-control matrix

**[DOCUMENTED]** Official copy: "Play your own style: Play on your Wii U GamePad or on TV. Use touch controls, Wii Remotes or the GamePad analog sticks." ([Wii U About page](https://web.archive.org/web/20160903223835/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com:80/wiiu/about.php), accessed 2026-09-24). All three schemes coexist: reviews confirm five people playing simultaneously across four Wii Remotes and one GamePad ([Cubed3](http://www.cubed3.com/review/1648/1/art-of-balance-wii-u.html), accessed 2026-09-24). The Wii Remote path is the WiiWare IR-pointer scheme — point to aim, A to pick up/drop, B or D-pad left/right to rotate in 45° increments — whose precision reviewers called "super-accurate" ([Cubed3](http://www.cubed3.com/review/1648/1/art-of-balance-wii-u.html); rotation increment per [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_of_Balance), tertiary, accessed 2026-09-24).

This tri-control breadth is the historical justification for the provider abstraction in §7: the Wii U edition is proof that one puzzle core can sit above three unrelated input idioms. The mapping:

| Wii U scheme | Documented behavior | Our provider (§7) | v1 platforms |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wii Remote IR pointer | Pointer-follow cursor; A pick/drop; B or D-pad L/R rotate | `MousePointerInputProvider` (pointer-follow, button rotate) | Windows, macOS (mouse) |
| GamePad touch | Direct touch placement | `TouchDragInputProvider` (drag to move, tap zones/buttons to rotate) | Android, iOS; touch-capable PCs |
| GamePad sticks + buttons | Cursor move via stick; face buttons pick/rotate/drop | `GamepadInputProvider` | All platforms (Xbox pad primary, §19) |
| (Wii Remote "motion" wording) | NWR's "motion controls using the Wii Remote" most likely denotes IR-pointing plus twist; the pointer is the corroborated mechanism | `MotionPointerInputProvider` (gyro attitude pointer) as the true-motion analog | Android/iOS gyro; gamepad gyro post-v1 |

**[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** The provider-to-scheme mapping table above is our design; the historical fact it encodes (three coexisting schemes, one game core) is the documented part. The gyro provider is included because the Input System exposes `AttitudeSensor` (orientation quaternion) on mobile platforms ([Input System sensors documentation, Unity-Technologies/InputSystem develop tree](https://github.com/Unity-Technologies/InputSystem/tree/develop/Packages/com.unity.inputsystem/Documentation~), accessed 2026-09-24), and because the Switch edition's Patch 1.1 motion addition (§13) demonstrates that a post-launch control scheme is a config-plus-provider event, not a rewrite.

One Wii U-specific control nuance: Cubed3 reports that for gravity-inverter levels — which place platforms at both the top and bottom of the screen and flip the stack — "turning the GamePad helps" **[DOCUMENTED]** ([Cubed3 review](http://www.cubed3.com/review/1648/1/art-of-balance-wii-u.html), accessed 2026-09-24). The sentence is ambiguous between physically tilting the GamePad to reorient the play view and rotating one's seating relative to the screen; we do not replicate either reading. Our gravity-inverter (§8) stays a deterministic, button-triggered flip with a screen-rotation camera option — **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** — because a hardware-tilt-dependent camera is untestable across our v1 device matrix and unverifiable from the sources.

### 11.3 Multiplayer topology — and the online player-count correction

**[DOCUMENTED]** The verified multiplayer matrix ([NWR](http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/review/38619/art-of-balance-wii-u-review), [NL](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24):

| Mode | Local | Online | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Arcade | up to 5 (co-op, mixed devices) | — | 5-player local co-op confirmed by NWR |
| Endurance | up to 5 (co-op) | leaderboards | score = speed + lives + difficulty; 3 lives per session |
| Swift Stacker | 2 teams, split-screen | yes — "locally, online or even a combination of the two" | teams of two; team that solves first wins |
| Tower Tumble | up to 4, local-only | no | turn-based; toppler loses |
| Special Challenges | solo context | — | Time/Height/Balance variants for extra points |

Correction that binds this plan: the claim "**10 players online across 2 consoles**" appears in franchise folklore but is supported by no fetched source. The best-documented online figure is NWR's "Online: 1–5" for the Wii U edition; no page supports a 10-player figure anywhere in the franchise. Our design documents use **online cap 5, unverified beyond that** — and since v1 ships no online multiplayer at all (§2 non-goal; the original had it, we defer it), the number only matters as a historical datum and a post-v1 ceiling.

The deferral is not arbitrary. Unity's physics engines are deterministic on the same device but "not 100% deterministic across devices" per Unity staff ([Unity Discussions, MelvMay, 2023-02-27](https://discussions.unity.com/t/fully-deterministic-physics/910507/10), accessed 2026-09-24), so cross-device lockstep over a physics stacker is unsafe (§6, §21). When online play is revisited post-v1, the architecture is host-authoritative pose snapshots, not lockstep — the standard casual-multiplayer choice enumerated in §6's determinism options. **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (the deferral and the snapshot-sync posture; the determinism facts are documented).

### 11.4 Dual-screen use and GamePad asymmetry

What is documented about the second screen:

- **Off-TV play**: the full game runs on the GamePad screen alone ([About page](https://web.archive.org/web/20160903223835/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com:80/wiiu/about.php), accessed 2026-09-24).
- **Simultaneous mixed-device play**: TV plus GamePad in the same session with five players (§11.2).
- **GamePad physicality**: the "turning the GamePad helps" gravity-level note (§11.2).
- **Queue placement**: not documented for Wii U. The 3DS sibling explicitly put the piece selection tray on the lower screen and the stack on the upper screen ([Der Spiegel, 2012-07-12](https://www.spiegel.de/netzwelt/games/3ds-spiel-art-of-balance-touch-im-test-a-843861.html), accessed 2026-09-24); whether the Wii U GamePad screen carried the queue during TV play is not stated in any fetched source. <!-- TODO-VERIFY: whether Wii U GamePad screen hosted the piece queue or any exclusive HUD during TV play -->

The design reading: Wii U asymmetry was **input-side** (who holds which device) rather than **information-side** (no documented private-screen role, hidden hand, or asymmetric-knowledge mechanic). That is convenient for us — nothing in the mode specs below depends on a second screen existing.

| Wii U capability | Closest analog in our v1 target set | v1 status |
|---|---|---|
| Off-TV play (GamePad-only) | Native on Android/iOS; on PC, Steam Deck / laptop handheld use | Free — no design work; UI must be legible at small sizes (§9 safe-area + resolution anchors) |
| TV + second screen simultaneous | None targeted | Out of scope; single-screen rendering everywhere |
| 5-device mixed local play | 4 gamepads + 1 mouse/touch on PC (§7 PlayerInputManager, per-player cursors) | Supported by input architecture; mode caps set in §11.7 |
| GamePad tilt assist (gravity levels) | Gyro attitude on mobile (§7 MotionPointerInputProvider) | Not wired to gravity flip; deterministic camera option instead (§11.2) |

**[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** The analog table is our scoping decision: no second-screen or companion-device feature is designed for v1, and any streaming-based off-TV play (platform handheld/remote-play functionality) is treated as incidental platform capability, not a designed feature.

### 11.5 The "240 fps physics" claim — status, meaning, and replication

**Claim status: unconfirmed.** The "up-to-240fps physics simulation" line is absent from all five official microsites, both live press sheets, all Nintendo product pages, and all seven reviews fetched for this project; it was either console-eShop copy that was never web-archived or it is apocryphal. It must not be stated as fact anywhere in this plan. <!-- TODO-VERIFY: primary source for the "up to 240fps physics" claim (suspected Wii U eShop store copy or a period interview; not in any fetched archive capture) -->

**What the claim would have to mean** (analysis, not attribution): a fixed-rate physics integrator running decoupled from — and faster than — the 60 fps render loop. At a 1/240 s step, a freely falling piece at 1 g drops at most ½·g·dt² ≈ 0.085 mm per step, so contact and settling resolution are effectively continuous for stack-scale bodies; jitter that a 20 ms step would leave visible (a 50 Hz step covers ~1.96 mm of fall) is numerically gone. For a game whose entire win condition is "the stack visibly stops moving," sim rate *is* game feel.

**How we replicate it today [ORIGINAL DESIGN], grounded in verified Unity 6.6 facts (§6):**

1. **Option A (default):** `Time.fixedDeltaTime = 1f/240f` (Fixed Timestep 0.0041667) with Physics 2D Simulation Mode = Fixed Update. FixedUpdate-driven game code (input application, StabilityMonitor checks) inherits the 240 Hz cadence. ([Time project settings](https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/class-TimeManager.html), accessed 2026-09-24)
2. **Option B (fallback):** Simulation Mode = Script with a fixed-step accumulator calling `Physics2D.Simulate(fixedStep)` — never a `Time.deltaTime`-derived value, which the docs explicitly call less deterministic. ([Physics2D.Simulate](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Physics2D.Simulate.html), accessed 2026-09-24)
3. **Terminology guard:** Unity's Physics2D *substepping* (`useSubStepping`, `maxSubStepCount`, `minSubStepFPS`) is a low-frame-rate "simulation explosion" guard that only operates in Update/Script simulation modes — it is **not** a mechanism for raising the base simulation rate and does nothing in Fixed Update mode. Our "240 Hz class" loop is a timestep choice, with substepping as the safety net only if Option B is used. ([Physics2D.useSubStepping](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Physics2D-useSubStepping.html), accessed 2026-09-24)
4. **Cost:** ~4.8× physics CPU versus the 50 Hz default — trivial at our body counts (a level holds well under 100 active bodies), per the §6 budget table.
5. **Interpolation:** `Rigidbody2D.interpolation = None` when sim rate exceeds render rate; every rendered frame samples fresh physics state.

Acceptance test for the feel (§10, exit criterion of the physics epic): a scripted drop-and-settle scenario must produce visually identical settle behavior at 30/60/120/240 Hz render rates, and the three-green-light stability window (§3) must complete on fixed-step count, not frame count. Whether or not the 2014 game ever ran 240 Hz, the clone's settle feel is specified to that bar.

### 11.6 Modes introduced on Wii U

The WiiWare original shipped only Arcade, drop-in co-op, and a 2-player split-screen Versus with selectable 5/7/9-round matches **[DOCUMENTED]** ([NL WiiWare review](https://web.archive.org/web/20210420192755/https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/2010/02/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24). The Wii U edition is where the competitive lineup received its persistent names and structure: NWR identifies Swift Stacker as "The Wii's multiplayer mode, now known as Swift Stacker," and Tower Tumble debuts as the turn-based "reverse Jenga" ([NWR](http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/review/38619/art-of-balance-wii-u-review), accessed 2026-09-24). Infinity mode is **not** named on Wii U official pages — it first appears in the fetched record on the PS4/Switch press sheets (§12) — so our five-mode set (§5) draws Infinity from the later editions, not from Wii U.

#### 11.6.1 Swift Stacker — full mechanical spec

**[DOCUMENTED]** basis:

| Rule | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Format | Split-screen head-to-head race to solve the same puzzle; "team that solves first wins" | [NL](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24 |
| Teams | Two teams of two | NL (above) |
| Connectivity | "locally, online or even a combination of the two" | [NWR](http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/review/38619/art-of-balance-wii-u-review), accessed 2026-09-24 |
| Retries | Unlimited | NL (above) |
| Ancestry | WiiWare 2p Versus: same levels as Arcade, best-of 5/7/9 selectable | [NL WiiWare review](https://web.archive.org/web/20210420192755/https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/2010/02/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24 |
| Later wording | "Play against others in split-screen head-to-head matches. At home, online or on the go - Who can solve the puzzles faster?" (Switch) | [Shin'en Switch press sheet](http://shinen.com/press/sheet.php?p=art_of_balance(Switch)), accessed 2026-09-24 |

Not documented anywhere fetched: round/match length on Wii U, tie-break rules, whether teammates alternate placements or share one queue freely, queue seeding, handicap options, and how a fifth local player participates in a 2v2 format. <!-- TODO-VERIFY: Wii U Swift Stacker round count and team turn rules (reviews describe format only at team-race level) --> Each gap below is filled explicitly.

**[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** fill — our competitive spec (v1: local split-screen; the same rules are the post-v1 online spec unchanged, since seeding makes queues wire-cheap):

1. **Match structure:** first to `roundsToWin` round wins, default 3 (best-of-5), user-selectable 2/3/4 (best-of 3/5/7/9) — honoring the documented WiiWare 5/7/9-round ancestry.
2. **Identical queues by seed:** both teams load the same `LevelDefinition` with the same queue seed; round level order drawn deterministically from a shared match seed (replayable per §6 determinism discipline; online-safe because only the seed crosses the wire).
3. **Team turn alternation:** within a team, placements strictly alternate (teammate A places, then B); the carrying player is whoever's turn it is. This makes 2v2 a real team mode rather than two players sharing a hand, and degrades cleanly: 1v1 = single placement turns; 2v2 = alternating; a 3- or 5-player local session rotates odd players across rounds.
4. **Retries:** unlimited, per the documented rule — but self-penalizing: a retry resets the stack and costs the reset downtime (default 2 s) while the opponent's clock keeps running. No artificial penalty is needed; with median failed attempts wasting ~35 s of a ~90–120 s par solve (§3 par data), expected round time ≈ parTime × (1 + failRate × refailFraction), which keeps races inside a 2–3 minute band at a 30% fail rate.
5. **Round win:** first team whose stack passes the full stability window (§3, §6 StabilityMonitor) — the three-green-light rule is the finish line, not piece depletion.
6. **Draws:** if both teams clear within the same fixed-step tick (possible online with snapshot sync), the round is replayed with a fresh seed.

```csharp
using System;
using UnityEngine;

/// <summary>
/// Arbitrates a Swift Stacker match: two teams race to clear identical,
/// seed-locked level queues in parallel split-screen instances. The first
/// team whose stack passes the stability window wins the round. Documented
/// basis: split-screen team race on the same puzzle, unlimited retries.
/// Round structure, seeding and turn alternation are [ORIGINAL DESIGN].
/// </summary>
public sealed class SwiftStackerRaceController : MonoBehaviour
{
    #region Serialized Fields

    [Header("Match Configuration")]
    [SerializeField] private int roundsToWin = 3;
    [SerializeField] private int retryResetCostSteps = 480;          // 2 s at 240 Hz fixed step (§6)
    [SerializeField] private LevelDefinition[] roundLevelPool;       // candidate levels per round

    [Header("References")]
    [SerializeField] private LevelManager[] teamLevelManagers = new LevelManager[TeamCount];
    [SerializeField] private ScoreController scoreController;

    #endregion

    #region Public Properties

    /// <summary>Round wins per team index; read-only outside this class.</summary>
    public int[] TeamRoundWins { get; private set; }

    /// <summary>Zero-based index of the round currently being raced.</summary>
    public int CurrentRound { get; private set; }

    public bool MatchInProgress { get; private set; }

    #endregion

    #region Private Fields

    private const int TeamCount = 2;

    private int _raceSeed;
    private bool _roundResolved;

    #endregion

    #region Unity Lifecycle

    private void Awake()
    {
        TeamRoundWins = new int[TeamCount];
    }

    #endregion

    #region Public Methods

    /// <summary>
    /// Starts a match. The seed is shared by both teams and, in a future
    /// online build, crosses the wire so both sides simulate identical queues.
    /// </summary>
    /// <param name="raceSeed">Deterministic seed for round and queue draws.</param>
    public void BeginMatch(int raceSeed)
    {
        _raceSeed = raceSeed;
        Array.Clear(TeamRoundWins, 0, TeamRoundWins.Length);
        CurrentRound = 0;
        MatchInProgress = true;
        StartRound();
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// Callback target for a team's StabilityMonitor stack-cleared event.
    /// First arrival wins the round; later arrivals in the same tick are ignored.
    /// </summary>
    /// <param name="teamIndex">Zero-based team index.</param>
    public void NotifyTeamCleared(int teamIndex)
    {
        if (!MatchInProgress || _roundResolved)
        {
            return;
        }

        _roundResolved = true;
        TeamRoundWins[teamIndex]++;
        scoreController.RecordSwiftStackerRound(teamIndex, CurrentRound);
        // … round-win VFX via VFXDirector, then next round or match end
    }

    #endregion

    #region Private Methods

    private void StartRound()
    {
        _roundResolved = false;
        LevelDefinition level = DrawRoundLevel(CurrentRound);
        for (int i = 0; i < TeamCount; i++)
        {
            teamLevelManagers[i].LoadLevel(level, _raceSeed + CurrentRound);
        }
    }

    private LevelDefinition DrawRoundLevel(int roundIndex)
    {
        // Deterministic draw: identical seed => identical round order on every
        // machine; allocation-free (System.Random instance per round, cold path).
        System.Random rng = new System.Random(_raceSeed + roundIndex * 31);
        return roundLevelPool[rng.Next(roundLevelPool.Length)];
    }

    #endregion
}
```

#### 11.6.2 Tower Tumble — full mechanical spec

**[DOCUMENTED]** basis:

| Rule | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Format | Turn-based: players alternate placing blocks; whoever topples the tower loses the round | [NL](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24 |
| Scoring | The toppler loses; everyone else scores a point | NL (above) |
| Piece feed | Randomly generated per round | NL (above) |
| Players | Up to 4; local multiplayer-only on Wii U | [NWR](http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/review/38619/art-of-balance-wii-u-review); [Switch press sheet](http://shinen.com/press/sheet.php?p=art_of_balance(Switch)), accessed 2026-09-24 |
| Nickname | "Reverse Jenga" | NWR (above) |

Not documented anywhere fetched: round end condition (piece budget? height target?), whether any stability gate applies between turns, match length, rotation rules, feed composition (which shapes/specials), or tie handling. <!-- TODO-VERIFY: Tower Tumble round end condition and per-turn settle rules (reviews describe turn order and scoring only) -->

**[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** fill — our hotseat spec (v1: local pass-and-play up to 4, matching the edition's local-only posture):

1. **Piece budget per round:** default 12 pieces drawn from a weighted `PieceDefinition` pool, seeded per round for replay determinism. At 4 players that is 3 placements each; at 2 players, 6 each.
2. **Per-turn settle gate:** after each placement the stack must pass a shortened 1.0 s stability check (one-third of the Arcade window) before the next player's piece is offered — long enough to propagate topples to the rightful placer, short enough to keep pace. Round pacing math: roundDuration ≈ piecesPerRound × (meanPlacementSeconds + turnSettleWindowSeconds) ≈ 12 × (6 + 1) ≈ 84 s; match = first to 3 points ≈ 4–5 rounds ≈ a 6–7 minute session.
3. **Round end, two exits:** (a) any water contact (§3 fail rule) — the acting player is the toppler, scores nothing, all others +1; (b) budget exhausted with the tower standing — all surviving players +1 (a defensive-play reward; the documented rules only cover exit (a), so the clean-budget case is ours).
4. **Feed composition:** base shapes plus breakable and timed specials by weight; gravity-inverters excluded from the default multiplayer feed (a mid-round gravity flip punishes whoever happens to be on turn — random-feeling, not read-based); fire shapes allowed only in an explicit "chaos" variant. Weights live in GameModeDefinition (§5).
5. **Match structure:** first to `pointsToWinMatch` (default 3); tie at match point triggers a sudden-death round with half budget.
6. **Turn input:** one active `IPieceInputProvider` at a time, gated by InputRouter (§7); gamepad hotseat passes on placement, or per-player cursors when 2–4 devices are paired (Wii U's mixed-device table, §11.2, is the precedent).

```csharp
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;

/// <summary>
/// Arbitrates a Tower Tumble round: players alternate placing randomly
/// generated pieces; the player who topples the tower loses the round and
/// every other player scores one point. Documented basis: turn order,
/// random feed, toppler-loses scoring, up to 4 players, local-only. Feed
/// budget, settle gate and match length are [ORIGINAL DESIGN].
/// </summary>
public sealed class TowerTumbleRoundController : MonoBehaviour
{
    #region Serialized Fields

    [Header("Round Configuration")]
    [SerializeField] private int piecesPerRound = 12;
    [SerializeField] private int pointsToWinMatch = 3;
    [SerializeField] private float turnSettleWindowSeconds = 1f;
    [SerializeField] private int playerCount = 2;

    [Header("References")]
    [SerializeField] private LevelManager levelManager;
    [SerializeField] private StabilityMonitor stabilityMonitor;
    [SerializeField] private List<PieceDefinition> feedPool = new List<PieceDefinition>();

    #endregion

    #region Public Properties

    public int[] PlayerScores { get; private set; }

    /// <summary>Index of the player currently placing; input is gated to them.</summary>
    public int ActivePlayerIndex { get; private set; }

    public int PiecesRemaining { get; private set; }

    #endregion

    #region Private Fields

    private const int MaxPlayers = 4;
    private const int MinPlayers = 2;

    private System.Random _feedRng;

    #endregion

    #region Unity Lifecycle

    private void Awake()
    {
        PlayerScores = new int[MaxPlayers];
    }

    private void OnDestroy()
    {
        if (stabilityMonitor != null)
        {
            stabilityMonitor.WaterContact -= HandleWaterContact;
        }
    }

    #endregion

    #region Public Methods

    /// <summary>Begins a round with a deterministic feed seed (replay-safe, §6).</summary>
    /// <param name="feedSeed">Seed for the piece-feed draw.</param>
    public void BeginRound(int feedSeed)
    {
        if (playerCount < MinPlayers || playerCount > MaxPlayers)
        {
            Debug.LogWarning($"{nameof(TowerTumbleRoundController)}: invalid player count {playerCount}.");
            return;
        }

        _feedRng = new System.Random(feedSeed);
        PiecesRemaining = piecesPerRound;
        ActivePlayerIndex = 0;
        stabilityMonitor.WaterContact += HandleWaterContact;
        OfferNextPiece();
    }

    /// <summary>Advances the turn after the acting player's piece settles.</summary>
    public void CompleteTurn()
    {
        PiecesRemaining--;
        if (PiecesRemaining <= 0)
        {
            EndRound(topplerIndex: -1); // budget exhausted, tower standing
            return;
        }

        ActivePlayerIndex = (ActivePlayerIndex + 1) % playerCount;
        OfferNextPiece();
    }

    #endregion

    #region Private Methods

    private void OfferNextPiece()
    {
        PieceDefinition piece = DrawFeedPiece();
        levelManager.OfferPiece(piece);
        // … InputRouter gates control to ActivePlayerIndex's provider (§7)
    }

    private PieceDefinition DrawFeedPiece()
    {
        // Weighted draw from feedPool (weights in GameModeDefinition, §5);
        // seeded and allocation-free on the hot path.
        int index = _feedRng.Next(feedPool.Count);
        return feedPool[index];
    }

    private void HandleWaterContact(PieceController piece)
    {
        // §6 surface: Action<PieceController> — the monitor reports the piece
        // that hit the water, not whose turn it is; resolve the acting player
        // (the toppler) from Tower Tumble turn state (§3/§7), not the payload.
        EndRound(topplerIndex: ActivePlayerIndex);
    }

    private void EndRound(int topplerIndex)
    {
        stabilityMonitor.WaterContact -= HandleWaterContact;
        for (int i = 0; i < playerCount; i++)
        {
            if (i != topplerIndex)
            {
                PlayerScores[i]++;
            }
        }
        // … score UI, sudden-death or next round at pointsToWinMatch
    }

    #endregion
}
```

### 11.8 What stays historical

Permanent Wii U specifics with no clone analog: the GamePad's second physical screen and off-TV mode as a designed feature; the Wii Remote IR light-gun-style pointing (our mouse/gyro providers approximate its *feel* — pointer-follow with button rotation — not the IR mechanism); the 1+4 device topology as a hardware fact; the mixed local+online session topology; and the edition's eShop distribution context. One feel-level lesson does carry forward as a test criterion: reviewers across editions praised the Wii-pointer scheme's precision ([Cubed3](http://www.cubed3.com/review/1648/1/art-of-balance-wii-u.html), accessed 2026-09-24), so pointer-latency parity between mouse, touch, and gamepad-cursor providers is an explicit §7 acceptance test rather than a nice-to-have.

**[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** The historical/modern split in §11.7–§11.8 is a scoping decision by this plan; every documented fact it rests on is cited in §11.1–§11.6, and the two competitive-mode specifications carry their own per-rule provenance markers so a future maintainer can tell exactly which rule is Shin'en's and which is ours.

## 12. Deep Dive — PlayStation Edition

The 2016 PlayStation 4 release is the franchise's only PlayStation SKU and the first edition whose own press material names Infinity mode. For our clone it serves two purposes: (a) the historical record for the five-mode set, the 4-player offline/online topology, and online leaderboards that our mode layer replicates; and (b) the anchor for Infinity's full mechanical spec (§12.2), which the historical record covers in exactly one sentence. PlayStation is **not** in the v1 target set — the decided order is Windows + macOS (Steam) first, then Android, then iOS, then Xbox gated on ID@Xbox access (see §2, §19) — so this section closes with a stretch-port work breakdown rather than build instructions.

### 12.1 Historical specification — Art of Balance (PS4, 2016)

The PS4 edition belongs to the post-Wii content generation (200 levels / 8 worlds / 16+5 shapes, shared with 3DS, Wii U, and Switch) and to the post-Wii rules generation: reviews document that from Wii U onward the 3-second stability countdown was made "significantly shorter" than the WiiWare original's ([Nintendo Life Wii U review](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24). The exact shortened duration was never published (§21 open question); the PS4-era value is therefore unknowable from sources and our default comes from §3's tuning instead.

#### 12.1.2 Mode set as shipped on PS4

Official mode wording captured verbatim from the press sheets (PS4 and, where identical, Switch):

| Mode | PS4-documented behavior | Provenance |

Two generation-level facts fill out the PS4 picture, both documented for the Wii U/3DS siblings and undocumented separately for PS4: Endurance grants exactly 3 lives/retries per session (triple-sourced: [Nintendo Life](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24) with score composed of speed + lives kept + puzzle difficulty feeding an online leaderboard; Arcade levels carry Time / Height / Balance Challenges for extra points (official pages of the Wii→Wii U generation and reviews). Treat both as carried into PS4 (medium confidence) — the fetched PS4 capture does not restate them. Note also the leaderboard history: 3DS Endurance leaderboards were offline-only ([Cubed3 3DS review](https://www.cubed3.com/games/reviews/nintendo-3ds/art-of-balance-touch), accessed 2026-09-24); the Wii U edition (2014) already documented online leaderboards alongside online multiplayer ([Nintendo Life Wii U review](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/wiiu-eshop/art_of_balance), accessed 2026-09-24; T01 src 17/18), and PS4 continues that pattern (T01 src 10) — the online leaderboard requirement in our §19 service layer descends from that Wii U→PS4 feature line, not from a PS4 first.

A historical nuance worth recording: Infinity is *named* on the PS4 and Switch press sheets but **not** on the archived Wii U official pages. Whether a Wii U build contained an unnamed endless mode is unknowable from the fetched sources; the plan treats Infinity as PS4-generation-documented and designs the rest itself (§12.3).

#### 12.1.3 DualShock 4 mapping — what is and is not documented

**[DOCUMENTED]**: the press sheet lists DualShock 4 as the controller (accessed 2026-09-24). That is the entire public record. The following were checked and are **not documented in any fetched source**: touchpad use, lightbar use, motion/gyro scheme, speaker use, and any specific PS4 button mapping. The WiiWare edition's documented mapping (A picks up/drops, B or D-pad L/R rotates) has no published PS4 counterpart.

Consequences for the clone:

- No DS4-specific affordance is required for faithfulness — our standard gamepad scheme from §7 (left stick moves the cursor, face buttons rotate in 45° increments, one button picks up/drops) satisfies everything the historical record demands of a PlayStation controller.
- We deliberately design **out** of DualShock/DualSense-exclusive features: Unity's public Input System package does not expose DualSense adaptive triggers at all (code-verified against the package source, Input System v1.20.1 develop branch, research track T09, 2026-09-24), and lightbar/haptics over Bluetooth are unsupported in the desktop HID path. Any such feature would need the PlayStation console SDK anyway (see §12.3.2), breaking input parity across our six targets.
- The Input System's standard gamepad layout aliases cross/circle/square/triangle onto the same positional controls as every other pad (buttonNorth/East/South/West; track T09, code-verified v1.20.1), so §7's `GamepadInputProvider` and PS glyph set work unchanged on a PlayStation target; `DualShock4GamepadHID` and `DualSenseGamepadHID` device classes exist on desktop platforms for development testing today. <!-- TODO-VERIFY: PlayStation regional confirm-button convention (cross vs circle) and whether system-level remap must be honored — not in research notes; validate against platform requirements under NDA before any PS port. -->

#### 12.1.4 Localization, trophies, demo

- **Localization:** the PS4 supported-language list was never captured (per-region PS Store pages unfetchable during research). The documented contrast is the Switch language list — Japanese, American English, British English, French, Canadian French, German, Spanish, Latin American Spanish — eight entries on the Switch press sheet/Nintendo.com ([Nintendo.com store page](https://www.nintendo.com/store/products/art-of-balance-switch/), accessed 2026-09-24). A "four languages" figure for PS4 circulates in task material but has no source behind it. <!-- TODO-VERIFY: PS4 per-region PS Store language list; do not quote any count until captured. --> Our §5 localization is string-table-driven, so the shipped language set is pure configuration; the design carries no PS4-language assumptions.
- **Trophies:** presence is documented (§12.1.1); the actual trophy list of the original was not captured and is unknown to this plan. Our own 13-trophy sketch is therefore **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** (§12.3.4).
- **Demo:** a free demo shipped on day one. Whether our clone ships a demo is a §2/§10 scope decision; the historical precedent (also on 3DS, Wii U, and Switch) is that every post-Wii edition launched or gained one.

#### 12.1.5 What the PS4 edition changes relative to Wii U (§11)

| Dimension | Wii U (2014, see §11) | PS4 (2016) |
|---|---|---|
| Local players | Up to 5 — 1 GamePad + 4 Wii Remotes | Up to 4 — DualShock 4 |
| Control schemes | Tri-control: Wii Remote pointer, GamePad touch, GamePad sticks | Single scheme: DualShock 4; no touch/motion documented |
| Screen topology | TV + GamePad dual-screen asymmetry | Single screen; split-screen for Swift Stacker |
| Online | Leaderboards + online multiplayer (Swift Stacker local/online/mixed) | Leaderboards + online multiplayer (Swift Stacker local/online) |
| Mode naming | Infinity not named on official pages | Infinity named and described on the press sheet |
| Hardware claims | "Up-to-240fps physics" claim — unverified, §11/§21 | None |

Port-forward into our clone: the PS4 edition's 4-player local cap on standard gamepads (no special hardware) is the model our multiplayer takes on every platform — §7's PlayerInputManager pairing supports 4 pads without a pointer peripheral, unlike the Wii/Wii U designs. What stays historical: DualShock-specific unknowns (§12.1.3), the couch split-screen SKU geometry, and PS4-era leaderboard infrastructure.

### 12.2 Infinity mode — full mechanical specification

**[DOCUMENTED]**, in full, from the press sheets: "Infinity Mode: The blocks don't stop. Build the highest possible stack." (PS4 + Switch press sheets, accessed 2026-09-24). Everything below this line is **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** — the fill our clone implements, built on the shared systems of §3/§5/§6/§8.

#### 12.2.1 Design goals and the mode loop

Infinity is the score-attack complement to Endurance: Endurance tests breadth (survive a string of levels on 3 lives, score = speed + lives + difficulty, per §12.1.2), Infinity tests depth (one endless tower, height is the goal). Design goals:

1. Zero authored content — the mode must run forever from the §5 `PieceDefinition` inventory plus one generator asset (matches the "blocks don't stop" wording; no level select, no queue preview beyond the next piece).
2. Deterministic per run — seeded RNG so ghost replays and §14's determinism replay tests work identically to Arcade.
3. Escalating tension with no authored difficulty curve — difficulty emerges from tower height via the weight model in §12.2.2.
4. Reuse, not fork — the mode reuses `LevelManager` lifecycle, `StabilityMonitor` settling, `IBlockBehaviour` specials (§8), `ScoreController`, and `GameStateMachine` mode states (§3); only the queue source and the win condition differ.

Loop micro-states (extension of §3's stack loop): `Offered → Carrying → Released → Settling → (settle-gated) Offered → …` with no terminal `Cleared`. The 3-second three-green-light window does **not** apply — that rule is documented as triggering after *all* pieces are placed, which never happens here. Instead:

- **Piece offering is settle-gated:** the next piece is offered only when `StabilityMonitor` reports the tower settled (velocity-below-threshold predicate from §6), with a serialized failsafe timeout (4 s) so a slowly-drifting tower cannot stall the feed forever.
- **Fail rule (unchanged, global):** any piece touching the water at any time ends the run immediately — this is the documented franchise-wide fail condition (§3) and needs no per-mode variant.
- **Run end:** water contact → results screen (height reached, pieces placed, score) → leaderboard submission via the §19 platform-service seam.

#### 12.2.2 Procedural queue generation — the math

Height is measured in block units above the waterline (1 unit = nominal small-square edge, matching §5's `PieceDefinition` scale conventions). Let `h` = current tower height, and define the difficulty ramp:

```
d(h) = clamp01(h / H_ramp),   H_ramp = 60 units
```

**Shape selection weights.** For each shape class `s` in the pool with base weight `b_s` and difficulty slope `a_s`:

```
w(s, h) = b_s · (1 + a_s · d(h))
P(s)   = w(s, h) / Σ w(s', h)
```

| Shape class | b_s | a_s | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flat rectangles (2×1, 4×1) | 1.00 | −0.40 | Easy foundations dominate early, fade late |
| Squares | 1.00 | −0.20 | Neutral filler, gently displaced at height |
| Small planks (1×½) | 0.80 | +0.30 | Shims gain value as towers narrow |
| Triangles | 0.60 | +0.70 | Awkward stacking surfaces become common late |
| Circles | 0.35 | +0.90 | The punisher piece; rare at ground, near-parity at cap |

**Special-block injection** (specials excluded from the shape table; drawn by a separate gate):

```
p_special(d) = 0.05 + 0.25·d        →  5 % at ground, 30 % at the ramp cap
```

Special mix within a gated draw:

```
P(timed)     = 0.20 + 0.20·d        →  20 % → 40 %   (urgency ramps)
P(fire)      = 0.40 − 0.20·d        →  40 % → 20 %   (detonation risk fades)
P(breakable) = 0.40                 →  constant      (load-management always relevant)
P(gravity)   = 0                    →  excluded from random draws (see milestones)
```

**Gravity milestones.** The gravity-inverter (documented franchise behavior: inverts gravity, flipping the stack to a platform at the top of the screen — §8) is too structural for random draws. It is force-offered each time the tower crosses a milestone: `h ∈ {15, 30, 45, 60, …}` units (interval 15). Accepting the flip converts the run to top-down building against a ceiling platform — the same documented behavior, now a rhythm device that re-grounds the player every 15 units and resets visual context.

**Size constraint.** Above `h > 30` units, pieces wider than one-third of the basin are excluded from the draw (their `b_s` is zeroed) — keeps late-game towers precision work rather than slab stacking.

**Determinism.** One `System.Random` seeded per run (`runSeed`), recorded in the save/ghost header (§6); a second independent stream (different seed offset) rolls cosmetic variation (spawn jitter within tolerance) so gameplay RNG is never perturbed by presentation. The generator performs no per-draw heap allocations (pre-allocated cumulative-weight array).

#### 12.2.3 Scoring and leaderboards — the math

Height is the primary leaderboard key (the documented goal is "the highest possible stack"); score is the secondary key. Per piece `k` that settles at height `h_k` (center-of-mass height at settle, in units):

```
points_k = 10 + floor(h_k / 2)                 + 15  if settle time ≤ 0.5 s (perfect settle)
Score    = Σ_k points_k
```

Worked example — a 30-piece run whose pieces settle evenly across h = 10…25: 10 pieces near h≈10 give 10·(10+5) = 150; 10 near h≈17 give 10·(10+8) = 180; 10 near h≈24 give 10·(10+12) = 220; Σ = 550, plus 15 per perfect settle (a skilled run might add ~10 × 15 = 150 → 700). The linear-with-height term makes each successive placement worth more than the last, which is the intended risk/reward gradient: the marginal piece at h = 40 is worth 3× the marginal piece at h = 0.

Leaderboard set (mode-scoped, one per mode, via the §19 platform seam): `InfinityHeight` (primary sort: height units; tiebreak: score) and `InfinityScore` — mirroring the original's per-mode online leaderboards documented on PS4 (§12.1.2). Anti-cheat considerations (score validation server-side where available, replay attachment where the platform supports UGC) follow §14's DevSecOps guidance.

#### 12.2.4 C# skeletons

`InfinityQueueGenerator` — a `ScriptableObject` referenced by the §5 `GameModeDefinition` for Infinity, so the mode is data-configured like every other mode:

```csharp
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;

namespace AoB.Gameplay.Modes
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Endless procedural piece feed for Infinity mode. Implements the weight model of
    /// §12.2.2 — w(s,h) = b_s * (1 + a_s * d(h)) — with milestone-forced gravity pieces.
    /// Seeded for determinism; performs no per-draw heap allocations.
    /// </summary>
    [CreateAssetMenu(fileName = "InfinityQueueGenerator",
        menuName = "AoB/Modes/Infinity Queue Generator")]
    public class InfinityQueueGenerator : ScriptableObject
    {
        #region Serialized Fields

        [Header("Shape Pool (PieceDefinition assets, §5)")]
        [SerializeField] private List<PieceDefinition> shapePool;
        [SerializeField] private List<float> baseWeights;
        [SerializeField] private List<float> difficultySlopes;

        [Header("Special Pieces (§8 behaviours)")]
        [SerializeField] private PieceDefinition breakablePiece;
        [SerializeField] private PieceDefinition timedPiece;
        [SerializeField] private PieceDefinition firePiece;
        [SerializeField] private PieceDefinition gravityPiece;

        [Header("Ramp (§12.2.2)")]
        [SerializeField] private float rampHeightUnits = 60f;
        [SerializeField, Range(0f, 1f)] private float specialChanceAtGround = 0.05f;
        [SerializeField, Range(0f, 1f)] private float specialChanceAtCap = 0.30f;
        [SerializeField] private float maxPieceWidthLateUnits = 0.33f;
        [SerializeField] private float lateGameHeightUnits = 30f;

        [Header("Milestones")]
        [SerializeField] private float gravityFlipIntervalUnits = 15f;

        #endregion

        #region Private Fields

        private System.Random _rng;
        private float[] _cumulative;
        private float _nextGravityFlipHeight;

        #endregion

        #region Public Properties

        /// <summary>Height that will force the next gravity-inverter offer.</summary>
        public float NextGravityFlipHeight => _nextGravityFlipHeight;

        #endregion

        #region Public Methods

        /// <summary>
        /// Resets the deterministic RNG stream for a new run.
        /// The seed is persisted with the run for ghost replays (§6).
        /// </summary>
        public void Initialize(int runSeed)
        {
            _rng = new System.Random(runSeed);
            _cumulative = new float[shapePool.Count];
            _nextGravityFlipHeight = gravityFlipIntervalUnits;
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Draws the next piece for a tower at <paramref name="towerHeightUnits"/> above
        /// the waterline. Gravity-inverter overrides the draw at milestone heights.
        /// </summary>
        public PieceDefinition Next(float towerHeightUnits, float basinWidthUnits)
        {
            if (towerHeightUnits >= _nextGravityFlipHeight)
            {
                _nextGravityFlipHeight += gravityFlipIntervalUnits;
                return gravityPiece;
            }

            float d = Mathf.Clamp01(towerHeightUnits / rampHeightUnits);
            if (_rng.NextDouble() < (double) Mathf.Lerp(specialChanceAtGround, specialChanceAtCap, d))
            {
                return DrawSpecial(d);
            }

            return DrawShape(d, towerHeightUnits, basinWidthUnits);
        }

        #endregion

        #region Private Methods

        private PieceDefinition DrawShape(float d, float h, float basinWidthUnits)
        {
            float total = 0f;
            bool late = h > lateGameHeightUnits;
            for (int i = 0; i < shapePool.Count; i++)
            {
                bool tooWide = late && shapePool[i].WidthUnits > maxPieceWidthLateUnits * basinWidthUnits;
                float w = tooWide ? 0f : baseWeights[i] * (1f + difficultySlopes[i] * d);
                total += w;
                _cumulative[i] = total;
            }

            if (total <= 0f)
            {
                return shapePool[shapePool.Count - 1];
            }

            double pick = _rng.NextDouble() * total;
            for (int i = 0; i < shapePool.Count; i++)
            {
                if (pick < _cumulative[i])
                {
                    return shapePool[i];
                }
            }

            return shapePool[shapePool.Count - 1];
        }

        private PieceDefinition DrawSpecial(float d)
        {
            // §12.2.2 mix: timed 0.20+0.20d, fire 0.40-0.20d, breakable remainder.
            double r = _rng.NextDouble();
            double timed = 0.20 + 0.20 * d;
            double fire = 0.40 - 0.20 * d;
            if (r < timed)
            {
                return timedPiece;
            }

            return r < timed + fire ? firePiece : breakablePiece;
        }

        #endregion
    }
}
```

`InfinityRunController` — the runtime driver; event surface names follow `StabilityMonitor` as defined in §6, extended with one event: `PieceSettled(settleSeconds, heightUnits)`, added to §6's StabilityMonitor Events region and consumed here for §12.2.3's per-piece scoring:

```csharp
using System;
using UnityEngine;

namespace AoB.Gameplay.Modes
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Drives one Infinity run: settle-gated piece offering, height/score accounting,
    /// water-contact termination. Mode states live in the GameStateMachine (§3);
    /// scoring events flow through ScoreController exactly as in Arcade.
    /// </summary>
    public class InfinityRunController : MonoBehaviour
    {
        #region Serialized Fields

        [Header("References")]
        [SerializeField] private StabilityMonitor stabilityMonitor;
        [SerializeField] private ScoreController scoreController;
        [SerializeField] private InfinityQueueGenerator queueGenerator;
        [SerializeField] private PieceSpawner pieceSpawner;

        [Header("Scoring (§12.2.3)")]
        [SerializeField] private int basePointsPerPiece = 10;
        [SerializeField] private float heightDivisor = 2f;
        [SerializeField] private int perfectSettleBonus = 15;
        [SerializeField] private float perfectSettleSeconds = 0.5f;

        [Header("Pacing")]
        [SerializeField] private float settleFailsafeSeconds = 4f;

        #endregion

        #region Public Properties

        /// <summary>Tower height in units above the waterline (primary leaderboard key).</summary>
        public float CurrentHeightUnits { get; private set; }

        /// <summary>Run score (secondary leaderboard key).</summary>
        public int Score { get; private set; }

        /// <summary>Pieces placed this run.</summary>
        public int PiecesPlaced { get; private set; }

        #endregion

        #region Private Fields

        private float _settleTimer;
        private bool _runActive;

        #endregion

        #region Unity Lifecycle

        private void Awake()
        {
            if (stabilityMonitor == null)
            {
                Debug.LogError($"{nameof(stabilityMonitor)} unassigned on {gameObject.name}", this);
            }
        }

        private void OnEnable()
        {
            stabilityMonitor.PieceSettled += HandleSettled;
            stabilityMonitor.WaterContact += HandleWaterContact;
        }

        private void OnDisable()
        {
            stabilityMonitor.PieceSettled -= HandleSettled;
            stabilityMonitor.WaterContact -= HandleWaterContact;
        }

        private void Update()
        {
            if (!_runActive)
            {
                return;
            }

            _settleTimer += Time.deltaTime;
            if (_settleTimer >= settleFailsafeSeconds)
            {
                OfferNextPiece();
            }
        }

        #endregion

        #region Public Methods

        /// <summary>Starts a deterministic run; the seed is persisted for ghost replays (§6).</summary>
        public void BeginRun(int runSeed)
        {
            CurrentHeightUnits = 0f;
            Score = 0;
            PiecesPlaced = 0;
            queueGenerator.Initialize(runSeed);
            _runActive = true;
            OfferNextPiece();
        }

        #endregion

        #region Private Methods

        private void OfferNextPiece()
        {
            _settleTimer = 0f;
            pieceSpawner.Offer(queueGenerator.Next(CurrentHeightUnits, pieceSpawner.BasinWidthUnits));
        }

        private void HandleSettled(float settleSeconds, float heightUnits)
        {
            if (!_runActive)
            {
                return;
            }

            CurrentHeightUnits = heightUnits;
            int points = basePointsPerPiece + (int) (heightUnits / heightDivisor);
            if (settleSeconds <= perfectSettleSeconds)
            {
                points += perfectSettleBonus;
            }

            Score += points;
            PiecesPlaced++;
            scoreController.NotifyPieceScored(points, heightUnits);
            OfferNextPiece();
        }

        private void HandleWaterContact(PieceController piece)
        {
            if (!_runActive)
            {
                return;
            }

            _runActive = false;
            RunEnded?.Invoke(CurrentHeightUnits, Score, PiecesPlaced);
        }

        #endregion

        #region Events

        /// <summary>Raised once when the run terminates on water contact.</summary>
        public event Action<float, int, int> RunEnded;

        #endregion
    }
}
```

Presentation coupling (no new systems): the camera rises with the tower top under the §6 camera director's dead-zone framing — the water plane stays world-anchored so height remains legible; the §9 gravity-flip and shatter VFX fire from the same `IBlockBehaviour` events as Arcade. The 3-green-light HUD widget is suppressed in this mode (§3 mode HUD config).

#### 12.2.5 Interaction with special blocks

| Behaviour (§8) | Infinity-specific role | Edge case handled |
|---|---|---|
| Breakable (load limit ~3 regulars, documented) | Load management becomes the core late-game skill as `p_special` rises | Shatter mid-settle re-arms the settle gate via `StabilityMonitor`; no offering during collapse |
| Timed (starts when stacked upon, documented) | Time pressure on placement order; ramps to 40 % of special draws | Expiry of a supporting piece can strand the tower — by design; water-contact rule ends the run |
| Fire (explodes on pair contact, documented) | Spatial-planning constraint; fades with height | Detonation debris is non-colliding (§8), so it cannot chain into water cheaply |
| Gravity (inverts gravity, documented) | Milestone rhythm device every 15 units | Flip mid-carry cancels the carry and re-offers (§3 retry semantics); ceiling platform is spawned by LevelManager on flip acceptance |

### 12.3 Our PlayStation stance — v1 exclusion and the stretch-port plan

#### 12.3.1 Why PS4/PS5 is not in v1

The decision is already fixed at plan level (§2): v1 ships Windows + macOS via Steam, then Android, then iOS, then Xbox gated on ID@Xbox. PlayStation would follow Xbox, reusing the console hardening that Xbox forces us to build anyway (cert process, kit hardware, platform services, controller-first UX polish). The research record supports the sequencing: every PlayStation-adjacent technical surface our notes touched is NDA-gated — Unity's console platform-module mechanics are a closed surface (documented for Xbox in track T08; the same pattern must be assumed for PlayStation), and console-specific input package contents are explicitly unverifiable from public sources (track T09). Nothing about a PlayStation port can be pre-verified from public docs, so it carries the highest planning uncertainty of any target (§21 risk entry).

#### 12.3.2 What a port would require

| # | Requirement | Grounding / status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sony developer/partner registration and concept approval | Not researched — no PlayStation partner-program facts were captured. The documented Xbox analogue (ID@Xbox: 18+, NDA, reside in a supported country; Unity listed among supported engines — [Microsoft GDK docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/gaming/gdk), accessed 2026-09-24) is the model, not evidence <!-- TODO-VERIFY: PlayStation partner-program entry requirements, fees, timeline -- capture from Sony's developer portal under NDA --> |
| 2 | Unity PlayStation platform module + per-platform Player Settings | Module install mechanics and settings are NDA-gated (pattern per track T08's Xbox finding) <!-- TODO-VERIFY: module availability for Unity 6.6, install steps, settings surface -- requires partner access --> |
| 3 | Input layer | Zero new work expected: §7's `GamepadInputProvider` targets the standard layout, which aliases cross/circle/square/triangle positionally (track T09, code-verified); PS glyphs are already in §7's glyph set. No DS4/DS5-exclusive features are used (§12.1.3), deliberately avoiding the public-package gaps (adaptive triggers unexposed; lightbar/Bluetooth haptics unsupported) |

## 13. Deep Dive — Switch Edition

This section studies the 2018 Nintendo Switch edition of Art of Balance as a historical reference and derives forward-looking design guidance for our clone. Per the chief-architect decision, Switch is **not** in the v1 target order (Windows + macOS via Steam → Android → iOS → Xbox); the Switch SKU appears here only as a study object whose content structure, mode set, input history, and docked/handheld duality feed our data model (§5), input architecture (§7), and quality-tier plan (§9). Every externally verifiable fact below carries its source from the research notes; anything the sources could not confirm is flagged `<!-- TODO-VERIFY -->` or marked **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**.

Primary sources for this section: the archived official Switch microsite ([web.archive.org capture, 2020-10-15](https://web.archive.org/web/20201015074209/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com/switch/), accessed 2026-09-24), the live Shin'en press sheet ([shinen.com press sheet: Art of Balance (Switch)](http://shinen.com/press/sheet.php?p=art_of_balance(Switch)), accessed 2026-09-24), and the live Nintendo.com store page ([nintendo.com/store/products/art-of-balance-switch](https://www.nintendo.com/store/products/art-of-balance-switch/), accessed 2026-09-24). Caution when citing Shin'en's *current* games page: it shows the Switch release as "4-Oct-2014" — a live-site typo for 2018 ([shinen.com games page](https://www.shinen.com/games/game.php3?art%20of%20balance), accessed 2026-09-24); every other official surface says 2018.

| Languages | Japanese, American English, British English, French, Canadian French, German, Spanish, Latin American Spanish (8) | **[DOCUMENTED]** (press sheet, accessed 2026-09-24) |

| Core rules | 3-second post-placement stability window with three green lights; any piece touching water fails the attempt; countdown "significantly shorter" than WiiWare's in post-Wii editions | **[DOCUMENTED]** (see §1 and §3 for the multiply-sourced rule set) |

Mode-by-mode, the Switch press sheet copy is the cleanest mode definition in the franchise record and is adopted verbatim as the semantic contract for our `GameModeDefinition` assets (§5):

| Mode | Official Switch copy (verbatim) | Structural reading for our clone |
|---|---|---|
| Arcade | "Watch out: Don't let any shape fall into the water!" † | Campaign queue-runner — rotate/place all shapes; co-op drop-in (the 1–4 single-system figure covers this) |
| Endurance | "Play a never ending string of puzzles to go for the best scores" | Random level string, 3 lives per session, score = speed + lives kept + difficulty (§3) |
| Infinity | "The blocks don't stop. Build the highest possible stack." | Endless feed, height score — no puzzle completion state |
| Swift Stacker | "Who can solve the puzzles faster?" — playable "at home, online or on the go" | Split-screen team race on an identical puzzle; the "on the go" phrasing is the Switch-specific local-wireless framing |
| Tower Tumble | "Who will topple the tower first? A multiplayer competition mode for up to 4 players" | Turn-based reverse-Jenga; random pieces; toppler loses, others score (§11) |

† Arcade-cell provenance — the one row not anchored to the Switch press sheet: track-t01-franchise.md registers this exact wording from the official Wii U About page (Quotations, T01 src 6 — [archived Wii U About, 2016-09-03 capture](https://web.archive.org/web/20160903223835/http://art-of-balance.shinen.com:80/wiiu/about.php), accessed 2026-09-24), with the same string corroborated by the Switch and PS4 press sheets (T01 src 9/10, claims section). "Rotate and place all shapes" in the structural column is our paraphrase of T01's own mode summary, not official copy.

Reception context for the Switch SKU specifically is a research gap: no Nintendo Life Switch review was reachable (likely URLs 404), so mode verification for this SKU rests on the Shin'en press sheets — acceptable because they are primary (§1, open threads). Metacritic 82 figures on Wikipedia cover the Wii U and 3DS editions, not Switch ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_of_Balance), accessed 2026-09-24).

### 13.3 Patch 1.1 (2018-11-13): motion controls as an input-layering case study

**Documented record.** The Switch SKU shipped 2018-10-04 *without* motion controls; the official microsite news item "13-Nov-2018 Patch 1.1 adds Motion Controls!" announces their addition 40 days (~six weeks) after launch, and the live Nintendo.com store page still carries the "Motion controls" feature tag (**[DOCUMENTED]**, sources in §13.1). Detailed patch notes text beyond that headline were not locatable in any fetched source — treat the patch's internal scope (which modes, which grip styles, sensitivity options) as unknown:

<!-- TODO-VERIFY: Patch 1.1 detailed notes (scope: modes covered, Joy-Con grip vs dual-hand styles, sensitivity settings, whether the eShop news channel archive or Nintendo support pages preserve the text). No public copy found during research; retry via Nintendo Help article archives and the eShop news-history community captures. -->

**What the patch proves about the original's architecture.** A post-launch control scheme added without breaking three existing schemes (touch, Joy-Con buttons/sticks, Pro Controller) implies the original routes all control input through an indirection layer where *device readings* are translated into *game intents* (move cursor, rotate ±45°, pick up, drop) rather than each mode polling hardware directly. The franchise record reinforces this: the Wii original was pointer-first (Wii Remote IR: A pick-up/drop, B or D-pad L/R rotate — §1), the Wii U edition stacked three schemes (§11), and the Switch edition re-added a motion/pointer scheme after players spent 40 days (~six weeks) without one in TV/Tabletop modes. The reasonable inference — flagged as reasoning, not documentation — is that launch-version TV-mode players were served by stick-driven cursor movement, and Patch 1.1 restored the franchise's native pointing idiom.

**Lesson institutionalized in §7.** Our `IPieceInputProvider` abstraction (MoveDelta, RotateCW/RotateCCW, RotateTo, Drop/Release, Pause, UI passthrough) exists precisely so that "Patch 1.1" is, for us, a *provider + config addition* rather than a refactor:

| Patch 1.1 concern | Our equivalent (see §7) |
|---|---|
| New device reading (Joy-Con attitude) | `MotionPointerInputProvider` consuming an orientation source |
| Cursor from device tilt | Gyro attitude → screen-space cursor with recenter action; `<AttitudeSensor>/attitude` quaternion on mobile (sensors exist on Android/iOS/Web only, not desktop — §7/T09) |
| Coexistence with existing schemes | Provider registry + active-provider switching + hot-swap, already built for mouse/gamepad/touch parity |
| Glyph/prompt updates | Per-scheme button glyph system (Switch/Pro prompts already a glyph set in the §7 table) |
| Rebinding | `PerformInteractiveRebinding()` pipeline with `SaveBindingOverridesAsJson` persistence (§7) |

Development-time stand-in hardware note: Unity's public Input System exposes `SwitchProControllerHID` on desktop over **Bluetooth only** (wired USB does not work — proprietary HID protocol), and Joy-Cons are unsupported on Windows/macOS (**[DOCUMENTED]**, [Input System docs source repo](https://github.com/Unity-Technologies/InputSystem/tree/develop/Packages/com.unity.inputsystem/Documentation~), accessed 2026-09-24). On-console Joy-Con gyro itself routes through Nintendo's console-specific input package, which is SDK-gated (§13.6). Our provider therefore reads a normalized `Quaternion Attitude` from an injected source so the desktop stand-in (Pro Controller over Bluetooth, no gyro) and the console path (SDK gyro) differ only in binding, not in code — the same discipline §7 applies to every device.

### 13.4 HD Rumble: documented absence, and our haptic design

The historical record is a *negative*: **no fetched source documents HD rumble for the original** — it is absent from the press sheet's controller/features list and from every review captured (medium-confidence negative, §1 open threads). We therefore treat rumble as absent in the original and design our own haptics as **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**, applying it uniformly across all rumble-capable targets rather than as a Switch homage.

Rumble plumbing facts that shape the design (**[DOCUMENTED]**, [Input System docs source repo](https://github.com/Unity-Technologies/InputSystem/tree/develop/Packages/com.unity.inputsystem/Documentation~), accessed 2026-09-24): `Gamepad.SetMotorSpeeds(lowFrequency, highFrequency)` drives the left (low-frequency) and right (high-frequency) motors with 0..1 floats; global `InputSystem.PauseHaptics()/ResumeHaptics()/ResetHaptics()` gate output; the 1.20.x support matrix lists Switch controllers rumbling **only on their own console via console-specific input packages** — desktop `SwitchProControllerHID` is not in the desktop rumble list, PS4 pads rumble on Mac/Windows/UWP, Xbox pads on Windows, Android requires Unity 6000.6+, iOS 6000.7+.

**[ORIGINAL DESIGN]** Haptic event map — **the plan's single canonical map**: §7.4.5 and §18.14 defer to this table and do not restate envelope values. Each row fires from an existing system event; envelopes are intensity × duration pairs for `SetMotorSpeeds`, tuned so the low motor carries weight and the high motor carries texture. Water-contact fail and stack collapse are deliberately two separate events, matching §4's distinct `Ev_WaterContact` and `Ev_StackCollapsed` channels — not one combined splash/fail pulse:

| Game event (source system) | Low freq | High freq | Duration | Intent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Piece picked up (LevelManager) | 0.05 | 0.15 | 40 ms | Feather-light tick |
| Piece released (LevelManager) | 0.10 | 0.25 | 50 ms | Commitment cue |
| Piece settled (StabilityMonitor) | 0.15 | 0.30 | 60 ms | Wooden "clunk" analog (pairs with the placement SFX, §9) |
| Stability light 1/2/3 lit (StabilityMonitor) | 0.10 | 0.55 | 50 ms | Rising pitch feel per light |
| Level failed — water contact (StabilityMonitor) | 0.40 | 0.20 | 150 ms | Dull splash thud |
| Breakable shattered (IBlockBehaviour driver, §8) | 0.70 | 0.40 | 120 ms | Sharp crack |
| Stack collapsed (StabilityMonitor) | 0.90 | 0.90 | 250 ms | Full collapse rumble |
| Tower Tumble turn hand-off (GameStateMachine turn token, §7.7) | 0.20 | 0.40 | 90 ms | Turn-change cue in hotseat play |
| UI confirm (InputRouter) | 0.05 | 0.35 | 30 ms | Subtle nav tick |

```csharp
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.InputSystem;

/// <summary>
/// Event-driven haptics director. The original Switch edition has no documented
/// HD Rumble feature; every envelope here is [ORIGINAL DESIGN]. Events arrive from
/// LevelManager, StabilityMonitor and the block-behaviour driver (see §6, §8).
/// </summary>
public sealed class HapticsDirector : MonoBehaviour
{
    #region Nested Types

    /// <summary>Immutable motor envelope: two motor speeds held for a duration.</summary>
    private readonly struct HapticEnvelope
    {
        public HapticEnvelope(float lowFrequency, float highFrequency, float durationSeconds)
        {
            LowFrequency = lowFrequency;
            HighFrequency = highFrequency;
            DurationSeconds = durationSeconds;
        }

        public float LowFrequency { get; }
        public float HighFrequency { get; }
        public float DurationSeconds { get; }
    }

    #endregion

    #region Constants

    private const float StopTimeEpsilon = 0.001f;

    private static readonly HapticEnvelope PiecePickedUp = new HapticEnvelope(0.05f, 0.15f, 0.04f);
    private static readonly HapticEnvelope PieceSettled = new HapticEnvelope(0.15f, 0.30f, 0.06f);
    private static readonly HapticEnvelope StabilityLightLit = new HapticEnvelope(0.10f, 0.55f, 0.05f);
    private static readonly HapticEnvelope BlockShattered = new HapticEnvelope(0.70f, 0.40f, 0.12f);
    private static readonly HapticEnvelope StackCollapsed = new HapticEnvelope(0.90f, 0.90f, 0.25f);

    #endregion

    #region Serialized Fields

    [Header("Configuration")]
    [SerializeField] private bool enableHaptics = true;
    [SerializeField] [Range(0f, 1f)] private float masterIntensity = 1f;

    #endregion

    #region Private Fields

    private Gamepad _activeGamepad;
    private float _motorStopTime;

    #endregion

    #region Unity Lifecycle

    private void Awake()
    {
        CacheActiveGamepad();
    }

    private void Update()
    {
        // Time-based motor stop: avoids per-event coroutine allocation.
        if (_activeGamepad == null || Time.unscaledTime + StopTimeEpsilon < _motorStopTime)
        {
            return;
        }

        _activeGamepad.SetMotorSpeeds(0f, 0f);
        _motorStopTime = 0f;
    }

    private void OnEnable()
    {
        InputSystem.onDeviceChange += HandleDeviceChange;
    }

    private void OnDisable()
    {
        InputSystem.onDeviceChange -= HandleDeviceChange;
        StopAllHaptics();
    }

    #endregion

    #region Public Methods

    /// <summary>Plays a named game-event envelope. Safe to call from any system event.</summary>
    public void PlayPiecePickedUp() => Play(PiecePickedUp);

    /// <summary>Placement feedback paired with the settle SFX (see §9).</summary>
    public void PlayPieceSettled() => Play(PieceSettled);

    /// <summary>One of the three stability lights lit (see §6 StabilityMonitor).</summary>
    public void PlayStabilityLightLit() => Play(StabilityLightLit);

    /// <summary>Breakable-block shatter (see §8).</summary>
    public void PlayBlockShattered() => Play(BlockShattered);

    /// <summary>Full stack collapse / level failure.</summary>
    public void PlayStackCollapsed() => Play(StackCollapsed);

    /// <summary>Pauses all haptic output; call when GameStateMachine enters Paused.</summary>
    public void PauseAllHaptics() => InputSystem.PauseHaptics();

    /// <summary>Resumes haptic output after unpause.</summary>
    public void ResumeAllHaptics() => InputSystem.ResumeHaptics();

    /// <summary>Stops motors and clears the pending stop time.</summary>
    public void StopAllHaptics()
    {
        if (_activeGamepad != null)
        {
            _activeGamepad.SetMotorSpeeds(0f, 0f);
        }

        _motorStopTime = 0f;
    }

    #endregion

    #region Private Methods

    private void Play(in HapticEnvelope envelope)
    {
        if (!enableHaptics || _activeGamepad == null)
        {
            return;
        }

        _activeGamepad.SetMotorSpeeds(
            envelope.LowFrequency * masterIntensity,
            envelope.HighFrequency * masterIntensity);
        _motorStopTime = Time.unscaledTime + envelope.DurationSeconds;
    }

    private void CacheActiveGamepad()
    {
        _activeGamepad = Gamepad.current;
        if (_activeGamepad == null)
        {
            Debug.LogWarning($"{nameof(HapticsDirector)}: no gamepad present; haptics dormant.", this);
        }
    }

    private void HandleDeviceChange(InputDevice device, InputDeviceChange change)
    {
        if (change is InputDeviceChange.Added or InputDeviceChange.Removed or InputDeviceChange.Reconnected)
        {
            CacheActiveGamepad();
        }
    }

    #endregion
}
```

<!-- TODO-VERIFY: on-console rumble routing. The public Input System's rumble matrix covers Switch controllers only via Nintendo's console-specific input package (SDK-gated). Confirm the exact SetMotorSpeeds pass-through behavior — including whether single Joy-Cons map to one motor each — inside the Switch platform module before finalizing the dual-Joy-Con envelope split. -->

Platform note for the paused state: `PauseHaptics` on menu entry matches the cert-friendly expectation that rumble stops when gameplay does not own the input focus; the Android auto-stop-after-~10 s behavior documented in §7/T09 is the same class of platform rule to respect on console.

### 13.5 Docked and handheld: resolution, frame pacing, quality tiers

**Documented base.** The press sheet lists TV / Tabletop / Handheld play modes and the touch screen among controllers (**[DOCUMENTED]**, §13.2 sources). Touch input is therefore available only in handheld (and tabletop-with-console-in-hand) contexts — a runtime input-surface fact our provider registry already models through device presence rather than platform defines (§7).

**Resolution targets.** The specific 1080p-docked / 720p-handheld envelope is **community convention, not a citable primary**: Nintendo Switch player settings and performance budgets are NDA-gated by design — Unity's public Player settings reference states "You can find details of closed platform Player settings in their respective documentation" (**[DOCUMENTED]**, [Unity 6.0 Manual — Player settings reference](https://docs.unity3d.com/6000.0/Documentation/Manual/class-PlayerSettings.html), accessed 2026-09-24), meaning the Nintendo developer portal. We adopt the convention as a working budget and flag it:

<!-- TODO-VERIFY: Switch docked/handheld resolution and performance targets (conventional 1080p docked / 720p handheld, 60 fps). No public primary can exist for a closed platform; validate against NDA documentation if a Switch target is ever greenlit, and treat all numbers in this subsection as conventions. -->

**Quality-tier design.** Unity's Quality settings assign one URP asset per quality level in a levels × platforms matrix with a single green default per platform, and each level carries its own Render Pipeline asset (**[DOCUMENTED]**, [Unity 6.0 Manual — Quality settings reference](https://docs.unity3d.com/6000.0/Documentation/Manual/class-QualitySettings.html), accessed 2026-09-24). That is exactly the mechanism a dock-transition needs: two named levels, `Switch_Docked` and `Switch_Handheld`, differing only in their URP asset, selected at runtime on dock-state change. The tier values below are **[ORIGINAL DESIGN]**, derived from the Switch-class recipe in §9/T10 (bandwidth-bound hardware, stylized low-poly content, forward path):

| URP asset setting | `Switch_Docked` | `Switch_Handheld` | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Render Scale | 1.0 | 0.85 + FSR 1.0 upscale | Handheld panel is smaller; FSR stays active at 1.0 and smooths 0.99↔1.0 transitions (**[DOCUMENTED]** behavior, [URP asset reference](https://docs.unity3d.com/6000.0/Documentation/Manual/urp/universalrp-asset.html), accessed 2026-09-24) |
| HDR | On | Off (LDR grading fallback) | Bloom is core to the lounge look; docked has bandwidth, handheld trades to LDR grading (tier recipe §9) |
| MSAA | 2x | 2x | Forward paths only; 4x buys little on stylized low-poly geometry |
| Depth Texture / Opaque Texture | On / On | On / On | Water depth fade + refraction on every tier (§9 recipe); Opaque Downsampling 2x Bilinear on handheld |
| Main light shadows | Pixel, atlas 1024, 1 cascade, max distance 25 | Per Vertex, atlas 512, 1 cascade, max distance 20 | Shadow cost is the biggest docked/handheld delta |
| Additional lights | Per Vertex, limit 4 | Per Vertex, limit 2 | Few lights in scenes; per-object limit honored under Forward |
| Post-processing | Bloom (low) + Neutral tonemap | Bloom (low) + LDR tonemap only | Minimal fill-rate overhead |
| SRP Batcher / Dynamic Batching | On / Off | On / Off | SRP Batcher precedence documented; dynamic batching obsolete with GPU instancing available |

Frame pacing follows the documented rule set: with `QualitySettings.vSyncCount != 0`, `Application.targetFrameRate` is ignored, and docs recommend vSync when smooth pacing is needed; on console-class fixed-refresh hardware we target 60 fps with the platform's presentation interval (**[DOCUMENTED]** semantics, [Application.targetFrameRate](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Application-targetFrameRate.html), accessed 2026-09-24; platform-specific application is console-gated). The frame-time budget split (16.67 ms across sim/render/UI/audio) and its profiling markers are owned by §14; the physics substepping cost that concerns Switch-class CPUs is risk-tracked in §21.

UI correctness in TV mode rides on the documented `Screen.safeArea` semantics — it already folds in TV overscan, bottom-left origin matching UGUI RectTransforms (**[DOCUMENTED]**, [Screen.safeArea](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Screen-safeArea.html), accessed 2026-09-24), plus the ~10% title-safe inset convention from §9.

```csharp
using System;
using UnityEngine;

/// <summary>
/// Watches dock-state transitions and swaps the active quality level (and with it
/// the per-level URP asset). [ORIGINAL DESIGN]: the tier split itself; on-platform
/// dock detection is bound through IDockStateProvider in the platform assembly.
/// </summary>
public sealed class QualityTierController : MonoBehaviour
{
    #region Nested Types

    /// <summary>Physical disposition of a hybrid console.</summary>
    public enum DockState
    {
        Unknown = 0,
        Docked = 1,
        Handheld = 2
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// Platform hook for dock events. The Switch implementation lives in the
    /// NDA-gated platform module; tests inject a fake provider.
    /// </summary>
    public interface IDockStateProvider
    {
        DockState Current { get; }

        event Action<DockState> DockStateChanged;
    }

    #endregion

    #region Serialized Fields

    [Header("Quality Level Indices (Project Settings > Quality)")]
    [SerializeField] private int dockedQualityLevelIndex = -1;
    [SerializeField] private int handheldQualityLevelIndex = -1;

    #endregion

    #region Private Fields

    private IDockStateProvider _dockStateProvider;
    private DockState _appliedState = DockState.Unknown;

    #endregion

    #region Unity Lifecycle

    private void Start()
    {
        if (_dockStateProvider == null)
        {
            Debug.LogWarning($"{nameof(QualityTierController)}: no {nameof(IDockStateProvider)} bound; tiers static.", this);
            return;
        }

        ApplyTier(_dockStateProvider.Current);
    }

    private void OnEnable()
    {
        if (_dockStateProvider != null)
        {
            _dockStateProvider.DockStateChanged += HandleDockStateChanged;
        }
    }

    private void OnDisable()
    {
        if (_dockStateProvider != null)
        {
            _dockStateProvider.DockStateChanged -= HandleDockStateChanged;
        }
    }

    #endregion

    #region Public Methods

    /// <summary>Injects the platform dock-state provider (called by the platform bootstrap, see §4).</summary>
    /// <param name="provider">Platform implementation or test fake.</param>
    public void Bind(IDockStateProvider provider)
    {
        _dockStateProvider = provider ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(provider));
    }

    /// <summary>Applies the quality level matching a dock state. Idempotent.</summary>
    /// <param name="state">Dock state to apply.</param>
    public void ApplyTier(DockState state)
    {
        int levelIndex = ResolveLevelIndex(state);
        if (levelIndex < 0 || _appliedState == state)
        {
            return;
        }

        QualitySettings.SetQualityLevel(levelIndex, true);
        _appliedState = state;
    }

    #endregion

    #region Private Methods

    private void HandleDockStateChanged(DockState newState)
    {
        ApplyTier(newState);
    }

    private int ResolveLevelIndex(DockState state)
    {
        return state switch
        {
            DockState.Docked => dockedQualityLevelIndex,
            DockState.Handheld => handheldQualityLevelIndex,
            _ => -1
        };
    }

    #endregion
}
```
